name: Hasmonean Kingdom
description: The Hasmonean Kingdom entered a period of Roman clientage in 63 BC after the Roman general Pompey intervened in a dynastic civil war and besieged Jerusalem. Under reduced boundaries that detached several Hellenistic cities, the realm retained administrative authority over Judea, Galilee and Idumea under the leadership of High Priest Hyrcanus II and his advisor Antipater the Idumaean. This protectorate arrangement subordinated Jewish internal governance to the proconsuls of Syria until Parthian forces temporarily overran the region. \n\n Status: Client kingdom of the Roman Republic; Capital: Jerusalem; Common languages: Middle Aramaic, Classical Hebrew and Koine Greek; Religion: Second Temple Judaism; Government: Theocratic client monarchy; Historical era: Hellenistic and Roman antiquity; Established: 141 BC; Reorganised: 63 BC; Disestablished: 37 BC

name: Kingdom of Pontus
description: The Kingdom of Pontus endured as a diminished client realm along the northern coast of Anatolia following the defeat of Mithridates VI in the Mithridatic Wars in 63 BC. While western coastal districts were annexed directly into the Roman province of Bithynia and Pontus, the eastern Pontic lands remained entrusted to local client dynasts who governed from centres such as Amasya. These vassal rulers maintained domestic order and secured Black Sea trade routes on behalf of Rome until direct provincial administration was imposed under Emperor Nero. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Roman Republic and Roman Empire; Capital: Amasya; Common languages: Koine Greek, Persian and Anatolian; Religion: Greco-Iranian syncretism and Anatolian polytheism; Government: Client monarchy; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 281 BC; Disestablished: 62 AD

name: Northern Satraps
description: The Northern Satraps comprised an Indo-Scythian dynasty that established sovereign authority across the eastern Punjab and the Mathura region during the 1st century BC. Displacing earlier Indo-Greek monarchs and indigenous Datta and Mitra rulers, these Saka governors assumed the titles of Kshatrapa and Mahakshatrapa while overseeing thriving urban trade networks. Their realm served as an influential patron of Buddhist, Jain and early Hindu art traditions before becoming subordinated to the expanding Kushan Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Mathura; Common languages: Gandhari Prakrit, Sanskrit and Greek; Religion: Buddhism, Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Antiquity; Established: 60 BC; Disestablished: 2nd century AD

name: Silla
description: Silla was an ancient Korean kingdom established in the south-eastern sector of the Korean Peninsula, traditionally tracing its foundation to 57 BC under King Hyeokgeose. Originating as the chiefdom of Saro within the Jinhan confederacy, the state gradually consolidated control over neighbouring valleys and developed a rigid aristocratic bone-rank social system. Governed from its capital at Gyeongju, Silla developed into one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, ultimately forging alliances that enabled it to unify most of the peninsula centuries later. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Gyeongju; Common languages: Old Korean and Classical Chinese; Religion: Korean shamanism and Buddhism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Historical era: Three Kingdoms of Korea; Established: 57 BC; Disestablished: 935 AD

name: Roman Republic
description: The Roman Republic during the civil war of 50 to 46 BC designates the central government and provincial territories brought under the direct military control of Julius Caesar. After crossing the Rubicon in early 49 BC and prompting his senatorial rivals under Pompey to evacuate Italy, Caesar secured the treasury at Rome, defeated opposing legions in Hispania and pursued his adversaries into Greece and North Africa. Operating under emergency consular and dictatorial authority, this administration laid the structural groundwork for the transformation of republican governance into autocracy. \n\n Status: Republic under dictatorial emergency rule; Capital: Rome; Official languages: Latin; Religion: Roman polytheism; Government: Dictatorship and consular republic; Historical era: Late Roman Republic; Established: 509 BC; Disestablished: 27 BC

name: Roman Republic
description: The Roman Republic under the Liberatores comprised the eastern senatorial faction mobilised in 43 BC by Marcus Junius Brutus and Gaius Cassius Longinus following the assassination of Julius Caesar. Deprived of a conventional municipal capital after fleeing Rome, the republican conspirators established control across Greece, Macedonia, Asia Minor and Syria, levying heavy taxation and requisitioning provincial legions for the coming conflict. This mobile wartime authority maintained the pretence of defending constitutional liberties until its decisive defeat by Mark Antony and Octavian at the Battle of Philippi. \n\n Status: Sovereign civil war faction; Administrative seat: Mobile military command; Official languages: Latin; Common languages: Latin and Koine Greek; Religion: Roman polytheism; Government: Republican military confederacy; Historical era: Late Roman Republic; Established: 43 BC; Disestablished: 42 BC

name: Hasmonean Kingdom
description: The Hasmonean Kingdom experienced a brief anti-Roman restoration between 40 and 37 BC when Antigonus II Mattathias seized power in Jerusalem with the military assistance of the invading Parthian Empire. Backed by Parthian cavalry under Pacorus, Antigonus deposed his uncle Hyrcanus II, forced Herod to flee abroad and claimed the dual offices of high priest and king. This Parthian protectorate resisted Roman counter-offensives for three years until Roman and Herodian legions besieged Jerusalem, capturing Antigonus and permanently ending Hasmonean dynastic rule. \n\n Status: Protectorate of the Parthian Empire; Capital: Jerusalem; Common languages: Middle Aramaic, Classical Hebrew and Koine Greek; Religion: Second Temple Judaism; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Historical era: Hellenistic and Roman antiquity; Established: 40 BC; Disestablished: 37 BC

name: Kingdom of Galatia
label: celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Galatia was a Celtic realm in central Anatolia that operated as a Roman client state under King Amyntas during the final decades of the 1st century BC. Centred around regional strongholds such as Ancyra, modern Ankara, the kingdom consolidated authority over several tribal Gaulish confederacies while expanding into neighbouring districts of Lycaonia and Pisidia with Roman approval. The protectorate supplied auxiliary troops and guarded strategic transit corridors for Rome until Amyntas died in battle in 25 BC, prompting the immediate annexation of his realm as a Roman imperial province. \n\n Status: Protectorate of the Roman Republic and Roman Empire; Capital: Ankara; Common languages: Galatian, Koine Greek and Latin; Religion: Celtic polytheism and Anatolian syncretism; Government: Client monarchy; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 40 BC; Disestablished: 25 BC

name: Goguryeo Kingdom
description: The Goguryeo Kingdom was a powerful Korean realm established in 37 BC by King Dongmyeong along the valleys of the Yalu and Tongtian rivers. Initially governed from Jolbon and later from fortified capitals at Gungnae and Pyongyang, the state developed formidable cavalry forces that subjugated neighbouring Buyeo clans and repelled repeated Chinese military expeditions. Goguryeo grew into the pre-eminent military power across northern Korea and Manchuria, patronising Mahayana Buddhism and dominating trade routes throughout East Asia until a combined Silla and Tang offensive overcame the state in 668. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Jolbon, later Ji-an and Pyongyang; Common languages: Goguryeo and Classical Chinese; Religion: Korean shamanism, Buddhism, Confucianism and Daoism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Three Kingdoms of Korea; Established: 37 BC; Disestablished: 668 AD

name: Herodian Kingdom of Judea
description: The Herodian Kingdom of Judea was an expansive Roman client monarchy established in 37 BC when Herod the Great captured Jerusalem with Roman military backing. Ruling under the titular designation of King of the Jews, Herod consolidated internal authority through extensive patronage, ruthless dynastic purges and monumental urban architecture, including the reconstruction of the Second Temple and the foundation of the port at Caesarea Maritima. The realm served as a loyal Roman protectorate safeguarding the eastern Mediterranean frontier until Herod's death in 4 BC precipitated its partition among his heirs. \n\n Status: Client kingdom of the Roman Empire; Capital: Jerusalem; Common languages: Koine Greek, Middle Aramaic, Hebrew and Latin; Religion: Second Temple Judaism, Samaritanism and Hellenistic polytheism; Government: Autocratic client monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Herodian dynasty; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 37 BC; Disestablished: 4 BC

name: Kingdom of Cappadocia
description: The Kingdom of Cappadocia functioned as a strategic Anatolian client state governed by King Archelaus, whom Mark Antony elevated to the throne in 36 BC. Centred upon the fortified royal capital of Mazaca, later renamed Caesarea, the kingdom navigated the rivalries of late republican Rome while serving as a defensive buffer against Parthian advances. Archelaus promoted Hellenistic municipal civic culture and preserved internal autonomy until Emperor Tiberius summoned him to Rome, incorporating the territory directly as an imperial province upon the monarch's death in 18 AD. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Roman Republic and Roman Empire; Capital: Kayseri; Common languages: Koine Greek, Cappadocian, Old Persian and Aramaic; Religion: Greco-Iranian syncretism and Anatolian polytheism; Government: Client monarchy; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 36 BC; Disestablished: 18 AD

name: Roman Empire
description: The Roman Empire was the pre-eminent power of classical antiquity, established in 27 BC when Octavian received the title of Augustus and consolidated imperial administrative authority over the former territories of the Roman Republic. Governing a vast domain that encompassed the Mediterranean basin, western Europe and portions of the Near East, the state combined centralised military command with provincial autonomy and Roman civil law. The empire maintained internal peace known as the Pax Romana, promoted extensive urban networks and underwent profound transformations until administrative partitions permanently divided the realm in 395. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Rome, later Milan; Official languages: Latin; Common languages: Latin and Koine Greek; Religion: Roman polytheism, imperial cult and Nicene Christianity; Government: Autocratic principate and dominate; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 27 BC; Disestablished: 17 January 395

name: Kingdom of Mauretania
description: The Kingdom of Mauretania was a North African client state established in 25 BC when Augustus appointed King Juba II to govern the Berber coastal lands of modern Morocco and western Algeria. From his seaside capital at Caesarea, modern Cherchell, Juba and his successor Ptolemy transformed the realm into a flourishing centre of Greco-Roman culture, Punic scholarship and Mediterranean commerce, exporting purple dyes, grain and timber. The kingdom remained an essential regional partner of Rome until Emperor Caligula executed Ptolemy in 40 AD, triggering a provincial rebellion and direct Roman annexation. \n\n Status: Client kingdom of the Roman Empire; Capital: Cherchell; Common languages: Berber, Punic, Latin and Koine Greek; Religion: Berber religion, Punic polytheism and Roman imperial cult; Government: Client monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Numidian-Mauretanian dynasty; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 25 BC; Disestablished: 44 AD

name: Odrysian Kingdom
description: The Odrysian Kingdom operated as a Thracian client protectorate under the Sapaean dynasty during the early decades of the Roman Empire. Based at Bizye in eastern Thrace, its monarchs governed the fragmented tribal populations across the eastern Balkans while fielding auxiliary units and safeguarding Roman lines of communication toward the Danube. Plagued by frequent aristocratic rebellions and dynastic assassinations, the realm lost its political viability until Emperor Claudius intervened directly in 46 AD, disestablishing the native monarchy and converting the territory into the Roman province of Thracia. \n\n Status: Protectorate of the Roman Empire; Capital: Bizye; Common languages: Thracian and Koine Greek; Religion: Thracian polytheism; Government: Client monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sapaean dynasty; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 20 BC; Disestablished: 46 AD

name: Baekje
description: Baekje was an influential Korean kingdom founded in 18 BC by King Onjo in the south-western sector of the Korean Peninsula. Initially ruling from Wiryeseong near modern Seoul, the court later relocated its administrative seat southwards to Ungjin and finally to Sabi, modern Buyeo, following pressure from northern rivals. Baekje developed sophisticated maritime commerce, cultivated diplomatic alliances with southern Chinese dynasties and the Yamato court of Japan, and served as a vital conduit for the transmission of Buddhism until falling to a combined Tang and Silla campaign in 660. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Buyeo; Common languages: Baekje and Classical Chinese; Religion: Korean shamanism, Buddhism, Confucianism and Daoism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Three Kingdoms of Korea; Established: 18 BC; Disestablished: 18 July 660

name: Apracharajas
description: The Apracharajas constituted an autonomous Indo-Scythian dynasty that exercised regional dominion across Gandhara and the surrounding highlands of modern north-western Pakistan during the 1st century. Stating their authority on silver coinage and Kharosthi inscriptions, its rulers governed from administrative strongholds such as Bajaur and fostered matrimonial ties with neighbouring border princely houses. The dynasty distinguished itself through deep patronage of Gandharan Buddhism, dedicating monumental stupas and commissioning reliquaries in monastic settlements until its territories were absorbed into the rising Kushan Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Apamea Ragiana; Common languages: Gandhari Prakrit; Religion: Gandharan Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Antiquity; Established: 15 BC; Disestablished: 51 AD; Currency: Tetradrachm

name: Bosporan Kingdom
description: The Bosporan Kingdom functioned as an enduring Greco-Scythian client state along the shores of the Cimmerian Bosporus, encompassing the Crimean peninsula and the Taman peninsula. Entering formal clientage under King Aspurgus during the reign of Augustus, the kingdom supplied Rome with vital shipments of grain, dried fish and leather while maintaining naval squadrons against Pontic piracy. Although briefly suspended under Emperor Nero, the client dynasty maintained local administrative autonomy and Hellenistic royal traditions until nomadic invasions by Greuthungi and Huns overran the region in the late 4th century. \n\n Status: Client kingdom of the Roman Empire; Capital: None recorded; Historical region: Black Sea and Crimea; Common languages: Koine Greek and Scythian; Religion: Hellenistic polytheism and Sarmatian religious cults; Government: Client monarchy; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 8 BC; Disestablished: 371 AD

name: Ethnarchy of Judea
label: herodian tetrarchy
description: The Ethnarchy of Judea was an autonomous territorial division created in 4 BC following the death of Herod the Great, when the Roman emperor Augustus confirmed Herod Archelaus as ruler over Judea, Samaria and Idumea. Governed from Jerusalem, the ethnarchy struggled with widespread domestic unrest, bitter religious opposition from Pharisaic leadership and administrative harshness from the ethnarch. Following formal delegations of Jewish and Samaritan elders who appealed against his oppressive governance, Augustus deposed Archelaus in 6 AD, exiling him to Gaul and converting the territory directly into the Roman province of Judaea. \n\n Status: Protectorate of the Roman Empire; Capital: Jerusalem; Common languages: Middle Aramaic, Hebrew, Koine Greek and Latin; Religion: Second Temple Judaism and Samaritanism; Government: Client ethnarchy; Ruling dynasty: Herodian dynasty; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 4 BC; Disestablished: 6 AD

name: Tetrarchy of Galilee and Perea
label: herodian tetrarchy
description: The Tetrarchy of Galilee and Perea was a Roman client domain established in 4 BC under the rule of Herod Antipas following the partition of his father Herod the Great's kingdom. Comprising two non-contiguous territories along the Jordan rift, the regime focused heavily on urban reconstruction, transforming Sepphoris into an administrative centre before founding the new lakeside capital of Tiberias in honour of Emperor Tiberius. Antipas maintained stable internal authority for four decades until imperial suspicion and accusations of treason led Emperor Caligula to depose and exile him to Gaul in 39 AD. \n\n Status: Protectorate of the Roman Empire; Capital: None recorded; Common languages: Middle Aramaic and Koine Greek; Religion: Second Temple Judaism; Government: Client tetrarchy; Ruling dynasty: Herodian dynasty; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 4 BC; Disestablished: 39 AD

name: Tetrarchy of Philip
label: herodian tetrarchy
description: The Tetrarchy of Philip was a northeastern Levantine principality created in 4 BC through the division of Herod the Great's realm, allocated to his son Philip. Ruling a diverse population across Batanaea, Trachonitis, Auranitis and Gaulanitis, Philip established his capital at Caesarea Philippi near the springs of the Jordan and gained a reputation as a calm and equitable administrator. His reign witnessed peaceful civic development and moderate taxation until his death in 34 AD, after which his territories were temporarily placed under the proconsul of Syria. \n\n Status: Client principality of the Roman Empire; Capital: Caesarea Philippi; Common languages: Koine Greek, Middle Aramaic and Old Arabic; Religion: Hellenistic polytheism and Second Temple Judaism; Government: Tetrarchy; Ruling dynasty: Herodian dynasty; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 4 BC; Disestablished: 34 AD

name: Toparchy of Jamnia
label: herodian tetrarchy
description: The Toparchy of Jamnia was a coastal Levantine enclave established in 4 BC for Salome I, the sister of Herod the Great, following Augustus's imperial ratification of Herod's will. Governed from the coastal city of Jamnia, the toparchy encompassed surrounding agricultural fertile lands and inland estates at Phasaelis in the Jordan Valley. Salome managed her autonomous patrimony with fiscal autonomy and close adherence to Roman interests until her death, whereupon her properties and revenues were bequeathed directly to Empress Livia and incorporated into imperial provincial estates. \n\n Status: Protectorate of the Roman Empire; Capital: Jamnia; Common languages: Middle Aramaic, Koine Greek and Hebrew; Religion: Second Temple Judaism; Government: Client toparchy; Ruling dynasty: Herodian dynasty; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 4 BC; Disestablished: 10 AD

name: Early Nazca Culture
description: The Early Nazca Culture developed as an advanced pre-Columbian civilisation along the arid river valleys of the southern Peruvian coast, particularly within the Rio Grande de Nazca drainage. Emerging from earlier Paracas cultural traditions, this society constructed the monumental ceremonial complex of Cahuachi, which served as a focal pilgrimage centre for religious assemblies and communal rituals. The Nazca excelled in crafting vibrant polychrome ceramics, complex woven textiles and engineered subterranean puquio aqueducts that supported agricultural communities in a hyper-arid desert landscape. \n\n Status: Sovereign archaeological culture; Capital: Cahuachi; Common languages: Unrecorded indigenous languages; Religion: Pre-Columbian Andean polytheism; Government: Theocratic ceremonial polity; Historical era: Early Intermediate Period; Established: 2 AD; Disestablished: 450 AD

name: Igneri
description: The Igneri constituted an Arawakan-speaking indigenous society that settled across the southern Lesser Antilles, establishing maritime villages from Trinidad northwards towards the Leeward Islands. Identified archaeologically with the Saladoid ceramic horizon, these island communities cultivated cassava, fished coastal reefs and navigated open Caribbean waters in large wooden canoes. Over several centuries, the Igneri sustained autonomous lineage-based settlements governed by local headmen before their material culture and dialect merged into subsequent Island Carib populations prior to the arrival of Christopher Columbus in 1493. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal society; Capital: Fort-de-France; Common languages: Igneri Arawakan; Religion: Traditional Taíno and Antillean animism; Government: Tribal chieftaincy; Historical era: Pre-Columbian era; Established: 2 AD; Disestablished: 14 November 1493

name: Western Satraps
description: The Western Satraps were an enduring Indo-Scythian dynasty that exercised sovereign dominion over western and central India, including Saurashtra, Gujarat and Malwa. Ruling from commercial centres such as Ujjain and Bharuch, the Saka monarchs, titled Kshatrapas and Mahakshatrapas, minted sophisticated dated silver coinage and patronised both Brahmanical and Buddhist establishments. The realm engaged in sustained territorial rivalries with the southern Satavahana Empire before reviving under the Kardamaka dynasty and eventually falling to the military conquests of Chandragupta II of the Gupta Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ujjain; Common languages: Sanskrit, Pali and Maharashtri Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Mahakshatrapa; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 2 AD; Disestablished: 415 AD

name: Xin
description: The Xin dynasty was a short-lived imperial realm founded in China on 10 January 9 AD when the prominent Confucian scholar and regent Wang Mang usurped the Han throne. Governing from Chang'an, modern Xi'an, Wang introduced sweeping egalitarian economic reforms that nationalised agricultural land, abolished private slavery, overhauled the coinage system and revitalised classical Zhou rituals. However, disastrous flooding of the Yellow River coupled with aristocratic resistance and widespread agrarian insurgencies, notably the Red Eyebrows, collapsed imperial authority and led to Wang's violent overthrow in October 23 AD. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Xi'an; Common languages: Old Chinese and Middle Chinese; Religion: Confucianism, Chinese folk religion and Taoism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Wang; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Imperial China; Established: 10 January 9; Disestablished: 5 October 23

name: Suren Kingdom
description: The Suren Kingdom, frequently designated in modern historiography as the Indo-Parthian Kingdom, was founded around 20 AD when Gondophares I, a nobleman of the Parthian House of Suren, asserted independence in Sakastan and expanded eastward. Controlling a vast expanse across eastern Iran, Arachosia, modern Pakistan and the Punjab, the monarch ruled from Taxila and adopted syncretic Persian and Hellenistic royal traditions. The kingdom prospered through Silk Road commerce and sponsored Gandharan Buddhist monuments such as Takht-i-Bahi before Kushan incursions and Sasanian conquests dismantled its authority. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Taxila; Common languages: Parthian, Gandhari Prakrit, Greek and Sanskrit; Religion: Zoroastrianism, Buddhism and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Suren; Historical era: Antiquity; Established: 20 AD; Disestablished: 228 AD

name: Tribal Kingdom of the Iazyges
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Tribal Kingdom of the Iazyges was a nomadic Sarmatian confederacy that established permanent encampments between the Danube and Tisza rivers on the Hungarian plain during the 1st century AD. Maintaining a decentralised tribal order headed by hereditary chieftains and mobile cavalry war-bands, the Iazyges functioned alternately as Roman frontier buffers, trading partners and dangerous raiders across the Pannonian limes. Although severely weakened during the Marcomannic Wars by Marcus Aurelius, the tribe preserved its autonomous pastoral life in the Tisza basin until Gothic and Hunnic migrations overwhelmed them. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal confederacy; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Sarmatian Iranian; Religion: Sarmatian polytheism and animism; Government: Tribal kingship; Ruler title: Tribal Chieftain; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 21 AD; Disestablished: 436 AD

name: Kushan Empire
description: The Kushan Empire was a syncretic imperial state established in the early 1st century AD when Kujula Kadphises unified the five principalities of the Yuezhi confederation in Bactria. Expanding rapidly across the Hindu Kush, the empire absorbed Gandhara, Punjab and the northern Gangetic plains, establishing primary administrative centres at Purushapura and Mathura. Reaching its zenith under Emperor Kanishka the Great, the realm fostered international Silk Road trade, patronised the dissemination of Mahayana Buddhism and Hellenistic Gandharan sculpture, and minted magnificent gold coinage before fragmenting under Sasanian and Gupta pressure. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: None recorded; Common languages: Bactrian, Gandhari Prakrit, Greek and Sanskrit; Religion: Buddhism, Hinduism and Zoroastrianism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kushan dynasty; Ruler title: King of Kings; Historical era: Antiquity; Established: 31 AD; Disestablished: 376 AD

name: Kingdom of Manipur
description: The Kingdom of Manipur was an ancient sovereign principality located in the fertile Imphal Valley of north-eastern India along the frontier with Upper Burma. Traditionally dated to the accession of King Nongda Lairen Pakhangba in 36 AD, the Meitei monarchy developed a distinct civil administration centred upon the royal stronghold of Kangla. The state maintained political autonomy through disciplined martial traditions, developed intricate agrarian wet-rice cultivation and resisted territorial encroachments from neighbouring Burmese and Shan principalities over many centuries before facing British colonial integration in the late 19th century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: None recorded; Common languages: Meitei; Religion: Sanamahism, animism and later Vaishnavite Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ningthouja dynasty; Ruler title: Meidingu; Historical era: Antiquity to modern era; Established: 36 AD; Disestablished: 27 April 1891

name: Lạc Việt
description: The Lac Viet state of 41 to 44 AD emerged from a widespread patriotic insurrection led by the Trung sisters, Trung Trac and Trung Nhi, against the oppressive administration of the Chinese Han dynasty in northern Vietnam. Drawing enthusiastic support from indigenous Lac lords and agricultural communities across the Red River Delta, Trung Trac was acclaimed queen regnant and liberated more than sixty walled settlements from imperial command. The restored native realm maintained independent governance until General Ma Yuan launched a massive counter-offensive that defeated the uprising in 43 AD. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Hanoi; Common languages: Lac Viet and Old Austroasiatic; Religion: Indigenous animism; Government: Monarchy; Head of state: Queen Trung Trac; Historical era: Antiquity; Established: 40 AD; Disestablished: 43 AD

name: Western Satraps
description: The Western Satraps during this phase exercised sovereign authority over the affluent trade provinces of Malwa, Gujarat and the Konkan coast from their administrative seat at Ujjain. Under prominent monarchs of the Kardamaka dynasty such as Chashtana and Rudradaman I, the realm repulsed territorial thrusts from the neighbouring Satavahana Empire and expanded control into Rajasthan and the lower Indus valley. The state enriched itself through bustling maritime commerce with the Roman Empire at the port of Barygaza, while royal inscriptions famously recorded the renovation of the Sudarshana lake reservoir. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ujjain; Common languages: Sanskrit, Maharashtri Prakrit and Gandhari; Religion: Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kardamaka dynasty; Ruler title: Mahakshatrapa; Historical era: Antiquity; Established: 41 AD; Disestablished: 191 AD

name: Gaya Confederacy
description: The Gaya Confederacy was a dynamic league of small city-states established in 43 AD across the Nakdong River basin in southern Korea, evolving out of the earlier Byeonhan confederacy. Centred initially upon Geumgwan Gaya at Gimhae and later upon Daegaya at Goryeong, the confederation derived enormous economic wealth from abundant iron ore deposits, exporting refined iron and armour to neighbouring Silla, Baekje and the Wa of Japan. Despite sophisticated metallurgy and maritime trade, Gaya remained politically fragmented and was gradually annexed by the expanding kingdom of Silla by 562. \n\n Status: Sovereign confederacy; Capital: Gimhae; Common languages: Gaya and Old Korean; Religion: Korean shamanism and Buddhism; Government: Aristocratic confederacy; Historical era: Three Kingdoms of Korea; Established: 42 AD; Disestablished: 562 AD

name: Northern Xiongnu
description: The Northern Xiongnu formed an independent nomadic confederacy on the northern Mongolian plateau following the political fracture of the Xiongnu Empire in 48 AD. Refusing submission to the Han dynasty, their chanyus maintained a traditional pastoral warrior existence across the Orkhon and Tuul river valleys without establishing a fixed stone capital. The confederacy sustained bitter hostilities against the Southern Xiongnu and the Chinese empire until combined Han and allied nomadic campaigns, culminating in the Battle of the Altai Mountains and the rise of the Xianbei, drove them westward. \n\n Status: Sovereign nomadic confederacy; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Xiongnu; Religion: Tengrism and shamanism; Government: Nomadic tribal confederacy; Ruler title: Chanyu; Historical era: Antiquity; Established: 49 AD; Disestablished: 156 AD

name: Southern Xiongnu
description: The Southern Xiongnu emerged in 49 AD when eight southern tribes under Chanyu Bi broke away from the main nomadic empire following succession disputes and devastating regional famines. Operating initially as a sovereign nomadic force along the northern frontiers of China, the confederacy established headquarters near Meiji in modern Inner Mongolia. Seeking security against their northern kin, the Southern Xiongnu quickly entered into diplomatic negotiations with Emperor Guangwu of Han, transitioning into a frontier tributary buffer that defended Chinese borders in exchange for grain and trade privileges. \n\n Status: Sovereign nomadic confederacy; Capital: Meiji; Common languages: Xiongnu and Old Chinese; Religion: Tengrism and shamanism; Government: Nomadic tribal confederacy; Ruler title: Chanyu; Historical era: Antiquity; Established: 49 AD; Disestablished: 51 AD

name: Coba
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Coba was a prominent pre-Columbian Maya city-state established around two natural lagoons in the north-eastern lowlands of the Yucatan Peninsula. Beginning its urban florescence during the 1st century AD, the city expanded into a powerful regional metropolis characterised by towering ceremonial pyramids such as Nohoch Mul and carved commemorative stelae documenting dynastic lineages. Coba constructed the most extensive network of elevated white limestone causeways, known as sacbeob, in the Maya world, dominating inland trade and agricultural production until regional influence shifted toward emerging northern centres such as Chichen Itza. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Coba; Common languages: Yucatec Maya and Classic Maya; Religion: Maya polytheism; Government: Theocratic hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Ajaw; Historical era: Pre-Columbian Mesoamerica; Established: 51 AD; Disestablished: 1001 AD

name: Kingdom of Margiana
description: The Kingdom of Margiana was an autonomous Central Asian state centred on the lush, irrigated oasis of Merv along the Murghab River in modern Turkmenistan. Previously an administrative satrapy of the Parthian Empire, local rulers asserted sovereign independence around the middle of the 1st century AD, issuing their own distinctive bronze and silver coinage. Positioned at a pivotal crossroads along the Silk Road, Margiana thrived on caravan trade connecting Persia, India and China while sustaining Zoroastrian and early Buddhist communities until returning to Parthian and subsequent Sasanian oversight. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Merv; Common languages: Parthian and Bactrian; Religion: Zoroastrianism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 51 AD; Disestablished: 201 AD

name: Kingdom of Armenia
description: The Kingdom of Armenia during these spans was governed as an Arsacid client state aligned closely with the Parthian Empire following the diplomatic campaigns of King Vologases I. Ruled by King Tiridates I and his successors from the capital at Artaxata, the Armenian monarchy maintained domestic administrative autonomy while relying on Parthian military backing to counterbalance Roman expansion in the Caucasus. This delicate geopolitical status triggered recurring Roman-Parthian conflicts until the Treaty of Rhandeia established a compromise where Arsacid princes ruled Armenia subject to formal investiture by the Roman emperor. \n\n Status: Client kingdom of the Parthian Empire; Capital: Artaxata; Common languages: Armenian, Parthian and Koine Greek; Religion: Zoroastrianism and Armenian polytheism; Government: Client monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Arsacid dynasty of Armenia; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 56 AD; Disestablished: 165 AD

name: Nakoku
description: Nakoku was an early Yayoi period chiefdom located around modern Hakata Bay and Fukuoka City on the northern coast of Kyushu. In 57 AD, its ruler dispatched diplomatic envoys across the sea to the court of Emperor Guangwu of Han, receiving an imperial gold seal inscribed to the King of Na of Wa that confirmed recognised regional prestige. Controlling vital sea routes connecting western Japan with the Korean Peninsula, Nakoku prospered through maritime trade and ironworking before being gradually eclipsed by the expanding Yamato polity during the 3rd century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Nakoku; Common languages: Proto-Japonic; Religion: Shinto animism; Government: Tribal monarchy; Ruler title: King of Na; Historical era: Yayoi period; Established: 57 AD; Disestablished: 301 AD

name: Kingdom of Khotan
label: tarim basin
description: The Kingdom of Khotan was an enduring Saka Buddhist realm established along the southern rim of the Tarim Basin bordering the Taklamakan Desert. Governed from its oasis capital at Yotkan, near modern Hotan, the kingdom flourished as a vital hub of Silk Road commerce, celebrated for its exports of exquisite nephrite jade, fine mulberry silk and glazed ceramics. Khotan maintained sovereign domestic authority through flexible diplomacy with steppe nomadic confederacies and Chinese empires, while its flourishing Buddhist monasteries attracted scholarly pilgrims and preserved Sanskrit and Khotanese literary manuscripts for centuries. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Hotan; Common languages: Khotanese Saka and Gandhari Prakrit; Religion: Mahayana Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Antiquity to Middle Ages; Established: 62 AD; Disestablished: 1006 AD

name: Kingdom of Funan
description: The Kingdom of Funan was the earliest recorded Indianised state in Mainland Southeast Asia, flourishing across the lower Mekong Delta and coastal plains of modern Cambodia and southern Vietnam. Governed from the inland capital of Vyadhapura and supported by the bustling entrepot port of Oc Eo, the kingdom controlled critical maritime trade networks linking India, China and the Malay Peninsula. Funan integrated Indic legal traditions, Sanskrit court culture and both Hindu and Buddhist religious institutions, constructing extensive canal networks for irrigation and navigation until being superseded by its northern vassal, Chenla. \n\n Status: Sovereign mandala kingdom; Capital: Vyadhapura; Common languages: Proto-Khmer and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Indianised mandala monarchy; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 68 AD; Disestablished: 550 AD

name: Nagvanshis of Chotanagpur
description: The Nagvanshis of Chotanagpur were an indigenous ruling dynasty that governed the rugged forested plateaus of modern Jharkhand from the 1st century AD. Traditionally established by Phani Mukut Rai, the dynasty administered its domain from fortified jungle seats including Khukhragarh and later Navratangarh, integrating local tribal communities with Sanskritic courtly traditions. The kingdom retained sovereign autonomy over regional trade and mineral resources for many centuries, resisting outside subjugation through its inaccessible topography until the expansion of the Mughal Empire under Akbar forced the dynasty into tributary vassalage. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Khukhragarh; Common languages: Sadri, Mundari and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and indigenous Sarnaism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Nagvanshi dynasty; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Antiquity to early modern era; Established: 84 AD; Disestablished: 1585 AD

name: Sarangarh State
description: Sarangarh State was an ancient indigenous principality founded across the fertile plains and forested hill tracts of modern Chhattisgarh in central India. Established according to regional traditions during the 1st century AD by a Raj Gond ruling lineage, the state governed its agrarian territories from the fortified town of Sarangarh. The principality preserved local political autonomy through shifting regional alliances with neighbouring Garhjat kingdoms and imperial dynasties, retaining its distinct cultural traditions and decentralised clan-based administration until early modern political reorganisations altered the central Indian feudal landscape. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Sarangarh; Common languages: Chhattisgarhi and Odia; Religion: Hinduism and Gond animism; Government: Clan-based principality; Ruling dynasty: Raj Gond dynasty; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Antiquity to early modern era; Established: 92 AD; Disestablished: 1551 AD

name: Xianbei Confederation
description: The Xianbei Confederation was a formidable nomadic empire that arose across the eastern Eurasian steppe and Inner Mongolia following the collapse of Xiongnu supremacy in the late 1st century AD. Governed through a decentralised assembly of clan chieftains without a permanent fixed capital, the confederacy reached its military height under leader Tanshihuai in the mid-2nd century, repeatedly repelling Han imperial armies and dominating northern trade routes. After Tanshihuai's death, the confederation fractured into autonomous tribal branches, including the Murong and Tuoba, who later established dynastic kingdoms across northern China. \n\n Status: Sovereign nomadic confederacy; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Xianbei and Para-Mongolic; Religion: Shamanism and Tengrism; Government: Nomadic tribal confederacy; Ruler title: Khagan; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 93 AD; Disestablished: 235 AD

name: Kingdom of Hatra
description: The Kingdom of Hatra was an autonomous Arab desert monarchy centred on the heavily fortified circular caravan city of Hatra in northern Mesopotamia. Buffeted between the Roman and Parthian empires, the city-state maintained its independence through formidable stone bastions, skilled camel archers and strategic diplomacy with nomadic desert clans. Hatra prospered as a cosmopolitan commercial nexus where Mesopotamian, Greco-Roman and Arabian religious traditions syncretised around the great temple complex of Shamash until the Sasanian ruler Shapur I conquered and razed the settlement in 241. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Hatra; Common languages: Hatran Aramaic and Old Arabic; Religion: Mesopotamian, Greek and Arabian polytheistic syncretism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 1st century AD; Disestablished: 1 May 241

name: Okjeo
description: Okjeo was an ancient tribal state occupying the coastal strip and mountainous hinterlands of north-eastern Korea along the Sea of Japan. Centred around settlements near modern Hamhung, the polity comprised two primary branches, Eastern Okjeo and Northern Okjeo, whose communities sustained themselves through fishing, agriculture and forest harvesting. Lacking centralised royal authority, Okjeo was organised under hereditary local elders who frequently paid tributary deliveries of cloth, fish and marine products to the militarily dominant kingdom of Goguryeo before being completely incorporated into its administrative fold. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal state; Capital: Hamhung; Common languages: Okjeo and Old Korean; Religion: Korean shamanism; Government: Tribal federation; Ruler title: Tribal Chieftain; Historical era: Proto-Three Kingdoms of Korea; Established: 101 AD; Disestablished: 401 AD

name: Tagaung
label: pyu city-states
description: Tagaung was an influential Pyu city-state established along the eastern banks of the Irrawaddy River in Upper Burma. Revered in traditional Burmese chronicles as the cradle of earliest royal lineages, the city developed as a fortified urban centre that regulated inland riverine trade, timber extraction and salt distribution from nearby deposits. The polity embraced early Buddhist and Hindu religious influences alongside indigenous animist worship, maintaining autonomous municipal governance until King Anawrahta unified the Irrawaddy valley under the Pagan Empire in the 11th century. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Tagaung; Common languages: Pyu, Old Burman and Sanskrit; Religion: Theravada Buddhism, Hinduism and Nat worship; Government: Urban monarchy; Historical era: Classical Burma; Established: 101 AD; Disestablished: 1051 AD

name: Kingdom of Dacia
description: The Kingdom of Dacia functioned briefly as a subjugated client realm under King Decebalus following his defeat in the First Dacian War by Emperor Trajan in 102 AD. Governed from the mountain stronghold of Sarmizegetusa Regia in the southern Carpathians, the Dacian state was forced to surrender siege weaponry, raze frontier fortresses and accept Roman garrisons on its territory. Decebalus covertly rearmed and attempted to rally anti-Roman tribal alliances across the Danube, precipitating Trajan's decisive Second Dacian War that destroyed the capital and annexed the kingdom as Roman Dacia. \n\n Status: Client kingdom of the Roman Empire; Capital: Sarmizegetusa; Common languages: Dacian and Latin; Religion: Zamolxism and Thracian polytheism; Government: Client monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 103 AD; Disestablished: 106 AD

name: Siljik
description: Siljik was an ancient coastal principality established around modern Samcheok in the Gangwon Province of eastern Korea. First documented in the early 2nd century when it contested territorial boundaries with neighbouring southern clans, the state commanded strategic maritime routes along the eastern coastline. Situated between the expanding spheres of Goguryeo to the north and Silla to the south, Siljik fiercely guarded its local autonomy under native rulers such as King Anil until Silla general Yi Sabu secured the region and incorporated it as a frontier county. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Samcheok; Common languages: Old Korean; Religion: Korean shamanism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Proto-Three Kingdoms of Korea; Established: 103 AD; Disestablished: 6th century AD

name: Tiwanaku Empire
description: The Tiwanaku Empire was a major pre-Columbian civilisation established in the high-altitude southern Lake Titicaca basin of modern western Bolivia. Governed from the monumental ceremonial metropolis of Tiwanaku, the polity pioneered extensive raised-field agricultural terraces known as sukakollos that sustained dense urban populations in a challenging altiplano environment. Tiwanaku projected religious and economic influence across western Bolivia, southern Peru and northern Chile through prestigious polychrome ceramics, sophisticated stone masonry and caravan trade rather than coercive territorial conquests, flourishing for centuries before climatic desiccation caused its decline. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Tiwanaku; Common languages: Puquina and Aymara; Religion: Pre-Columbian Andean polytheism; Government: Theocratic imperial federation; Historical era: Middle Horizon; Established: 111 AD; Disestablished: 1000 AD

name: Kingdom of Kucha
label: tarim basin
description: The Kingdom of Kucha was an ancient Tocharian oasis monarchy situated along the northern branch of the Silk Road between the Taklamakan Desert and the Tian Shan mountains. Inhabited by Tocharian speakers and governed from the fortified walled oasis of Kucha, the kingdom derived immense wealth from transit duties on luxury caravans, iron mining and agricultural irrigation. Kucha served as a renowned beacon of Sarvastivada Buddhism, celebrated for monastic scholarship, subterranean cave shrines at Kizil and classical musical traditions that profoundly influenced imperial courts across East Asia. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kucha; Common languages: Tocharian B and Kucha Prakrit; Religion: Sarvastivada Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Antiquity; Established: 112 AD; Disestablished: 384 AD

name: Kingdom of Osroene
description: The Kingdom of Osroene functioned as a vital Roman client state in Upper Mesopotamia centred upon the walled regional metropolis of Edessa, modern Şanlıurfa. Ruled by the Arab Abgarid dynasty, the kingdom occupied a contentious border zone between the Roman and Parthian empires, requiring its monarchs to balance imperial demands while securing vital trans-Euphrates caravan traffic. Under Roman clientage, Edessa blossomed into a vibrant centre of Syriac literary scholarship and early Eastern Christianity until Emperor Caracalla deposed the royal house and annexed Osroene directly as an imperial province. \n\n Status: Client kingdom of the Roman Empire; Capital: Şanlıurfa; Common languages: Classical Syriac, Aramaic, Koine Greek and Latin; Religion: Syrian polytheism and Syriac Christianity; Government: Client monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Abgarid dynasty; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 116 AD; Disestablished: 215 AD

name: Chutu Dynasty
description: The Chutu Dynasty was an autonomous southern Indian royal house that ruled parts of the south-western Deccan and coastal Karnataka from their historic capital at Banavasi. Originally serving as provincial administrators under the Satavahana Empire, the Chutus asserted sovereign independence as Satavahana central power waned in the 2nd century AD. Their rulers issued distinctive lead coinage bearing tree and hill motifs, patronised Buddhist monasteries and excavated early rock-cut shrines before being eclipsed and replaced by Mayurasharma, the founder of the native Kadamba dynasty. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Banavasi; Common languages: Prakrit and Old Kannada; Religion: Buddhism, Jainism and Shaivism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 126 AD; Disestablished: 346 AD

name: Kingdom of Khotan
label: tarim basin
description: The Kingdom of Khotan operated as a tributary protectorate under Chinese suzerainty during this extended historical span, maintaining its native Saka monarchy while acknowledging imperial oversight through the Western Regions administration. Governed from its oasis capital at Yotkan near modern Hotan, the kingdom guarded the southern caravan routes of the Taklamakan Desert and sent regular diplomatic embassies bearing exquisite nephrite jade and fine silk textiles to Chinese capitals. The protectorate arrangement insulated Khotan from nomadic incursions, allowing its renowned Mahayana Buddhist monastic centres to flourish in remarkable security. \n\n Status: Protectorate of the Chinese dynasties; Capital: Hotan; Common languages: Khotanese Saka, Gandhari Prakrit and Middle Chinese; Religion: Mahayana Buddhism; Government: Client monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Antiquity to Early Middle Ages; Established: 128 AD; Disestablished: 631 AD

name: Salakanagara Kingdom
description: The Salakanagara Kingdom was an early Indianised coastal realm recorded in regional Javanese traditions as having flourished across western Java around modern Pandeglang and the Sunda Strait. Known in classical manuscripts as the City of Silver, the polity is thought to have developed around maritime anchorages that traded spices, aromatic resins and metal ores with merchants from India and China. While largely known through later historiographical compilations such as the Wangsakerta manuscripts, tradition identifies Salakanagara as the cultural and political forerunner to the historical Tarumanagara kingdom. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Pandeglang; Common languages: Sanskrit and Old Sundanese; Religion: Hinduism and animism; Government: Indianised monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 130 AD; Disestablished: 362 AD

name: Ay Dynasty
description: The Ay Dynasty was an ancient Tamil ruling lineage that commanded the south-western extremity of peninsular India, encompassing the fertile plains of Nanjinad and the spice-rich slopes of the southern Western Ghats. Operating from regional strongholds such as Aykudi and the bustling maritime haven of Vizhinjam, the Ay chieftains derived significant revenues from the export of black pepper, pearls and aromatic woods. The dynasty balanced complex diplomatic relations between the neighbouring Chera and Pandya powers, preserving distinct lineage autonomy until Pandya expansion absorbed its principal territories in the 8th century. \n\n Status: Sovereign chieftaincy and monarchy; Capital: None recorded; Historical region: Kerala and Tamil country; Common languages: Old Tamil; Religion: Hinduism and indigenous animism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Historical era: Sangam period to Early Middle Ages; Established: 151 AD; Disestablished: 766 AD

name: Gangga Negara
description: Gangga Negara was an early Malay-Hindu coastal kingdom established along the western coastline of the Malay Peninsula, encompassing modern Beruas and the Dinding district of Perak. Guarding vital maritime approaches along the Malacca Strait, the kingdom flourished on the extraction of alluvial tin, gold panning and trade with passing Indian and Chinese merchant fleets. Governed by Indianised monarchs who fostered syncretic Brahmanical traditions, Gangga Negara preserved its commercial autonomy for centuries until the destructive naval raid launched by King Rajendra Chola I of Tamilakam dismantled the state around 1026. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Beruas; Common languages: Old Malay and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Classical era; Established: 2nd century AD; Disestablished: 1026 AD

name: Kalabhra Dynasty
description: The Kalabhra Dynasty comprised a powerful ruling line that established dominion over the ancient Tamil country, displacing the traditional royal houses of the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas. Governing from urban centres such as Madurai and Kaveripumpattinam, the Kalabhras broke the conventional aristocratic social hierarchy and vigorously patronised non-Brahmanical monastic traditions, especially Jainism and Buddhism. Their era witnessed an extraordinary flowering of classical Tamil literature and ethical poetry before combined military counter-offensives by Simhavishnu of the Pallavas and Kadungon of the Pandyas permanently broke Kalabhra hegemony in the late 6th century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Madurai; Common languages: Old Tamil, Prakrit and Sanskrit; Religion: Jainism, Buddhism and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 151 AD; Disestablished: 576 AD

name: Kanker State
description: Kanker State was an enduring indigenous principality located within the rugged hills and dense sal and teak forests of the upper Mahanadi basin in modern southern Chhattisgarh. Centred upon the fortified riverside settlement of Kanker, the realm was governed by an ancient native dynasty that successfully maintained local territorial independence amidst the shifting fortunes of central Indian empires. The state's economic base relied on forest commodities, timber and subsistence agriculture, while its isolated upland geography shielded native Gond and tribal communities from foreign conquest for multiple centuries. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Kanker; Common languages: Chhattisgarhi, Gondi and Halbi; Religion: Hinduism and Gond animism; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Classical antiquity to early modern era; Established: 151 AD; Disestablished: 1810 AD

name: Kingdom of the Garamantes
description: The Kingdom of the Garamantes was an advanced Saharan civilisation centred in the arid Fezzan depression of south-western Libya, with its royal capital established at Garama. The Garamantes created an extraordinary desert agricultural economy through an extensive network of subterranean irrigation channels known as foggaras, which tapped fossil groundwater to cultivate dates, grains and grapes. As pioneers of early trans-Saharan commerce, they utilised horse-drawn chariots and caravans to trade salt, precious stones and slaves with Roman North Africa until depleted groundwater resources precipitated the realm's gradual decline. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Garama; Common languages: Garamantian Berber; Religion: Traditional Berber religion and Saharan animism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 151 AD; Disestablished: 670 AD

name: Langkasuka Kingdom
description: The Langkasuka Kingdom was one of the earliest Indianised states on the Malay Peninsula, established around the 2nd century AD with its primary urban and religious centre located at Yarang near modern Pattani. Controlling a strategic overland portage across the narrow Malay Isthmus, the kingdom provided a safe transit corridor for merchants seeking to avoid treacherous navigational routes through the Malacca Strait. Langkasuka patronised both Mahayana Buddhism and Shaivite Hinduism, dispatching diplomatic tribute to imperial China and developing extensive maritime links until being integrated into the maritime realm of Srivijaya. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Yarang; Common languages: Old Malay and Sanskrit; Religion: Buddhism and Hinduism; Government: Indianised monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Classical Southeast Asia; Established: 2nd century AD; Disestablished: 751 AD

name: Ulaidh
label: irish medieval kingdoms;celtic polities
description: Ulaidh was an ancient Gaelic over-kingdom situated in north-eastern Ireland, comprising territories east of the River Bann that encompass modern counties Antrim and Down. Centred politically on coastal bastions such as Dunseverick and later Downpatrick, the realm was dominated by rival royal dynasties of the Dal Fiatach and the Cruithin Dal nAraidi who held the title of Ri Ulad. Celebrated in early Irish mythology as the realm of the Red Branch warriors, historic Ulaidh fiercely defended its borders against Ui Neill encroachers until Norman knight John de Courcy overran the kingdom in 1177. \n\n Status: Sovereign over-kingdom; Capital: Dunseverick; Common languages: Old Irish, Middle Irish and Latin; Religion: Celtic polytheism, later Celtic Christianity; Government: Gaelic tanistry monarchy; Ruler title: Ri Ulad; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 151 AD; Disestablished: 1177 AD

name: Kingdom of Osroene
description: The Kingdom of Osroene passed briefly under the suzerainty of the Parthian Empire between 164 and 166 AD during the height of the Roman-Parthian War. Centred at Edessa, modern Şanlıurfa, the kingdom saw its pro-Roman monarch ousted and replaced by a Parthian nominee supported by the armies of King Vologases IV. This brief alignment integrated Upper Mesopotamia into the Parthian defensive perimeter until Roman counter-offensives commanded by Avidius Cassius and Lucius Verus recaptured Edessa, expelling the Parthian garrison and re-establishing Roman client status over the Abgarid monarchy. \n\n Status: Client kingdom of the Parthian Empire; Capital: Şanlıurfa; Common languages: Classical Syriac, Aramaic and Parthian; Religion: Mesopotamian polytheism and early Christianity; Government: Client monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Abgarid dynasty; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 164 AD; Disestablished: 166 AD

name: Kingdom of the Vandals
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Vandals during this initial era was established by the Hasdingi branch of the Germanic Vandal confederacy in the upper Tisza and Carpathian borderlands of modern western Romania. Emerging into prominence during the Marcomannic Wars, the Hasdingi concluded an alliance treaty with Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius, settling in lands near Roman Dacia with their regional base situated near Sarmizegetusa. These early Vandal clans maintained an autonomous martial kingship, clashing frequently with neighbouring Goths and Sarmatians until escalating nomadic pressures impelled their subsequent westward migrations across central Europe. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal kingdom; Capital: Sarmizegetusa; Common languages: Vandalic Germanic and Latin; Religion: Germanic paganism; Government: Tribal kingship; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical antiquity and Migration Period; Established: 170 AD; Disestablished: 336 AD

name: Kingdom of Leinster
label: irish medieval kingdoms;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Leinster was an enduring Gaelic realm in eastern Ireland, formed by the tribal confederation of the Laighin and traditionally active from the late 2nd century. Governing from fluctuating royal seats and defensive hillforts including Dun Ailinne, Naas and Kilkenny, its dynastic houses, notably the Ui Cheinnselaig, contested supremacy with the northern Ui Neill and the monarchs of Munster. Leinster sustained a distinct legal code, bardic literature and monastic foundations until King Diarmait Mac Murchada enlisted Anglo-Norman adventurers to restore his disputed throne in the late 12th century, precipitating the Norman conquest of Ireland. \n\n Status: Sovereign Gaelic kingdom; Capital: Kilkenny; Common languages: Old Irish, Middle Irish and Latin; Religion: Celtic polytheism, later Celtic Christianity; Government: Gaelic tanistry monarchy; Ruler title: Ri Laighean; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 186 AD; Disestablished: 1176 AD

name: Kingdom of Lâm Ấp
description: The Kingdom of Lam Ap was an early Cham maritime realm founded in 192 AD when the local leader Khu Lien led a successful rebellion against the Chinese Han dynasty in Xianglin county. Located in central Vietnam between the Hai Van Pass and the Thu Bon River valley, the kingdom governed from fortified administrative centres such as Tra Kieu. Lam Ap prospered through coastal seafaring, trade in spices and eaglewood, and pirate raids against southern Chinese coastal commanderies, laying the cultural, religious and political foundations for the historical civilisation of Champa. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Trà Kiệu; Common languages: Cham and Sanskrit; Religion: Cham folk religion, Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Indianised monarchy; Ruler title: King of Lam Ap; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 192 AD; Disestablished: 530 AD

name: Roman Empire
label: year of the five emperors
description: The Roman Empire under Septimius Severus during the spring of 193 comprised the Danubian and Italian faction of the imperial state formed during the Year of the Five Emperors. Following the assassination of Pertinax, Severus was acclaimed emperor by his legions at Carnuntum in Pannonia Superior and executed a rapid march across the Alps into Italy. Gaining recognition from the Senate in Rome and executing the disgraced incumbent Didius Julianus on 1 June 193, Severus secured the imperial capital and disbanded the Praetorian Guard before turning east to confront rival contenders. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Rome; Official languages: Latin; Common languages: Latin and Koine Greek; Religion: Roman polytheism and imperial cult; Government: Military autocracy; Ruling dynasty: Severan dynasty; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 28 March 193; Disestablished: 1 June 193

name: Roman Empire
label: year of the five emperors
description: The Roman Empire under Pescennius Niger designated the eastern provinces of the Roman world that proclaimed Niger emperor in Antioch following the murder of Pertinax in 193. Supported by the Syrian legions, Egypt and allied client rulers across the Near East, Niger established a rival imperial administration that controlled eastern trade routes and fortified the passes of the Taurus Mountains. However, his forces were outmanoeuvred in Anatolia by the veteran Danubian legions of Septimius Severus, culminating in Niger's decisive defeat at the Battle of Issus and his death near Antioch in 194. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Antioch; Official languages: Latin; Common languages: Koine Greek, Latin and Aramaic; Religion: Roman polytheism and imperial cult; Government: Military autocracy; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 28 March 193; Disestablished: 1 June 194

name: Roman Empire
label: year of the five emperors
description: The Roman Empire under Clodius Albinus comprised the western provincial administration established during the civil wars following the death of Emperor Pertinax in 193. Acclaimed by the legions of Britannia and Hispania, Albinus initially cooperated with Septimius Severus, accepting the title of Caesar, before declaring himself Augustus in 196 and transferring his headquarters to Lugdunum, modern Lyon. Mobilising extensive Gallo-Roman aristocratic support, his rival regime commanded significant military forces until Severus marched west and crushed Albinus's army in the massive and bloody Battle of Lugdunum on 19 February 197. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Lugdunum; Official languages: Latin; Common languages: Latin and Celtic; Religion: Roman polytheism and imperial cult; Government: Military autocracy; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 28 March 193; Disestablished: 19 February 197

name: Tanukhid Confederation
description: The Tanukhid Confederation was an influential league of Arab tribes that migrated from eastern Arabia to establish pastoral settlements along the Syrian desert frontier and the Euphrates borderlands. Functioning as a mobile martial alliance without a permanent fixed capital, the confederation was led by famous monarchs including Jadhima and the 4th-century warrior Queen Mavia. The Tanukhids embraced Orthodox Christianity and served as prominent foederati allies of the Eastern Roman Empire, guarding the imperial limes against Persian incursions until the Muslim conquest of the Levant culminated in the Battle of Yarmouk in 636. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal confederacy; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Old Arabic and Classical Syriac; Religion: Arabian polytheism, later Orthodox Christianity; Government: Tribal confederacy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late antiquity; Established: 197 AD; Disestablished: 20 August 636

name: Abhira Kingdom
description: The Abhira Kingdom was an influential Indian dynasty that rose to prominence across the western Deccan and Gujarat following the collapse of the Satavahana Empire in the early 3rd century. Controlling extensive territories spanning modern Maharashtra, northern Konkan and southern Madhya Pradesh, the Abhira monarchs issued royal inscriptions and established a calendar era that persisted in regional use for centuries. The kingdom patronised Hindu rituals and Buddhist rock-cut monasteries, notably at Nasik, maintaining substantial regional authority until the rise of the Vakatakas and Traikutakas fragmented their territorial holdings. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Dum Dum; Common languages: Sanskrit, Prakrit and Apabhramsha; Religion: Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 200 AD; Disestablished: 371 AD

name: Alupa Dynasty
description: The Alupa Dynasty was an ancient coastal realm that governed the Tulu Nadu region, encompassing modern coastal Karnataka and northern Kerala, under the dynastic territory known as Alvakheda. Administering their domain from the port capital of Udyavara, the Alupa monarchs navigated fluctuating relations with larger inland Deccan empires, preserving robust local sovereignty over maritime trade and agricultural valleys. The dynasty actively sponsored temple architecture, celebrated coastal trade with Mediterranean and Indian merchants, and maintained deep patronal commitments to Shaivism and Jainism throughout this early classical era. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Udyavara; Common languages: Tulu and Old Kannada; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Pandya-Chakravarti; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 200 AD; Disestablished: 451 AD

name: Kingdom of Margiana
description: The Kingdom of Margiana functioned as a loyal eastern vassal state of the Parthian Empire during the early decades of the 3rd century AD. Centred upon the affluent agricultural oasis of Merv in the Murghab basin of modern Turkmenistan, the realm was governed by local dynasts who recognised Arsacid imperial suzerainty. Margiana guarded northeastern frontier trade routes against nomadic steppe incursions and facilitated caravan traffic connecting Iran with Central Asia until the collapse of the Parthian dynasty at the Battle of Hormozdgan in 224 altered regional allegiances. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Parthian Empire; Capital: Merv; Common languages: Parthian and Bactrian; Religion: Zoroastrianism and Buddhism; Government: Client monarchy; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 201 AD; Disestablished: 28 April 224

name: Moche Polities
description: The Moche Polities comprised a network of autonomous river-valley states that flourished along the arid northern coast of Peru between the 2nd and 8th centuries AD. Sharing a cohesive religious and artistic tradition without a centralised imperial administration, these polities erected monumental adobe pyramid complexes such as the Huaca del Sol and Huaca de la Luna in the Moche Valley. The Moche achieved extraordinary artistic sophistication in realistic stirrup-spout ceramics, intricate metallurgy and elaborate mural paintings depicting ritual combat and sacrificial ceremonies, thriving through complex canal irrigation until climatic shocks undermined coastal agriculture. \n\n Status: Sovereign regional confederacy; Capital: Huaca del Sol; Common languages: Mochica; Religion: Pre-Columbian Andean polytheism; Government: Theocratic valley chiefdoms; Historical era: Early Intermediate Period; Established: 201 AD; Disestablished: 751 AD

name: Nagas of Padmavati
description: The Nagas of Padmavati were an indigenous north-central Indian dynasty that rose to prominence in the wake of declining Kushan imperial power across modern Madhya Pradesh. Governing from their fortified capital at Padmavati Pawaya near modern Gwalior, the Naga monarchs, identified in historical records with the Bharashiva clan, issued distinctive copper coinage and celebrated the revival of Brahmanical religious prestige through ten historic ashvamedha horse sacrifices. The dynasty dominated transit corridors between the Gangetic plain and Malwa until King Samudragupta incorporated their realm into the expanding Gupta Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Padmavati Pawaya; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Shaivite Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 201 AD; Disestablished: 341 AD

name: Quiriguá
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Quirigua was an ancient Maya city-state founded along the lower Motagua River valley in the Izabal department of south-eastern Guatemala. Occupying a pivotal juncture of overland trade corridors, the city controlled regional exchanges of precious jadeite, obsidian and cacao. Quirigua attained political and cultural renown during the 8th century under King K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat, who achieved sovereign independence from neighbouring Copan, captured its king and erected the tallest monolithic carved stelae and zoomorphic stone altars known in the pre-Columbian Maya world. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Quiriguá; Common languages: Classic Maya; Religion: Maya polytheism; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Ruler title: Ajaw; Historical era: Classic Maya period; Established: 201 AD; Disestablished: 1201 AD

name: Kingdom of the Alemanni
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Alemanni was a martial Germanic tribal confederacy that coalesced in the Main River basin and broke through the Roman limes into the Agri Decumates during the early 3rd century. Occupying south-western Germany, Alsace and the northern Alpine foreland, the Alemanni established rural settlements governed by confederated kings and war-band chieftains, maintaining regional strongholds near Augsburg. They mounted frequent trans-Rhenish incursions against Roman Gaul and Raetia for over two centuries until King Clovis I of the Franks decisively defeated them at the Battle of Tolbiac in 496. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal kingdom; Capital: Augsburg; Common languages: Alemannic Germanic and Latin; Religion: Germanic paganism; Government: Tribal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Migration Period; Established: 214 AD; Disestablished: 497 AD

name: Kingdom of Hanzhong
description: The Kingdom of Hanzhong was a transitional sovereign regime established in 219 and 220 AD by the warlord Liu Bei following his hard-fought victory over Cao Cao in the Hanzhong Campaign. Centred upon the strategic mountain commandery of Hanzhong and controlling the fertile Sichuan Basin, Liu Bei assumed the royal title of King of Hanzhong to assert legitimate dynastic continuity on behalf of the beleaguered House of Han. This administrative consolidation provided the essential political and military platform for Liu Bei to declare himself emperor of Shu Han shortly thereafter. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Hanzhong; Common languages: Eastern Han Chinese; Religion: Confucianism, Taoism and Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King of Hanzhong; Head of state: Liu Bei; Historical era: Three Kingdoms period; Established: 220 AD; Disestablished: 222 AD

name: Wei
label: three kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Wei, known historically as Cao Wei, was the dominant imperial dynasty of the Three Kingdoms period in northern China, established on 11 December 220 AD when Cao Pi received the abdication of Emperor Xian of Han. Administered from its grand capitals at Xuchang and Luoyang, the state controlled the vast agricultural heartland of the Yellow River plains, implementing the Nine-rank system for bureaucratic selection and state-run tuntian agricultural colonies. Wei conquered the rival state of Shu Han in 263 before the regent Sima Yan usurped the imperial throne to establish the Jin dynasty. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Luoyang; Common languages: Eastern Han Chinese; Religion: Confucianism, Taoism and Chinese folk religion; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Cao; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Three Kingdoms; Established: 11 December 220; Disestablished: 2 August 266

name: Wu
label: three kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Wu, designated in historical literature as Eastern Wu or Sun Wu, was an imperial Chinese state that ruled the southern Yangtze River basin and coastal regions throughout the Three Kingdoms period. Founded by Sun Quan and administered from fluctuating capitals at Wuchang and Jianye, modern Nanjing, the realm developed powerful naval squadrons that dominated the Yangtze and expanded maritime trade into Southeast Asia. Wu fostered the rapid economic development of the Jiangnan region and integrated southern non-Han indigenous peoples before finally succumbing to the overwhelming amphibious invasion launched by the Western Jin dynasty in 280. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Jianye, also Wuchang; Common languages: Eastern Han Chinese, Old Jiangdong and Proto-Wu; Religion: Taoism, Confucianism and Buddhism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Sun; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Three Kingdoms; Established: 221 AD; Disestablished: 31 May 280

name: Han
label: three kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Han, commonly referred to in historiography as Shu Han, was an imperial state established in 221 AD by Liu Bei to uphold the legitimate succession of the fallen Han dynasty. Governed from the fortified city of Chengdu in the fertile Sichuan Basin, the state commanded the mountain passes of south-western China and mobilised resources through the meticulous administration of Chancellor Zhuge Liang. Despite repeated Northern Expeditions aimed at dislodging Cao Wei and restoring the dynastic capital at Luoyang, Shu Han remained constrained by limited manpower and was conquered by Wei armies in 263. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Chengdu; Common languages: Ba-Shu Chinese and Eastern Han Chinese; Religion: Confucianism, Taoism and Chinese folk religion; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Liu; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Three Kingdoms; Established: 221 AD; Disestablished: 17 December 263

name: Kingdom of Margiana
description: The Kingdom of Margiana became an eastern vassal state of the nascent Sasanian Empire following the defeat and death of the last Arsacid monarch at the Battle of Hormozdgan in 224 AD. Maintaining its traditional regional administration at Merv, the oasis principality acknowledged the suzerainty of King Ardashir I and his successor Shapur I. The realm served as a vital forward military base and trade hub protecting north-eastern Persia from nomadic inroads, retaining subordinate dynastic privileges until the Sasanian crown reorganised the eastern provinces into direct imperial satrapies. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Sasanian Empire; Capital: Merv; Common languages: Middle Persian, Parthian and Bactrian; Religion: Zoroastrianism and Buddhism; Government: Client monarchy; Historical era: Late antiquity; Established: 28 April 224; Disestablished: 261 AD

name: Sasanian Empire
description: The Sasanian Empire, officially designated by its rulers as Eranshahr, was the last great pre-Islamic Iranian empire, established on 28 April 224 AD when Ardashir I overthrew the Parthian Arsacid dynasty. Governing from the sprawling imperial capital of Ctesiphon on the Tigris, the Sasanian monarchs, styled King of Kings, revived Achaemenid imperial traditions, established Zoroastrianism as the state religion and developed a formidable professional cavalry force known as the savaran. The empire contested hegemony over the Near East with the Roman and Byzantine empires until fracturing under the Arab Muslim conquests in the 7th century. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Ctesiphon; Official languages: Middle Persian; Common languages: Middle Persian, Parthian, Aramaic and Greek; Religion: Zoroastrianism, Christianity and Manichaeism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Sasan; Ruler title: King of Kings; Historical era: Late antiquity; Established: 28 April 224; Disestablished: 651 AD

name: Ikshvakus of Vijayapuri
description: The Ikshvakus of Vijayapuri, also known as the Andhra Ikshvakus, were a prominent dynasty that asserted sovereign control over the lower Krishna River valley following the fragmentation of the Satavahana Empire in 228 AD. Ruling from their monumental capital of Vijayapuri, modern Nagarjunakonda in Andhra Pradesh, the monarchs patronised Vedic sacrifices while royal women famously endowed magnificent Buddhist stupas, chaityas and monasteries. The realm developed vibrant riverine and maritime trade connecting the Deccan with Southeast Asia before the rising southern power of the Pallava dynasty subdued the state in the 4th century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Vijayapuri; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 228 AD; Disestablished: 351 AD

name: Kushano-Sasanian Kingdom
description: The Kushano-Sasanian Kingdom was a regional vassal state established by the Sasanian Empire in Bactria, Gandhara and Sogdia around 228 AD after conquering the western provinces of the declining Kushans. Administered by Sasanian princes titled Kushanshah from the ancient metropolis of Balkh, the polity issued distinctive bilingual coinage reflecting a syncretic blend of Sasanian, Bactrian and Indian royal iconography. The kingdom maintained domestic autonomy and patronised both Zoroastrian fire temples and Buddhist monastic sanctuaries until nomadic invasions by the Kidarite Huns dismantled Kushano-Sasanian authority in the late 4th century. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Sasanian Empire; Capital: Balkh; Common languages: Middle Persian, Bactrian and Gandhari Prakrit; Religion: Zoroastrianism, Buddhism and Hinduism; Government: Feudal sub-kingdom; Ruler title: Kushanshah; Historical era: Late antiquity; Established: 228 AD; Disestablished: 371 AD

name: Northern Satavahanas
description: The Northern Satavahanas comprised a remnant monarchical state that preserved royal Satavahana dynastic continuity in the north-western Deccan following the collapse of the imperial dynasty after the death of Pulumavi IV in 228 AD.
