Ruling from the historic ancestral capital of Pratishthana, modern Paithan on the Godavari River, this rump regime retained control over local agrarian tracts and commercial river routes. The kingdom struggled to preserve its authority against rival successor factions including the Abhiras and Western Satraps, finally dissolving as new regional powers partitioned the remnants of central Maharashtra. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Paithan; Common languages: Maharashtri Prakrit and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 228 AD; Disestablished: 301 AD

name: Pallava Dynasty
description: The Pallava Dynasty was a powerful southern Indian state that arose in Tondaimandalam and the southern Deccan following the dissolution of the Satavahana Empire in the early 3rd century AD. Establishing their royal capital at the temple city of Kanchipuram, the Pallavas developed into a major naval and cultural power that sponsored monolithic rock-cut shrines, shore temples at Mamallapuram and the influential Pallava script. The dynasty engaged in centuries-long rivalries with the Chalukyas of Vatapi and the southern Pandyas before being permanently eclipsed by the imperial Cholas in 898. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kanchipuram; Common languages: Tamil, Prakrit and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism, Jainism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 228 AD; Disestablished: 898 AD

name: Yan
label: three kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Yan was a short-lived breakaway kingdom established in July 237 on the Liaodong Peninsula when the regional warlord Gongsun Yuan declared independence from Cao Wei. Administered from Xiangping, modern Liaoyang, the regime controlled vital overland transit routes into the Korean Peninsula and sought maritime alliances with Eastern Wu to counterbalance Wei power. However, Gongsun Yuan's diplomatic gambits failed to deter a massive retaliatory expedition commanded by Sima Yi, whose siege of Xiangping led to the capture of the city and the dissolution of Yan in September 238. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Xiangping; Common languages: Eastern Han Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, Confucianism and Taoism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King of Yan; Head of state: Gongsun Yuan; Historical era: Three Kingdoms period; Established: July 237; Disestablished: 29 September 238

name: Abhira Kingdom
description: The Abhira Kingdom during this phase consolidated sovereign dynastic control across western Maharashtra and the northern Konkan coastline following the disintegration of Satavahana hegemony. Marking the inception of their royal calendar in 249 AD, the Abhira monarchs oversaw lucrative coastal ports and inland agricultural valleys from fortified seats across the northern Western Ghats. The realm supported religious tolerance by endowing Hindu temples alongside Buddhist rock-hewn caves at Kanheri and Nasik, sustaining independent regional authority until the expanding power of the Traikutakas and Vakatakas eclipsed the dynasty in the early 5th century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Dum Dum; Common languages: Sanskrit, Prakrit and Apabhramsha; Religion: Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 249 AD; Disestablished: 416 AD

name: Duan Tribe
description: The Duan Tribe was a prominent Xianbei nomadic clan that established an autonomous tribal principality across the Liaoxi region along the north-eastern frontier of China. Unlike pastoral groups confined to the deep steppe, the Duan settled within the borders of the Western Jin dynasty, maintaining a formidable equestrian military while adopting Chinese bureaucratic titles and court customs. Functioning as vital military allies for imperial Jin authorities during the upheavals of the Sixteen Kingdoms, the tribe fiercely defended its border territory until being conquered by the rival Murong Xianbei of Former Yan in 338. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal principality; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Xianbei and Middle Chinese; Religion: Shamanism and Chinese folk religion; Government: Nomadic tribal chieftaincy; Ruler title: Chieftain; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 251 AD; Disestablished: 338 AD

name: Empire of Japan
description: The Empire of Japan traces its political continuity to the coalescence of the Yamato state during the mid-3rd century AD, marked archaeologically by the emergence of monumental keyhole-shaped kofun burial mounds. Centred in the Kinai plain and long directed from historic imperial capitals including Kyoto, the realm gradually unified the Japanese archipelago through military campaigns, clan alliances and the integration of continental technology and continental writing systems. Under an unbroken imperial lineage, the state evolved from early tribal chiefdoms into an enduring centralised monarchy that shaped East Asian cultural and geopolitical history. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Kyoto; Common languages: Old Japanese, Classical Japanese and Japanese; Religion: Shinto and Buddhism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruler title: Tenno; Historical era: Antiquity to modern era; Established: 250 AD; Disestablished: 2 February 1946

name: Ghassanid Kingdom
description: The Ghassanid Kingdom, ruled by the Jafnid dynasty, was an Arab Christian monarchy that governed the Syrian desert frontier and the Golan as premier foederati of the Roman Empire. Establishing their primary political encampment and capital at Jabiyah, the Ghassanids defended imperial borderlands against nomadic raids and waged bitter desert wars against the pro-Sasanian Lakhmids of Al-Hira. Reaching their apex in the 6th century under King al-Harith ibn Jabalah, the Ghassanid monarchs patronised Miaphysite Christian churches and fostered sophisticated Arabic poetry until Arab Muslim armies conquered the region after the Battle of Yarmouk. \n\n Status: Foederatus kingdom of the Roman Empire; Capital: Jabiyah; Common languages: Old Arabic, Classical Syriac and Greek; Religion: Miaphysite Christianity; Government: Client monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jafnid dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late antiquity; Established: 251 AD; Disestablished: 20 August 636

name: Gupta Empire
description: The Gupta Empire was a pre-eminent classical Indian state established in the mid-3rd century AD by King Gupta, with its imperial capital situated at Pataliputra in the Gangetic basin. Reaching its zenith under monarchs such as Samudragupta and Chandragupta II, the empire unified northern and central India through military campaigns, diplomatic matrimonial ties and a decentralised administrative framework. The Gupta era witnessed an extraordinary flowering of Sanskrit literature, mathematics, astronomy and classical temple architecture, establishing enduring artistic standards across the subcontinent before nomadic invasions by the Hunas triggered its political decline. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Pataliputra; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Vaishnavite Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Gupta dynasty; Ruler title: Maharajadhiraja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 240 AD; Disestablished: 551 AD

name: Kingdom of Lazica
description: The Kingdom of Lazica, known natively as Egrisi, was an ancient Georgian realm in western Georgia that evolved out of the earlier kingdom of Colchis along the Black Sea coast. Governed from the fortified mountain citadel of Archaeopolis, the kingdom operated as a key Christian vassal of the Roman Empire, securing the Caucasus passes against steppe incursions and Persian expansionism. Lazica maintained internal dynastic governance while relying on Roman naval subsidies and military contingents, serving as a fierce battleground between Rome and Sasanian Persia during the prolonged Lazic War of the 6th century. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Roman Empire; Capital: Archaeopolis; Common languages: Zan, Old Georgian and Greek; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy and Georgian polytheism; Government: Client monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical antiquity to Late antiquity; Established: 131 AD; Disestablished: 563 AD

name: Vakataka Dynasty
description: The Vakataka Dynasty was a major classical Indian royal house founded around 250 AD by Vindhyashakti in the Deccan, succeeding to the former domains of the Satavahanas. Administering their territory from capital centres including Nandivardhana and Vatsagulma, the Vakatakas forged crucial dynastic alliances with the imperial Guptas and extended their influence from the Arabian Sea to the borders of Chhattisgarh. The dynasty is celebrated for its deep patronage of the arts, literature and religious public works, most prominently commissioning the magnificent rock-cut Buddhist viharas and chaityas at the Ajanta Caves. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Nandivardhana; Common languages: Maharashtri Prakrit and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Vakataka dynasty; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 250 AD; Disestablished: 544 AD

name: Veracruz Culture
label: mesoamerican polities
description: The Veracruz Culture was an influential pre-Columbian civilisation that flourished along the Gulf Coast lowlands of modern Mexico, concentrated across the Papaloapan River basin and the coastal plains. Functioning as a decentralised network of independent ceremonial centres rather than a unified empire, the culture built monumental civic plazas, ballcourts and tiered pyramids at sites such as Cerro de las Mesas and El Tajin. The society is celebrated for its sophisticated hieroglyphic inscriptions, advanced calendrical records and distinctive ceremonial stone sculptures, including intricately carved yokes, hachas and palmas associated with the Mesoamerican ballgame. \n\n Status: Sovereign archaeological culture; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Mixe-Zoquean and Totonacan; Religion: Mesoamerican polytheism; Government: Theocratic ceremonial centres; Historical era: Classic Mesoamerica; Established: 251 AD; Disestablished: 1001 AD

name: Kingdom of Armenia
description: The Kingdom of Armenia was subjected to repeated periods of Sasanian Persian clientage and indirect imperial rule across the 3rd and 4th centuries AD. Following the campaigns of Shapur I, Sasanian monarchs intermittently ousted pro-Roman Arsacid rulers, placing Persian princely governors on the Armenian throne and establishing administrative headquarters at Dvin. Despite aggressive Persian efforts to promote Zoroastrianism and dismantle native noble resistance, the Armenian aristocracy preserved its Christian identity and feudal nakharar institutions until the Sasanian crown formally abolished the monarchy in 428, reorganising the realm into a Persian marzpanate. \n\n Status: Client kingdom of the Sasanian Empire; Capital: Dvin; Common languages: Armenian, Middle Persian and Parthian; Religion: Armenian Christianity and Zoroastrianism; Government: Client monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Arsacid dynasty of Armenia; Historical era: Late antiquity; Established: 253 AD; Disestablished: 428 AD

name: Gallic Empire
label: crisis of the third century
description: The Gallic Empire was a sovereign breakaway state of the Roman world established on 1 October 260 AD when General Postumus was acclaimed emperor amidst barbarian invasions and administrative chaos in Rome. Encompassing the western provinces of Gaul, Britannia, Germania and temporarily Hispania, the empire governed from Rhine administrative centres at Cologne and Trier with its own senate, praetorian guard and consuls. Designed to provide effective local defence along the northern Rhine frontier rather than overthrow central Rome, the Gallic state endured until Emperor Aurelian defeated Tetricus I at the Battle of Chalons in 274. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Cologne, later Trier; Official languages: Latin; Common languages: Latin and Gaulish; Religion: Roman polytheism and imperial cult; Government: Military autocracy; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Crisis of the Third Century; Established: 1 October 260; Disestablished: 1 April 274

name: Kingdom of Iberia
description: The Kingdom of Iberia, known natively as Kartli in eastern Georgia, functioned as a strategic Caucasian client realm under Sasanian Persian suzerainty during several distinct phases of late antiquity. Occupying key trans-Caucasian mountain passes between the Black and Caspian seas, the Iberian monarchy maintained domestic feudal administration while paying tribute and fielding military levies for the Sasanian King of Kings. Despite intense imperial Persian religious and fiscal pressures, the Georgian nobility staunchly maintained their Christian church and royal traditions until Sasanian king Hormizd IV abolished the monarchy in 580, placing the territory under a Persian governor. \n\n Status: Client kingdom of the Sasanian Empire; Capital: None recorded; Common languages: Old Georgian, Middle Persian and Greek; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy and Zoroastrianism; Government: Client monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Chosroid dynasty; Historical era: Late antiquity; Established: 261 AD; Disestablished: 580 AD

name: Jin
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: The Jin dynasty was an imperial Chinese realm founded on 2 August 266 AD by Sima Yan, who usurped the throne of Cao Wei to establish the Western Jin at Luoyang. Reunifying China in 280 through the conquest of Eastern Wu, the dynasty soon fractured in the civil strife of the Eight Princes, allowing northern nomadic rebellions to sack the capital. Imperial survivors relocated south to Jiankang, modern Nanjing, establishing the Eastern Jin, which preserved classical Han cultural and bureaucratic traditions until Liu Yu established the Liu Song dynasty in 420. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Luoyang, later Nanjing; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Eastern Han Chinese; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Sima; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Six Dynasties; Established: 2 August 266; Disestablished: 7 July 420

name: Kingdom of Palmyra
label: crisis of the third century
description: The Kingdom of Palmyra, often designated the Palmyrene Empire, was a short-lived breakaway realm proclaimed in 270 AD by Queen Zenobia and her son Vaballathus in the Syrian desert oasis of Palmyra. Capitalising on the Crisis of the Third Century, Palmyrene armies launched rapid campaigns that wrested control of Syria, Palestine, Egypt and southern Anatolia from central Roman authority. Zenobia ruled from her opulent caravan metropolis, patronising philosophers and maintaining disciplined heavy cataphract cavalry until Emperor Aurelian conducted a vigorous counter-offensive, capturing Palmyra and parading the captured queen in Rome in 274. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Palmyra; Common languages: Palmyrene Aramaic, Koine Greek and Latin; Religion: Semitic polytheism and Greco-Roman syncretism; Government: Imperial autocracy; Ruler title: Augusta; Head of state: Queen Zenobia; Historical era: Crisis of the Third Century; Established: 1 November 270; Disestablished: 274 AD

name: Kingdom of the Ostrogoths
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Ostrogoths, representing the early Greuthungi branch of the Gothic people, established sovereign dominion across the Pontic steppe and the Dnieper basin north of the Black Sea from 272 AD. Centred near coastal trading hubs such as Olbia and associated archaeologically with the Chernyakhov culture, the kingdom developed into an expansive multi-ethnic confederation encompassing Slavs, Sarmatians and Dacians. Under the formidable king Ermanaric in the 4th century, the realm dominated inland European trade routes until the devastating onslaught of the nomadic Huns destroyed Ostrogothic hegemony around 377. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal kingdom; Capital: Olbia; Common languages: Gothic, East Germanic, Sarmatian and Greek; Religion: Germanic paganism; Government: Tribal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Migration Period; Established: 272 AD; Disestablished: 377 AD

name: Tuyuhun Kingdom
description: The Tuyuhun Kingdom was an enduring pastoral state founded in 285 AD around Qinghai Lake and the Qilian Mountains by Murong Tuyuhun, a chieftain of the Xianbei people. Governing their diverse realm from the walled city of Fusi, the monarchs ruled over a multi-ethnic population of Xianbei, Qiang and Tibetan pastoralists, controlling strategic northern branches of the Silk Road. The kingdom accumulated substantial wealth through livestock breeding, horse trading and copper mining, preserving its sovereign autonomy through skilful diplomacy with Chinese dynasties until Tang military expeditions subdued the realm in 635. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Fusi; Common languages: Tuyuhun and Mongolic; Religion: Shamanism, Tengrism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Khagan; Historical era: Six Dynasties; Established: 285 AD; Disestablished: 635 AD

name: Roman Empire
label: civil wars of the tetrarchy
description: The Roman Empire under Diocletian between 286 and 306 designates the eastern administrative domain established by the senior Augustus to inaugurate the system of the Tetrarchy. Administering his territory from the Bithynian capital of Nicomedia, Diocletian overhauled imperial governance by expanding the imperial bureaucracy, separating civil and military commands and introducing rigorous price controls and tax reforms. As the supreme architect of the Dominate, Diocletian defended the Danubian and Persian frontiers alongside his junior Caesar Galerius, providing administrative stability to the eastern Mediterranean until his unprecedented voluntary abdication in 305. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Nicomedia; Official languages: Latin; Common languages: Koine Greek and Latin; Religion: Roman polytheism and imperial cult; Government: Autocratic dominate; Ruling dynasty: Jovian dynasty; Ruler title: Augustus; Head of state: Diocletian; Historical era: Late antiquity; Established: 286 AD; Disestablished: 306 AD

name: Roman Empire
label: civil wars of the tetrarchy
description: The Roman Empire under Maximian comprised the western imperial realm established in 286 AD when Diocletian elevated Maximian as his co-Augustus to govern Italy, Hispania and North Africa. Operating primarily from administrative centres at Milan and Rome, Maximian exercised supreme military authority across the western provinces, successfully suppressing the Bagaudae insurgencies in Gaul and repelling Germanic tribal confederacies along the Rhine. Maximian reinforced frontier defences and pacified Berber insurrections in Mauretania, sustaining western administrative coherence until being compelled by Diocletian to abdicate his imperial office at Milan in May 305. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Rome; Official languages: Latin; Common languages: Latin and Celtic; Religion: Roman polytheism and imperial cult; Government: Autocratic dominate; Ruling dynasty: Herculian dynasty; Ruler title: Augustus; Head of state: Maximian; Historical era: Late antiquity; Established: 286 AD; Disestablished: 306 AD

name: Roman Empire
label: civil wars of the tetrarchy
description: The Roman Empire under Constantius Chlorus designates the north-western territorial command created within the Tetrarchy in 293 and 294 AD, encompassing Gaul, Britannia and the Rhine frontier. Governing from his imperial palace at Augusta Treverorum, modern Trier, Constantius restored imperial authority by recapturing the breakaway Britannic Empire under Carausius and Allectus and fortifying the Rhenish borderlands against Frankish incursions. Known for his administrative moderation and reluctant enforcement of anti-Christian persecutions, Constantius ruled as senior western Augustus from 305 until his death while campaigning at Eboracum, modern York, in 306. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Augusta Treverorum; Official languages: Latin; Common languages: Latin, Celtic and Germanic; Religion: Roman polytheism and Sol Invictus; Government: Autocratic dominate; Ruling dynasty: Constantinian dynasty; Ruler title: Caesar, later Augustus; Head of state: Constantius Chlorus; Historical era: Late antiquity; Established: 294 AD; Disestablished: 307 AD

name: Roman Empire
label: civil wars of the tetrarchy
description: The Roman Empire under Galerius comprised the Balkan and Danubian administrative sphere established in 293 and 294 AD under the original Tetrarchic partition instituted by Diocletian. Operating from his fortified regional capital at Sirmium, modern Sremska Mitrovica, Galerius commanded the Danubian limes, repelling incursions by the Sarmatians and Carpi before winning a decisive victory against the Sasanian king Narseh in 298. Elevated to senior Augustus in 305, he struggled to preserve the crumbling Tetrarchic college against multiple usurpations, ultimately issuing the Edict of Serdica in 311 to concede official toleration to Christians. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Sirmium; Official languages: Latin; Common languages: Latin and Koine Greek; Religion: Roman polytheism and imperial cult; Government: Autocratic dominate; Ruling dynasty: Jovian dynasty; Ruler title: Caesar, later Augustus; Head of state: Galerius; Historical era: Late antiquity; Established: 294 AD; Disestablished: 312 AD

name: Chouchi Kingdom
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: The Chouchi Kingdom was an autonomous mountain principality established in 297 AD by the Di ethnic Yang clan in the rugged borderlands of modern southern Gansu and northern Sichuan. Administered from fortified mountain redoubts including Chouchi and regional centres such as Hanzhong, the state skilfully leveraged its inaccessible alpine terrain to survive the conflicts of the Sixteen Kingdoms period. The Yang rulers maintained independent governance by playing northern dynasties against southern courts, preserving local autonomy until the expanding Northern Wei permanently subdued the realm in 443. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Hanzhong; Common languages: Di and Middle Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion, Buddhism and Taoism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Yang clan; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 296 AD; Disestablished: 443 AD

name: Chiefdom of Mu'ege
label: four great native chiefdoms in guizhou
description: The Chiefdom of Mu'ege was an enduring Nasu Yi indigenous realm established around 300 AD across the highland karst plateaus of modern western Guizhou. Governed by hereditary clan chieftains from mountain strongholds such as Mugebaizhage in modern Dafang, Mu'ege developed into the most powerful tribal polity in south-western China, renowned historically as the Shuixi chieftaincy. The chiefdom preserved sovereign tribal autonomy through its disciplined indigenous warrior levies and mountainous terrain, cultivating distinct Bimoist religious rites and Nasu scripts for nearly a millennium before being integrated into imperial China's tributary tusi administrative framework. \n\n Status: Sovereign native chiefdom; Capital: None recorded; Historical region: Guizhou and Southwest China; Common languages: Nasu Yi; Religion: Bimoism and animism; Government: Hereditary tribal chiefdom; Ruler title: Chieftain; Historical era: Antiquity to Middle Ages; Established: 300 AD; Disestablished: 1373 AD

name: Djenné-Djenno
description: Djenne-Djenno was an ancient urban settlement established in the fertile Inland Niger Delta of modern Mali, flourishing as one of the earliest urbanised centres in sub-Saharan West Africa. Developed by ancestral Mande and Bozo communities, the city expanded into a sprawling occupational mound supported by domesticated African rice agriculture, advanced terracotta craftsmanship and iron metallurgy. Remarkably organised without evidence of centralised monarchical palaces or a rigid military aristocracy, Djenne-Djenno anchored extensive regional and trans-Saharan trading routes in copper, gold and dried fish centuries before northern Islamic trading contacts were initiated. \n\n Status: Sovereign urban polity; Capital: Djenné; Common languages: Proto-Mande and Bozo; Religion: West African traditional animism; Government: Egalitarian corporate urban federation; Historical era: Classical West African antiquity; Established: 301 AD; Disestablished: 901 AD

name: Federation of the Ripuarian Franks
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Federation of the Ripuarian Franks comprised an autonomous league of Germanic tribes established along the Middle Rhine basin around the former Roman provincial capital of Cologne. Operating independently from their western Salian kin, the Ripuarian Franks fortified strategic river crossings, cultivated fertile agricultural valleys and codified their own distinct customs in the Lex Ripuaria. Governed by native royal houses such as that of King Sigobert the Lame, the federation maintained independent political status until King Clovis I orchestrated the incorporation of Cologne into a unified Frankish kingdom around 511. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal federation; Capital: Cologne; Common languages: Old Frankish and Latin; Religion: Germanic paganism, later Nicene Christianity; Government: Tribal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Migration Period; Established: 301 AD; Disestablished: 511 AD

name: Federation of the Salian Franks
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Federation of the Salian Franks was an early Germanic tribal league that coalesced along the Lower Rhine delta and settled across Toxandria in modern Belgium and the Netherlands. Governed from regional strongholds such as Tournai, these riverine warriors established agrarian settlements and maintained loose confederated leadership under tribal chieftains. The federation clashed frequently with Roman border legions while also negotiating settlement rights in exchange for securing northern waterways, retaining sovereign tribal freedom until Caesar Julian defeated them in 358 and formally incorporated them as imperial foederati. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal federation; Capital: Tournai; Common languages: Old Frankish and Latin; Religion: Germanic paganism; Government: Tribal chieftaincy; Ruler title: Chieftain; Historical era: Migration Period; Established: 301 AD; Disestablished: 359 AD

name: Kingdom of Arakan
description: The Kingdom of Arakan was an independent coastal realm situated along the rugged Rakhine littoral between the Bay of Bengal and the Arakan Mountains in western Myanmar. Beginning with the ancient dynasties of Dhanyawadi and Waithali and culminating in the fortified capital of Mrauk U, the state served as a vital cultural and commercial bridge connecting Indian and Southeast Asian civilisations. Arakan maintained a powerful naval fleet, traded across the Indian Ocean and patronised Theravada Buddhism alongside Mahayana and Hindu court traditions, tenaciously guarding its sovereignty against Burmese and Bengali inland powers across many centuries. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Mrauk U; Common languages: Arakanese, Sanskrit and Pali; Religion: Theravada Buddhism, Mahayana Buddhism and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical era to early modern era; Established: 301 AD; Disestablished: 1517 AD

name: Kingdom of Kibi
description: The Kingdom of Kibi was an autonomous 4th-century regional state located across the fertile plains and coastal inlets of modern Okayama Prefecture along the Seto Inland Sea. Commanding rich agricultural lands and advanced iron smelting technology, Kibi emerged as a formidable political and cultural rival to the burgeoning Yamato court in the Kinai region. The rulers of Kibi erected colossal keyhole-shaped burial mounds, most notably the Tsukuriyama Kofun, demonstrating immense mobilised labour and wealth before the centralising Yamato polity gradually subjugated the dynasty and partitioned Kibi into smaller administrative provinces. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Okayama; Common languages: Old Japanese; Religion: Shinto animism; Government: Tribal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Kofun period; Established: 301 AD; Disestablished: 401 AD

name: Lakhmid Kingdom
description: The Lakhmid Kingdom was an influential Arab dynasty that established sovereign regional governance across southern Mesopotamia and north-eastern Arabia, ruling from their renowned desert capital at Al-Hira. Governed by the Nasrid dynasty of the Banu Lakhm, the kingdom guarded the western desert frontiers of the Sasanian Empire, fielding mobile cavalry units against Roman foederati, particularly the rival Ghassanids. Al-Hira developed into a glittering centre of pre-Islamic Arabic poetry, scholarship and Christian worship under the Church of the East until Sasanian king Khosrow II foolishly executed King al-Nu'man III in 602, abolishing the monarchy. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: None recorded; Historical region: Mesopotamia and Arabia; Common languages: Old Arabic and Classical Syriac; Religion: Church of the East and Arabian polytheism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Nasrid dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late antiquity; Established: 301 AD; Disestablished: 602 AD

name: Pan Pan Kingdom
description: The Pan Pan Kingdom was an early Indianised coastal principality established along the eastern littoral of the Malay Peninsula, encompassing territories around modern Pattani and the Gulf of Thailand. Located at a critical maritime junction along trans-isthmian portage routes, the kingdom flourished on maritime trade connecting India and China, dispatching regular tributary missions to Chinese imperial courts from the 5th century onwards. The state welcomed Brahmin scholars, endowed Hindu temples and patronised Buddhist foundations, maintaining commercial autonomy for several centuries until the expanding maritime thalassocracy of Srivijaya absorbed its territory in the late 8th century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Pattani; Common languages: Old Malay and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Indianised monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Classical Southeast Asia; Established: 3rd century AD; Disestablished: 776 AD

name: Samaskuta Kingdom
description: The Samaskuta Kingdom was an enigmatic ancient realm located in the mountainous interior of western Sumatra around the tectonic basin of modern Lake Singkarak. Mentioned in early Javanese historical chronicles such as the Pararaton, the kingdom was governed by local monarchs including King Prabhava Sangkala in the early 5th century. Benefiting from the fertile volcanic soils and upland river routes of the Minangkabau highlands, Samaskuta sustained agricultural and mining communities until regional catastrophic volcanic activity, traditionally linked with prehistoric caldera eruptions, caused widespread devastation and submerged the kingdom beneath the newly expanded lake. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Samaskuta; Common languages: Old Malayo-Polynesian and Sanskrit; Religion: Indigenous animism and early Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Head of state: King Prabhava Sangkala; Historical era: Classical antiquity; Established: 301 AD; Disestablished: 417 AD

name: Tamna
description: Tamna was an ancient maritime kingdom that ruled Jeju Island off the southern coast of the Korean Peninsula from antiquity. Governed by indigenous aristocratic clans, notably the Go lineage who bore the title of Seongju, the island state sustained an economy based on deep-sea fishing, diving, horse breeding and maritime trade across the Yellow and East China seas. Tamna maintained sovereign internal autonomy while dispatching diplomatic tribute to neighbouring peninsular powers, including Baekje and Silla, before gradually transitioning into an autonomous administrative dependency under the Goryeo dynasty in the 10th century. \n\n Status: Sovereign island kingdom; Capital: Jeju City; Common languages: Tamna and Old Korean; Religion: Korean shamanism and Buddhism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Seongju; Historical era: Three Kingdoms of Korea; Established: 301 AD; Disestablished: 939 AD

name: Usan
description: Usan, known in historical records as Usan-guk, was an insular kingdom that encompassed the volcanic island of Ulleungdo and neighbouring islets in the Sea of Japan. Centred upon the coastal haven of Dodong, the islanders lived primarily by fishing, seafaring and forest foraging, fiercely maintaining independence from peninsular Korean states. Usan's geographic isolation and hazardous coastal waters long deterred external conquest until 512 AD, when the noted Silla general Kim Isabu launched an amphibious invasion, famously using carved wooden lions to intimidate the islanders into surrendering to Silla authority. \n\n Status: Sovereign island kingdom; Capital: Dodong; Common languages: Old Korean; Religion: Korean shamanism; Government: Island monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Three Kingdoms of Korea; Established: 301 AD; Disestablished: 512 AD

name: Utkala Kingdom
description: The Utkala Kingdom was an ancient sovereign realm established across the northern and eastern coastal plains of modern Odisha and adjoining districts of West Bengal. Administering its domain from regional administrative seats including the sacred city of Dantapura, modern Jajpur, the kingdom occupied a strategic coastal corridor along the Bay of Bengal. Celebrated in early Sanskrit epic literature, Utkala derived significant wealth from salt extraction, seafaring and fertile rice agriculture, preserving its distinct political identity through successive regional dynasties before being absorbed into the Somavamshi kingdom. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Dantapura; Common languages: Sanskrit and Old Odia; Religion: Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 301 AD; Disestablished: 901 AD

name: Cheng Han
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Cheng Han was a dynastic empire established in 304 AD in south-western China by Li Xiong, a chieftain of the Ba Di ethnic minority, during the upheavals of the Sixteen Kingdoms. Centred at Chengdu in the fertile Sichuan Basin, the state was initially proclaimed as Dacheng before being renamed Han under Emperor Li Shou. Cheng Han maintained internal stability, low taxation and agrarian prosperity while northern China was engulfed in civil warfare, preserving sovereign independence for over four decades until the prominent Eastern Jin general Huan Wen mounted an expedition that conquered Chengdu in 347. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Chengdu; Common languages: Ba-Shu Chinese and Middle Chinese; Religion: Daoism, Chinese folk religion and Buddhism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Li; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 304 AD; Disestablished: 347 AD

name: Zhao
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Zhao, recorded in Chinese historiography as Han-Zhao or Former Zhao, was the first non-Han dynastic empire of the Sixteen Kingdoms, founded in 304 AD by the Southern Xiongnu leader Liu Yuan. Initially claiming the imperial mantle of Han and later adopting the dynastic title Zhao under Liu Yao, the state captured and sacked the Western Jin capitals of Luoyang and Chang'an. Governed from Chang'an, the realm integrated nomadic cavalry with traditional Chinese court bureaucracy until its defeat and destruction by rival warlord Shi Le of Later Zhao in 329. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Chang'an; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Xiongnu; Religion: Tengrism, Buddhism and Chinese folk religion; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Liu; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 304 AD; Disestablished: 329 AD

name: Roman Empire
label: civil wars of the tetrarchy
description: The Roman Empire under Severus II designates the central western territorial division of the Roman state between 306 and 307 AD during the breakdown of the Tetrarchy. Elevated to the rank of Augustus following the death of Constantius Chlorus, Severus governed Italy, the Danubian provinces and North Africa from his imperial residence at Milan. His authority was immediately challenged by the usurpation of Maxentius in Rome, prompting Severus to march south and besiege the ancient capital. However, his troops defected to their former commander Maximian, leading to Severus's capture and eventual execution in late 307. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Milan; Official languages: Latin; Common languages: Latin; Religion: Roman polytheism and imperial cult; Government: Autocratic dominate; Ruler title: Augustus; Head of state: Severus II; Historical era: Late antiquity; Established: 306 AD; Disestablished: 307 AD

name: Roman Empire
label: civil wars of the tetrarchy
description: The Roman Empire under Maximinus Daza comprised the affluent eastern dioceses of the Orient, Egypt and parts of southern Anatolia during the civil wars of the Tetrarchy. Administering his realm from Antioch, Maximinus ruled initially as Caesar under Galerius before claiming the rank of Augustus in 310 and holding the ancient titular dignity of Pharaoh of Egypt. A committed defender of traditional paganism, he enforced vigorous persecutions against Christian communities until open conflict erupted with his rival Licinius, who decisively defeated Maximinus's army at the Battle of Tzirallum in Thrace in 313. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Antioch; Official languages: Latin; Common languages: Koine Greek, Latin, Aramaic and Coptic; Religion: Roman polytheism and Hellenistic cults; Government: Autocratic dominate; Ruler title: Augustus; Head of state: Maximinus Daza; Historical era: Late antiquity; Established: 306 AD; Disestablished: 313 AD

name: Roman Empire
label: civil wars of the tetrarchy
description: The Roman Empire under Constantine I during this formative phase represents the expanding western administration that transformed classical antiquity into the Christian imperial era. Proclaimed emperor at York in 306, Constantine consolidated control over Britannia and Gaul before marching into Italy to crush his rival Maxentius at the historic Battle of the Milvian Bridge in 312. Governing from Rome, Trier and Milan, Constantine co-authored the Edict of Milan granting religious toleration, introduced the stable gold solidus currency and eventually eliminated his eastern co-ruler Licinius in 324 to reunite the entire empire under sole rule. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Rome; Official languages: Latin; Common languages: Latin and Koine Greek; Religion: Christianity and Sol Invictus; Government: Autocratic dominate; Ruling dynasty: Constantinian dynasty; Ruler title: Augustus; Head of state: Constantine I; Historical era: Late antiquity; Established: 307 AD; Disestablished: 324 AD

name: Roman Empire
label: civil wars of the tetrarchy
description: The Roman Empire under Maxentius in 308 and 309 designates the Italian imperial administration centred at Rome following the usurpation of power by the son of Maximian. Defying the Carnuntum conference that branded him an illegitimate usurper, Maxentius governed the Italian peninsula, Sicily, Corsica and Sardinia with the support of the Roman Senate and the Praetorian Guard. He invested heavily in monumental architectural renovations across Rome, including a vast public basilica and circus, before temporarily losing vital grain supplies and revenues when Domitius Alexander staged a provincial revolt in North Africa. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Roma; Official languages: Latin; Common languages: Latin; Religion: Roman polytheism and imperial cult; Government: Autocratic dominate; Ruler title: Augustus; Head of state: Maxentius; Historical era: Late antiquity; Established: 308 AD; Disestablished: 309 AD

name: Roman Empire
label: civil wars of the tetrarchy
description: The Roman Empire under Domitius Alexander comprised an autonomous breakaway regime established in 308 and 309 AD when the vicarius of Africa was acclaimed emperor by his garrison. Based in the maritime metropolis of Carthage, Alexander held sway over North Africa and the island of Sardinia. By halting critical grain and olive oil shipments to Italy, Alexander disrupted metropolitan food supplies and allied cautiously with Constantine until Maxentius dispatched a punitive expedition commanded by Rufius Volusianus that defeated the usurper and recaptured Carthage around 310. \n\n Status: Sovereign breakaway empire; Capital: Carthage; Official languages: Latin; Common languages: Latin, Punic and Berber; Religion: Roman polytheism and early Christianity; Government: Military autocracy; Ruler title: Augustus; Head of state: Domitius Alexander; Historical era: Late antiquity; Established: 309 AD; Disestablished: 311 AD

name: Roman Empire
label: civil wars of the tetrarchy
description: The Roman Empire under Maxentius during this subsequent phase represents the restored dominion over Italy and North Africa following the military reconquest of Carthage in 310 AD. Re-securing the African grain supply and fortifying northern Italian alpine routes, Maxentius sought to consolidate his legitimacy against rival Augusti Licinius and Constantine through civic munificence and religious conciliation in Rome. However, Constantine launched a rapid transalpine offensive in 312, capturing Verona and routing Maxentius's army at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge, where Maxentius drowned in the Tiber on 28 October 312. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Rome; Official languages: Latin; Common languages: Latin; Religion: Roman polytheism and imperial cult; Government: Autocratic dominate; Ruler title: Augustus; Head of state: Maxentius; Historical era: Late antiquity; Established: 309 AD; Disestablished: 28 October 312

name: Roman Empire
label: civil wars of the tetrarchy
description: The Roman Empire under Licinius designates the eastern imperial dominion that governed the Balkans, Thrace, Anatolia and the Levant between 308 and 324 AD. Appointed Augustus at the Carnuntum conference, Licinius eliminated his eastern rival Maximinus Daza in 313, establishing his imperial court at Nicomedia and co-authoring the Edict of Milan with Constantine to ensure religious peace. Although Licinius initially governed the east with administrative and fiscal competence, recurring political tensions with Constantine escalated into outright civil wars, culminating in Licinius's decisive defeat at the Battle of Chrysopolis and his execution in 325. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Nicomedia; Official languages: Latin; Common languages: Koine Greek and Latin; Religion: Roman polytheism and imperial cult; Government: Autocratic dominate; Ruler title: Augustus; Head of state: Licinius; Historical era: Late antiquity; Established: 308 AD; Disestablished: 324 AD

name: Dai
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Dai was a Xianbei principality established by the Tuoba clan across the northern frontier steppes and modern Inner Mongolia during the Sixteen Kingdoms period. Originating when chieftain Tuoba Yilu received a ducal title from the Western Jin court for military assistance, the realm maintained its administrative base around Shengle. The state preserved nomadic cavalry traditions while gradually adopting Chinese administrative practices, until conquest by the Former Qin extinguished its autonomy in 376. \n\n Status: Autonomous principality; Capital: Shengle; Common languages: Xianbei and Middle Chinese; Religion: Tengrism and ancestral veneration; Government: Nomadic monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Tuoba; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 310; Disestablished: 376; Succeeded by: Former Qin

name: Zhao
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Zhao, commonly designated in historiography as the Later Zhao, was an expansive northern Chinese empire founded by the Jie general Shi Le during the collapse of Han-Zhao. Dominating substantial portions of the Central Plains from its successive capitals at Xiangguo and Yecheng, the realm sustained powerful nomadic shock cavalry alongside heavily fortified garrison cities. Following the brutal reign and eventual demise of emperor Shi Hu, internal succession strife rapidly eroded imperial cohesion, culminating in the violent usurpation of Ran Min. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Xiangguo; Common languages: Jie and Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism and Chinese folk religion; Government: Imperial autocracy; Ruling dynasty: Shi; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 319; Disestablished: 351; Succeeded by: Ran Wei and Former Qin

name: Itzá Empire
label: mesoamerican polities
description: The Itzá Empire was an enduring Maya kingdom originally rooted in the Chontal lowlands before migrating across the Yucatán Peninsula and establishing its final island stronghold at Nojpetén on Lake Petén Itzá. Resisting European encroachment for well over a century after neighbouring domains fell, the Itzá maintained an independent hereditary monarchy deeply tied to classical ritual traditions. Their fortified lacustrine capital successfully rebuffed multiple Spanish expeditions until an assault led by Martín de Ursúa breached the island defences in 1697. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Nojpetén; Common languages: Itza Maya and Chontal Maya; Religion: Maya polytheism; Government: Sacral elective monarchy; Historical era: Classical to Postclassic Mesoamerica; Established: 321; Disestablished: 1697; Succeeded by: Captaincy General of Guatemala

name: Liang
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Liang, distinguished in historical records as the Former Liang, was an autonomous dynastic state established along the vital Hexi Corridor by the Han Chinese Zhang family. Governing from their seat at Guzang, its hereditary rulers maintained nominal fealty to the Eastern Jin dynasty as dukes of Xiping while exercising complete territorial independence across modern Gansu and eastern Xinjiang. The realm served as a critical commercial sanctuary and cultural haven until mounting pressure from the Di-led Former Qin forced its capitulation in 376. \n\n Status: Autonomous principality; Capital: Guzang; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Confucianism, Taoism and Buddhism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Zhang; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 301; Disestablished: 376; Succeeded by: Former Qin

name: Kadaram Kingdom
description: Kadaram Kingdom was an ancient Indianised maritime realm located on the north-western coast of the Malay Peninsula in present-day Kedah. Anchored around the fertile Bujang Valley and riverine trade networks, the polity prospered through intensive trans-oceanic commerce linking South Asia with the South China Sea. Regional rulers patronised Shaivite Hinduism and Mahayana Buddhism, erecting prominent brick temple sanctuaries until the kingdom became progressively integrated into the expanding thalassocracy of Srivijaya. \n\n Status: Sovereign maritime kingdom; Capital: Kedah; Common languages: Old Malay and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Indianised monarchy; Historical era: Classical Southeast Asia; Established: 330; Succeeded by: Srivijaya

name: Rouran Khaganate
description: The Rouran Khaganate was a formidable nomadic steppe confederation founded by proto-Mongolic Donghu lineages across the Mongolian Plateau and adjacent regions of Central Asia. Operating under supreme leaders who popularised the imperial title of khagan, the realm commanded pastoralist cavalry forces that collected tribute from the Hephthalites and rivalled the Northern Wei. A devastating revolt initiated by their erstwhile Göktürk blacksmith vassals shattered the khaganate in the mid-sixth century, driving splinter groups westward. \n\n Status: Nomadic confederation; Capital: Mumocheng; Common languages: Rouran, Turkic and Mongolic; Religion: Tengrism, Shamanism and Buddhism; Government: Nomadic kurultai monarchy; Ruler title: Khagan; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 330; Disestablished: 555; Succeeded by: First Turkic Khaganate

name: Ananda Gotrika
description: Ananda Gotrika was a regional dynasty that governed coastal Andhra from its capital at Kandarapura following the decline of the Andhra Ikshvakus. Founded by King Kandara, who expelled Pallava forces from the Amaravati region, the kingdom maintained sovereignty across the lower Krishna River basin for nearly a century. Royal patrons sponsored lavish Vedic sacrifices alongside Shaivite and Buddhist foundations until expansionist Salankayana monarchs absorbed their coastal territories. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kandarapura; Common languages: Sanskrit and Telugu Prakrit; Religion: Shaivism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ananda; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 335; Disestablished: 425; Succeeded by: Salankayana dynasty

name: Kingdom of the Vandals
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Vandals in Pannonia emerged when Germanic Hasdingi and Silingi bands received imperial settlement rights from Constantine the Great following their defeat along the Maros River. Stationed as frontier foederati around the provincial hub of Aquincum, these warriors pledged military service to Rome in exchange for Danubian farmland and annual subsidies. Growing instability along the imperial borders and encroaching nomadic pressures eventually prompted the Vandals to abandon Pannonia at the turn of the fifth century. \n\n Status: Roman foederatus client kingdom; Capital: Aquincum; Common languages: Vandalic and Vulgar Latin; Religion: Germanic paganism and Arian Christianity; Government: Tribal client monarchy; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 335; Disestablished: 401; Succeeded by: Western Roman Empire

name: Roman Empire
label: civil war of the constantinian dynasty
description: The Roman Empire under Dalmatius comprised a brief regional partition of imperial administration encompassing Thrace, Macedonia and Achaea during the tumultuous succession that followed the demise of Constantine the Great. Appointed as a caesar by his imperial uncle in 335, Dalmatius directed Balkan border defences from his headquarters at Naissus. His reign ended abruptly within three months when provincial legionaries staged a dynastic purge that slaughtered Constantine's collateral relatives and partitioned their territorial allotments. \n\n Status: Imperial administrative division; Capital: Naissus; Common languages: Latin and Ancient Greek; Religion: Nicene Christianity; Government: Autocratic tetrarchic monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Constantinian; Head of state: Dalmatius; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 23 May 337; Disestablished: 25 August 337

name: Roman Empire
label: civil war of the constantinian dynasty
description: The Roman Empire under Constantine II encompassed the western praetorian prefectures of Gaul, Hispania and Britain following the tripartite division arranged among Constantine the Great's surviving sons. Operating from his administrative capital at Augusta Treverorum, Constantine claimed senior authority over his younger brothers and guarded the Rhine limes. Tensions escalated into open warfare when he marched an army into northern Italy against Constans, suffering defeat and death in an ambush near Aquileia. \n\n Status: Imperial administrative division; Capital: Augusta Treverorum; Common languages: Latin and Celtic dialects; Religion: Christianity; Government: Imperial autocracy; Ruling dynasty: Constantinian; Head of state: Constantine II; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 23 May 337; Disestablished: 340; Succeeded by: Constans

name: Roman Empire
label: civil war of the constantinian dynasty
description: The Roman Empire under Constans initially encompassed Italy, Illyricum and North Africa before expanding across Gaul, Hispania and Britain after the fall of Constantine II. Ruling primarily from Mediolanum, Constans championed orthodox Nicene Christianity, conducted campaigns against the Franks and became the final legitimate reigning emperor to visit Britain. Discontent within the Gallic army culminated in an insurrection led by the general Magnentius, who deposed and executed the emperor near the Pyrenean border. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Mediolanum; Common languages: Latin; Religion: Nicene Christianity; Government: Imperial autocracy; Ruling dynasty: Constantinian; Head of state: Constans; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 23 May 337; Disestablished: 350; Succeeded by: Magnentius

name: Roman Empire
label: civil war of the constantinian dynasty
description: The Roman Empire under Constantius II embraced the wealthy eastern provinces, Thrace and Egypt following the imperial partition that commenced upon his father's death. Ruling from Constantinople, Constantius engaged in prolonged and costly defensive operations against the Sasanian Empire along the Mesopotamian frontier. After western usurpers eliminated his brothers, he mobilised imperial armies, crushed Magnentius in a brutal civil war and briefly re-established unified autocracy across the Roman world. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Constantinople; Common languages: Greek and Latin; Religion: Semi-Arian Christianity; Government: Imperial autocracy; Ruling dynasty: Constantinian; Head of state: Constantius II; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 23 May 337; Disestablished: 353

name: Yan
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Yan, remembered in historiography as the Former Yan, was a northern Chinese realm founded by the Murong clan of the Xianbei from their traditional redoubt in Liaoning. Expanding southwestward through disciplined horse-archer armies, the state conquered Ran Wei, seized control of the Central Plains and proclaimed imperial dignity from Jicheng before shifting to Yecheng. Murong rule unified significant portions of northern China until political intrigue and military overextension left the empire vulnerable to complete conquest by the Former Qin in 370. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Yecheng; Common languages: Xianbei and Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism, Confucianism and Shamanism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Murong; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 23 November 337; Disestablished: 370; Succeeded by: Former Qin

name: Kadamba Dynasty
description: The Kadamba Dynasty was an indigenous Kannadiga royal house that established an independent kingdom in northern Karnataka and the coastal Konkan with its capital at Banavasi. Founded by Mayurasharma after defying the suzerainty of the Pallavas of Kanchi, the dynasty fostered administrative regionalism and patronised early Kannada literature alongside Sanskrit learning. Kadamba authority flourished through advantageous marital alliances with the imperial Guptas and Vakatakas before bowing to the Chalukyas of Badami in the mid-sixth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Banavasi; Common languages: Kannada and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kadamba; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 345; Disestablished: 540; Succeeded by: Chalukya dynasty

name: Gauda Kingdom
description: The Gauda Kingdom was an early medieval regional realm centred in Bengal with its principal royal seat at Karnasuvarna. Emerging from the fragmentation of imperial Gupta dominion, the polity achieved geopolitical prominence under King Shashanka, who established Shaivite institutions and vigorously contested supremacy against Harsha of Kanauj. Gauda maintained distinct regional coinage and administrative structures across the lower Ganges Delta until internal anarchy yielded to the rise of the Pala Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Karnasuvarna; Common languages: Sanskrit and Proto-Bengali; Religion: Shaivism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharajadhiraja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 351; Disestablished: 841; Succeeded by: Pala Empire

name: Ghana Empire
description: The Ghana Empire, known historically to its Soninke founders as Wagadu, was a major Sahelian imperial realm situated in present-day south-eastern Mauritania and western Mali. Governing from the bustling commercial metropolis of Koumbi Saleh, the ruling dynasty derived immense wealth and prestige by monopolising the trans-Saharan gold and salt trade networks. The empire maintained powerful cavalry levies and tributary vassal networks until nomadic incursions, trade disruptions and regional rebellions facilitated its eventual absorption by imperial Mali. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Koumbi Saleh; Common languages: Soninke and Mande; Religion: Traditional African religion and Islam; Government: Feudal monarchy; Historical era: Classical to Post-classical West Africa; Established: 350; Disestablished: 1240; Succeeded by: Mali Empire and Sosso Empire

name: Kamarupa Kingdom
description: Kamarupa Kingdom was the premier historical state of the Brahmaputra Valley, emerging in ancient Assam under the Varman dynasty founded by Pushyavarman. First recorded as an autonomous frontier ally on the Allahabad pillar of Gupta emperor Samudragupta, the realm developed sophisticated agricultural and administrative infrastructure around its capital at Pragjyotishpura. It successfully absorbed neighbouring Davaka and maintained vigorous cultural and diplomatic exchanges across northern India until succession shifts ushered in the Mlechchha dynasty. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Pragjyotishpura; Common languages: Kamarupi Prakrit and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Animism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Varman; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 350; Disestablished: 1258; Succeeded by: Kamata kingdom and Ahom kingdom

name: Kingdom of the Gepids
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Gepids was an early East Germanic polity established across the Carpathian Basin and Middle Danube frontier during the fourth century. Originating as a regional tribal confederation bordering Roman Dacia and Pannonia, the Gepids maintained a warlike monarchy anchored around fortified riverine settlements. Encroaching Hunnic expansion from the eastern steppes soon engulfed their independent dominion, incorporating Gepid warrior contingents into the imperial host of the Huns until the mid-fifth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal kingdom; Capital: Sirmium; Common languages: East Germanic and Latin; Religion: Germanic paganism; Government: Tribal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Migration Period; Established: 350; Disestablished: 377; Succeeded by: Hunnic Empire

name: Qi
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Qi, known in Chinese historiography as Duan Qi, was a short-lived regional state established on the Shandong Peninsula by the Xianbei general Duan Kan. Seizing territorial control amid the chaotic disintegration of the Later Zhao empire, Duan proclaimed himself King of Qi and governed independently from local strongholds. Despite briefly offering nominal allegiance to the Eastern Jin court to stave off northern rivals, the regime collapsed when the invading forces of Former Yan besieged and overran the peninsula in 356. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Linzi; Common languages: Xianbei and Middle Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion and Buddhism; Government: Military monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Duan; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 350; Disestablished: 356; Succeeded by: Former Yan

name: Roman Empire
label: civil war of the constantinian dynasty
description: The Roman Empire under Magnentius functioned as a rebellious western regime that seized control over Gaul, Hispania, Britain and Italy following the overthrow of Constans in 350. Proclaimed Augustus by Gallic troops at Augustodunum, Magnentius operated without a fixed capital, commanding his armies directly from mobile field headquarters across the western provinces. His refusal to accept subordinate status triggered a ruinous civil conflict with Constantius II, culminating in devastating battlefield defeats and his suicide at Mons Seleucus. \n\n Status: Contested imperial regime; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Latin; Religion: Christianity and Roman paganism; Government: Military autocracy; Head of state: Magnentius; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 350; Disestablished: 3 July 353; Succeeded by: Roman Empire

name: Wei
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Wei, designated in historical annals as Ran Wei, was an ephemeral northern Chinese state established by the Han Chinese general Ran Min following his violent usurpation of the Later Zhao throne. Operating from the fortified capital of Ye, Ran promulgated fierce edicts that triggered widespread slaughter of nomadic Jie and Xianbei populations throughout the Central Plains. Lacking enduring institutional support and beset by hostile neighbours, the regime was swiftly eradicated when Murong Jun led the horsemen of Former Yan to victory at Liantai. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Ye; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Chinese folk religion and Taoism; Government: Military autocracy; Ruling dynasty: Ran; Head of state: Ran Min; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 350; Disestablished: 8 September 352; Succeeded by: Former Yan

name: Western Ganga Dynasty
description: The Western Ganga Dynasty was a prominent royal lineage of ancient Karnataka that achieved sovereignty amid the geopolitical retreat of Pallava authority across southern India. Governing initially from Kolar before transferring their royal seat to Talakad along the Kaveri River, the Ganga rulers patronised Digambara Jainism, advanced irrigation works and built exquisite stone architecture. The kingdom maintained fierce regional independence before accommodating the suzerainty of the imperial Chalukyas and Rashtrakutas in later centuries. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Talakad; Common languages: Kannada and Sanskrit; Religion: Jainism and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Western Ganga; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 350; Disestablished: 1004; Succeeded by: Western Chalukya Empire and Chola Dynasty

name: Qin
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Qin, recognised in Chinese historiography as the Former Qin, was a powerful northern dynasty founded by the Fu clan of Di ethnicity amid the collapse of the Later Zhao. Under the leadership of Fu Jiān and his prime minister Wang Meng, the empire operated from Chang'an and achieved the unprecedented feat of unifying all of northern China under one throne. This hard-won hegemony disintegrated catastrophically after imperial forces suffered a rout at the Battle of Fei River in 383, igniting widespread ethnic rebellions. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Chang'an; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Di; Religion: Buddhism, Confucianism and Taoism; Government: Imperial autocracy; Ruling dynasty: Fu; Ruler title: Heavenly King; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 351; Disestablished: 394; Succeeded by: Later Yan and Later Qin

name: Kingdom of the Franks
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of the Franks was the largest post-Roman realm in Western Europe, originating when Salian Frankish warbands settled along the lower Rhine and Meuse rivers. Under the Merovingian dynamic leader Clovis I, the kingdom unified disparate Germanic tribes, embraced Chalcedonian Catholicism and drove the Visigoths from southern Gaul. Subsequent Carolingian restructuring expanded Frankish authority into central Europe, culminating when Charlemagne received the imperial crown in Rome on Christmas Day in 800. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Tournai, Paris and Aachen; Common languages: Frankish, Old High German and Vulgar Latin; Religion: Nicene Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Merovingian and Carolingian; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 359; Reorganised: 25 December 800; Succeeded by: Carolingian Empire

name: Tarumanagara Kingdom
description: Tarumanagara Kingdom was an early Sundanese Indianised realm situated in western Java, representing one of the earliest historically documented civilisations in the Indonesian archipelago. Anchored around its administrative centre at Sundapura near modern Jakarta, the state flourished under King Purnawarman, who recorded major hydraulic projects and religious endowments on rock inscriptions. The kingdom controlled maritime approaches to the Sunda Strait until weakening dynasties yielded their paramount status to the emergent Sunda Kingdom. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Sundapura; Common languages: Old Sundanese and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism, Buddhism and Sunda Wiwitan; Government: Indianised monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Classical Southeast Asia; Established: 358; Disestablished: 669; Succeeded by: Sunda Kingdom and Galuh Kingdom

name: Yaxchilan
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Yaxchilan was a dominant Classic Maya city-state established along a pronounced meander of the Usumacinta River in present-day Chiapas, Mexico. The kingdom exercised extensive hegemony over neighbouring secondary sites such as Bonampak while waging enduring dynastic conflicts against its chief regional rival, Piedras Negras. Renowned for its elaborately carved limestone lintels and hieroglyphic stairways erected under charismatic rulers like Bird Jaguar IV, the city experienced terminal political fragmentation early in the ninth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Yaxchilan; Common languages: Classic Maya; Religion: Maya polytheism; Government: Sacral city-state monarchy; Ruler title: Ajaw; Historical era: Classic Mesoamerica; Established: 23 July 359; Disestablished: 802

name: Alchon Huns
description: The Alchon Huns were a nomadic warrior confederation that established expansive dominions across Central Asia, Bactria and north-western India during Late Antiquity. Moving southward through the Hindu Kush passes, they displaced the Kidarites and drove deep into the Punjab and the Gangetic plains, delivering fatal shocks to the Gupta Empire. Led by formidable conquerors such as Toramana and Mihirakula from royal encampments and capitals like Sakala, the dynasty minted distinctive portraits before succumbing to regional Indian counter-offensives. \n\n Status: Nomadic empire; Capital: Sakala; Common languages: Bactrian; Religion: Hinduism, Buddhism and Zoroastrianism; Government: Nomadic military monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 370; Disestablished: 601; Succeeded by: Nezak Huns and Hephthalites

name: Hunnic Empire
description: The Hunnic Empire was a formidable nomadic steppe confederation that swept out of Inner Asia, subjugated the Alans and Goths north of the Black Sea and dominated the middle Danubian plains. Operating from mobile pastoral courts in the Hungarian basin, Hunnic chieftains subjected neighbouring Germanic tribes to strict vassalage and extracted enormous gold tributes from the Eastern Roman Empire. Under King Attila, the empire waged audacious campaigns into Gaul and Italy before fracturing irrecoverably following his death and the Battle of Nedao. \n\n Status: Nomadic confederation; Capital: Attila's Court; Common languages: Hunnic, Gothic and Sarmatian; Religion: Tengrism and Shamanism; Government: Tribal khaganate monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Migration Period; Established: 370; Disestablished: 469; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Gepids and Ostrogothic Kingdom

name: Kidarite Kingdom
description: The Kidarite Kingdom was an early Huna dynastic realm that established dominance across ancient Bactria, Gandhara and adjacent stretches of the upper Indus Valley. Supplanting the Kushano-Sasanians, the rulers styled themselves as heirs to Kushan imperial prestige and minted silver coinage bearing distinctively crown-topped portraits. The realm waged continuous defensive wars against the Sasanian monarchy to the west and Indian powers to the south until pressure from the encroaching Hephthalites extinguished their statehood. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Balkh; Common languages: Bactrian; Religion: Zoroastrianism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Kushanshah; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 360; Disestablished: 468; Succeeded by: Hephthalite Empire and Alchon Huns

name: Traikutaka Dynasty
description: The Traikutaka Dynasty was an Indian royal house that ruled northern Konkan, Aparanta and the coastal reaches of southern Gujarat and northern Maharashtra. Establishing their principal seat at Aniruddhapur, its monarchs emerged as autonomous sovereigns following the retreat of the Western Satraps, whose coinage designs they adapted with Sanskrit and Brahmi legends. Royal inscriptions commemorate extensive Shaivite patronages and Vedic horse sacrifices before the dynasty lost primacy to the expanding Vakataka and Maitraka regimes. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Aniruddhapur; Common languages: Sanskrit and Maharashtri Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Traikutaka; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 371; Disestablished: 457; Succeeded by: Maitraka dynasty and Kalachuris

name: Kingdom of the Ostrogoths
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Ostrogoths in Moesia was established when Greuthungi and Thervingi Gothic warbands entered an imperial foedus with Eastern Roman emperor Theodosius I following the Battle of Adrianople. Settled across Lower Moesia and Scythia Minor around Svishtov, Gothic warriors provided auxiliary defence along the Danube frontier while retaining internal autonomy under tribal commanders. Rising discontent over Roman food provisions and imperial court intrigue eventually spurred these federates to abandon their Danubian settlements for western campaigns. \n\n Status: Roman foederatus client kingdom; Capital: Svishtov; Common languages: Gothic, Vulgar Latin and Greek; Religion: Arian Christianity; Government: Tribal client monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 3 October 382; Disestablished: 403; Succeeded by: Roman Empire

name: Qin
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Qin, known in Chinese historiography as the Later Qin, was a major northern dynastic state established by the Qiang chieftain Yao Chang following the defeat of Former Qin at the Fei River. Governing from the historic imperial metropolis of Chang'an, the realm held sway over modern Shaanxi and Henan while reducing numerous neighbouring regimes to tributary vassalage. Under emperor Yao Xing, the court became a renowned centre of Buddhist translation and scholarship led by the monk Kumarajiva before surrendering to the Jin general Liu Yu. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Chang'an; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Qiang; Religion: Buddhism and Chinese folk religion; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Yao; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 384; Disestablished: 417; Succeeded by: Great Xia and Jin Dynasty

name: Yan
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Yan, remembered in historiography as the Western Yan, was a turbulent Xianbei dynastic state founded by Murong Hong in the immediate aftermath of the Former Qin collapse. Initially formed by relocated Xianbei warrior families attempting to march back to their north-eastern homeland, the state captured and briefly occupied Chang'an before relocating eastward to Zhangzi in Shanxi. Marked by persistent military revolts and rapid changes of monarchs, Western Yan was ultimately conquered and annexed by the rival Later Yan emperor Murong Chui. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Chang'an and Zhangzi; Common languages: Xianbei and Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism and Shamanism; Government: Military monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Murong; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 384; Disestablished: 394; Succeeded by: Later Yan

name: Yan
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Yan, designated as the Later Yan in Chinese historiography, was a powerful northern dynasty founded by Murong Chui as a deliberate restoration of the Former Yan imperium. Establishing its initial imperial seat at Zhongshan, the state reclaimed extensive swathes of the Central Plains across Hebei, Henan and Liaoning. A catastrophic defeat against the ascendant Tuoba Northern Wei at Canhe Slope in 395 shattered imperial authority, forcing the remaining Murong court to retreat to their northern fortress capital at Longcheng. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Zhongshan and Longcheng; Common languages: Xianbei and Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism and Confucianism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Murong; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 384; Disestablished: 409; Succeeded by: Northern Wei and Northern Yan

name: Qin
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Qin, styled in historiographical accounts as the Western Qin, was a regional Xianbei state established by the Qifu clan across the Longxi region of modern Gansu. Governing from shifting frontier strongholds such as Yongshi and Fuhan, its rulers relied on agile cavalry forces to control trade routes between the Hexi Corridor and the Tibetan plateau. After briefly submitting to the Later Qin in 400, the kingdom successfully re-established independence until being completely overwhelmed by the Helian Xia army in 431. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Yongshi and Fuhan; Common languages: Xianbei and Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism and Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Qifu; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 385; Disestablished: 1 June 431; Succeeded by: Great Xia

name: Wei
label: northern and southern dynasties (chinese history)
description: Wei, universally known as the Northern Wei, was an enduring Xianbei dynasty founded by Tuoba Gui that brought an end to the chaotic Sixteen Kingdoms era by unifying northern China. Governing initially from Pingcheng and subsequently from the classical capital of Luoyang, the state blended nomadic military institutions with comprehensive sinification policies instituted under Emperor Xiaowen. Despite fostering spectacular Buddhist art at Yungang and Longmen, court divisions between traditionalist northern garrisons and southern aristocrats sparked disastrous internal civil conflicts. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Pingcheng and Luoyang; Common languages: Tuoba Xianbei and Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Tuoba; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Northern and Southern Dynasties; Established: 386; Disestablished: 534; Succeeded by: Eastern Wei and Western Wei

name: Liang
description: Liang, established during the Sixteen Kingdoms era as the Later Liang by the Di general Lü Guang, governed the fertile Hexi Corridor from its administrative centre at Guzang. Dominating vital trade routes leading into Central Asia, the regime held nominal sway over oasis city-states and welcomed prominent Buddhist travellers. In later imperial historiography, the title also denoted the Five Dynasties realm founded at Kaifeng by Zhu Wen, whose initial regime supplanted the Tang court before yielding to the Later Tang. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Guzang and Kaifeng; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Di; Religion: Buddhism and Confucianism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms and Five Dynasties; Established: 386; Disestablished: 923; Succeeded by: Northern Liang and Later Tang

name: Wei
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Wei, designated in Chinese historiography as Zhai Wei, was a short-lived regional realm established across modern central Henan by Zhai Liao, a warlord of the nomadic Dingling people. Operating from his fortified headquarters at Huatai, Zhai maintained an aggressive stance along the Yellow River, shifting allegiances between the Later Yan and Eastern Jin. The state survived only four years under Zhai Liao and his son Zhai Zhao before powerful Later Yan armies led by Murong Chui overwhelmed their garrison and annexed the territory. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Huatai; Common languages: Dingling and Middle Chinese; Religion: Traditional steppe beliefs; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Zhai; Ruler title: Heavenly King; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 388; Disestablished: 392; Succeeded by: Later Yan

name: Roman Empire
description: The Roman Empire in the West originated as an independent administrative division upon the demise of Theodosius I, who bequeathed the western prefectures to his younger son Honorius. Governed successively from Mediolanum and the marsh-fortified citadel of Ravenna, the realm faced catastrophic barbarian incursions, shrinking provincial revenues and the autonomous rise of Germanic federate kingdoms. The Western court steadily lost territorial cohesion until the Germanic general Odoacer deposed the teenage emperor Romulus Augustulus in 476. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Mediolanum and Ravenna; Official languages: Latin; Common languages: Vulgar Latin and Celtic dialects; Religion: Nicene Christianity; Government: Autocratic imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Theodosian; Ruler title: Augustus; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 17 January 395; Disestablished: 4 September 476; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Italy

name: Roman Empire
description: The Roman Empire in the East, known in modern historiography as the Byzantine Empire, endured as the prosperous continuation of the Roman state centred upon the impregnable maritime capital of Constantinople. Maintaining deep Hellenistic cultural traditions alongside Roman administrative law, the empire under Justinian I reclaimed substantial western Mediterranean territories including Italy, North Africa and southern Hispania.
