Sustained warfare against the Sasanian Persians and devastating bubonic plagues strained imperial resources until the transformative accession of Heraclius in 610. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Constantinople; Official languages: Latin and Greek; Common languages: Ancient Greek, Latin and Coptic; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Autocratic imperial monarchy; Ruler title: Augustus; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 17 January 395; Reorganised: 5 October 610; Currency: Solidus

name: Liang
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Liang, distinguished in Chinese historiography as the Southern Liang, was a regional state established across eastern Qinghai and western Gansu by the Tufa clan of Xianbei ethnicity. Governing from their administrative base at Xining and later Ledu, its monarchs maintained skilled cavalry forces and asserted authority over local Qiang and Han populations. Beset by severe agricultural shortages and relentless hostile incursions from the neighbouring Northern Liang and Western Qin, the dynasty collapsed when its last ruler surrendered in 414. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Xining; Common languages: Xianbei and Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism and Chinese folk religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Tufa; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 397; Disestablished: 414; Succeeded by: Western Qin

name: Liang
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Liang, designated in historical records as the Northern Liang, was an important dynastic state established along the Hexi Corridor by the Lushuihu chieftain Juqu Mengxun. Governed from the strategic Silk Road oasis of Guzang, the realm flourished as a renowned bastion of Buddhist scholarship, cave temple construction and trans-continental commerce. Northern Liang maintained autonomous survival by adroitly balancing tribute diplomacy with southern courts until the expansive armies of Northern Wei conquered the corridor in 439. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Guzang; Common languages: Lushuihu, Middle Chinese and Sogdian; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Juqu; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 397; Disestablished: 439; Succeeded by: Northern Wei

name: Aulikara Dynasty
description: The Aulikara Dynasty was a prominent royal house of central India that governed the kingdom of Dasapura across the fertile Malwa plateau. Emerging from the declining periphery of the Gupta Empire, the dynasty attained imperial renown under Yashodharman Vishnuvardhana, who routed the invading Alchon Hun armies of Mihirakula and erected monumental victory pillars at Sondani. Aulikara monarchs patronised classical Sanskrit literature and grand Shaivite temples before internal fragmentation ceded regional influence to the Later Guptas. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Dasapura; Common languages: Sanskrit and Western Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Aulikara; Ruler title: Rajadhiraja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 350; Disestablished: 550; Succeeded by: Later Gupta dynasty

name: Davaka Kingdom
description: Davaka Kingdom was an ancient realm located across the fertile Kopili and Kolong river valleys of central Assam. Recorded on the fourth-century Allahabad pillar of Samudragupta as an autonomous frontier neighbour of the Gupta Empire, the kingdom maintained independent diplomatic relations and sent an embassy to the imperial Chinese court. Regional monarch Kalyana Varman eventually incorporated Davaka into the expanding realm of neighbouring Kamarupa during the fifth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign frontier kingdom; Capital: Lanka; Common languages: Kamrupi Prakrit and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 401; Disestablished: 501; Succeeded by: Kamarupa Kingdom

name: Kingdom of Makuria
label: christian kingdoms of nubia
description: The Kingdom of Makuria was a Christian Nubian monarchy established along the Nile Valley between the third and fourth cataracts in modern northern Sudan. Governed from its fortified capital at Old Dongola, the realm repulsed early Arab incursions and secured lasting diplomatic equilibrium with Islamic Egypt through the historic Baqt treaty. Makurian culture flourished through monumental brick architecture, distinct painted pottery and thriving monastic foundations until late medieval fragmentation enabled its dissolution. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Old Dongola; Common languages: Old Nubian, Greek and Coptic; Religion: Coptic Orthodox Christianity; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 401; Disestablished: 1519; Succeeded by: Funj Sultanate and Banu Kanz

name: Kingdom of Meath
label: irish medieval kingdoms;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Meath was an important Gaelic over-kingdom situated in the fertile central plains of Ireland, encompassing the modern counties of Meath and Westmeath. Ruled by the Southern Uí Néill dynasty from the ceremonial and inaugural summit at the Hill of Tara, the realm exercised substantial military influence over neighbouring provincial kings. Meath retained its territorial identity and legal institutions until Anglo-Norman invaders overran its heartland and partitioned the realm into feudal lordships in the late twelfth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign over-kingdom; Capital: Tara; Common languages: Old Irish and Middle Irish; Religion: Gaelic Christianity; Government: Tanistry monarchy; Ruler title: Rí; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 401; Disestablished: 1174; Succeeded by: Lordship of Meath

name: Kutai Martadipura
description: Kutai Martadipura was the earliest Indianised Hindu kingdom in the Indonesian archipelago, established along the lower Mahakam River in East Kalimantan on Borneo. Governed from its royal seat at Muara Kaman, the kingdom is celebrated through the Yupa stone inscriptions erected by King Mulavarman, which record lavish cattle donations and Brahminical rituals. The state drew sustained wealth from forest commodities and maritime riverine trade routes until its conquest by the Islamic Sultanate of Kutai Kartanegara. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Muara Kaman; Common languages: Sanskrit and Old Kutai; Religion: Shaivite Hinduism; Government: Indianised monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Martadipura; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Classical Southeast Asia; Established: 401; Disestablished: 1635; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Kutai Kartanegara

name: Liang
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Liang, known in Chinese historiography as the Western Liang, was an autonomous dynastic state established by the Han Chinese scholar-official Li Gao along the western fringes of the Hexi Corridor. Governing initially from Dunhuang and subsequently from Jiuquan, the regime maintained vigilant frontier garrisons to protect vital Silk Road transit corridors. Despite strong agricultural development and classical literary patronages, the kingdom was conquered by the forces of Northern Liang after two decades of regional rivalry. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Dunhuang and Jiuquan; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Confucianism, Buddhism and Taoism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Li; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 400; Disestablished: 421; Succeeded by: Northern Liang

name: Mathara Dynasty
description: The Mathara Dynasty was a regional royal family that governed the ancient territory of Kalinga along the eastern seaboard of India between southern Odisha and the Godavari River. Establishing their administrative centre at Simhapura following the withdrawal of imperial Gupta armies, its rulers styled themselves as lords of Kalinga. The dynasty actively patronised Brahminical learning and issued numerous land grants inscribed in classical Sanskrit before being eclipsed by the rival Pitrbhaktas. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Simhapura; Common languages: Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Mathara; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 401; Disestablished: 501; Succeeded by: Pitrbhakta dynasty and Vasishtha dynasty

name: Nobatia
label: christian kingdoms of nubia
description: Nobatia was a Christian Nubian kingdom that controlled Lower Nubia from the First Nile Cataract southward to the Third Cataract in modern southern Egypt and northern Sudan. Establishing its royal and ecclesiastical capital at Faras, the realm under King Silko defeated the nomadic Blemmyes and formally embraced Monophysite Christianity in the sixth century. Renowned for its vibrant cathedral frescoes and Greek-derived administrative titles, Nobatia was peacefully integrated into its southern neighbour Makuria during the seventh century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Faras; Common languages: Old Nubian, Greek and Coptic; Religion: Coptic Orthodox Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Basiliskos; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 400; Disestablished: 643; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Makuria

name: Salihid Confederation
description: The Salihid Confederation was an Arab tribal phylarchy that operated across the Syrian desert borderlands and the Wadi Sirhan region as prominent federates of the Eastern Roman Empire. Ruled by the Zokomid dynasty without a permanent urban capital, the confederates collected imperial frontier taxes and protected Roman agricultural settlements from nomadic desert raiders. Ardent practitioners of Christianity who constructed monumental desert monasteries, the Salihids lost their regional hegemony to the ascendant Ghassanids in the early sixth century. \n\n Status: Roman federate tribal phylarchy; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Arabic and Greek; Religion: Christianity; Government: Tribal phylarchy; Ruling dynasty: Zokomid; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 401; Disestablished: 501; Succeeded by: Ghassanids

name: Vasishtha Dynasty
description: The Vasishtha Dynasty was a regional Indian royal house that governed portions of Kalinga across present-day northern Andhra Pradesh during the fifth century. Operating from their capital at Devapura, the Vasishtha monarchs asserted autonomous authority following the retraction of imperial Gupta influence from the eastern Deccan. The dynasty maintained administrative autonomy and issued copperplate grants confirming royal patronages of Vedic scholars until regional hegemony consolidated under rival southern kingdoms. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Devapura; Common languages: Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Vasishtha; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 401; Disestablished: 501; Succeeded by: Vishnukundina dynasty

name: Yan
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Yan, designated in historical records as the Southern Yan, was a Xianbei dynastic state founded by Murong De after the territorial fracturing of the Later Yan. Moving southward across the Yellow River, the imperial court established its permanent capital at Guanggu on the Shandong Peninsula. The realm maintained aggressive frontier raids against the Eastern Jin court until the brilliant southern general Liu Yu mounted a massive expedition that besieged Guanggu and extinguished the dynasty in 410. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Guanggu; Common languages: Xianbei and Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism and Confucianism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Murong; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 398; Disestablished: 410; Succeeded by: Jin Dynasty

name: Zaculeu
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Zaculeu was a fortified highland Maya capital and ceremonial centre situated in the western mountains of modern Guatemala near Huehuetenango. Serving as the primary political seat of the Mam Maya kingdom, the city featured tiered temples, ballcourts and plazas constructed with distinctive stepped plaster architecture. The stronghold fiercely resisted regional expansion by the Kʼicheʼ Maya of Qʼumarkaj before succumbing to a protracted siege led by Spanish conquistador Gonzalo de Alvarado in 1525. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Zaculeu; Common languages: Mam Maya; Religion: Maya polytheism; Government: Highland city-state monarchy; Ruler title: Ajaw; Historical era: Classic to Postclassic Mesoamerica; Established: 401; Disestablished: 1451; Succeeded by: Kʼicheʼ Kingdom of Qʼumarkaj

name: Bacalar
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Bacalar was a Maya city-state established along the western shores of Lake Bacalar in the southern reaches of the Yucatán Peninsula in modern Quintana Roo. Occupying a critical transhipment point linking Caribbean coastal trading canoes with riverine routes extending into the Petén interior, the polity maintained substantial commercial influence. The city preserved its indigenous political autonomy until sixteenth-century Spanish conquistadors colonised the lakeshore and founded the fortified settlement of Salamanca de Bacalar. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Bacalar; Common languages: Yucatec Maya; Religion: Maya polytheism; Government: City-state monarchy; Ruler title: Batab; Historical era: Classic to Postclassic Mesoamerica; Established: 402; Disestablished: 1544; Succeeded by: Captaincy General of Yucatán

name: Kingdom of the Ostrogoths
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Ostrogoths in Italy was established when Theodoric the Great led his Germanic warriors westward from the Balkans, defeated Odoacer and took control of the Italian peninsula. Governing from Ravenna, Theodoric fostered a dual administration that preserved the Roman Senate, civil bureaucracy and classical legal codes alongside an Arian Gothic military elite. The kingdom reached its cultural and territorial zenith across Italy and Dalmatia before prolonged Byzantine reconquest campaigns under Justinian I shattered Gothic resistance in 553. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ravenna; Common languages: Gothic, Vulgar Latin and Pannonian Latin; Religion: Arian Christianity and Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Amal; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 493; Disestablished: 553; Succeeded by: Byzantine Empire

name: Chu
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Chu, designated in historiography as Huan Chu, was an ephemeral Chinese imperial regime established in the Yangtze River basin by the Eastern Jin general Huan Xuan. Usurping the imperial throne at Jiankang in early 404, Huan declared the founding of Chu and claimed sovereign authority over southern China. His autocratic reign provoked an immediate military uprising led by commander Liu Yu, who routed Huan's loyalists in battle and brought about his execution within six months. \n\n Status: Contested imperial regime; Capital: Jiankang; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Confucianism, Taoism and Buddhism; Government: Imperial autocracy; Ruling dynasty: Huan; Head of state: Huan Xuan; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 404; Disestablished: 25 June 404; Succeeded by: Jin Dynasty

name: Roman Empire
description: The Roman Empire under Constantine III emerged when legions stationed in Roman Britain proclaimed a common soldier as Augustus in 407 amid growing barbarian incursions. Crossing the Channel with the British field army, Constantine established his imperial seat at Arelate and secured control over Gaul and Hispania through strategic alliances. Although the Western court under Honorius briefly acknowledged him as co-emperor, military mutinies and a siege by imperial general Constantius led to Constantine's surrender and execution in 411. \n\n Status: Contested imperial regime; Capital: Arelate; Common languages: Latin and Celtic dialects; Religion: Nicene Christianity; Government: Imperial autocracy; Head of state: Constantine III; Ruler title: Augustus; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 407; Disestablished: 411; Succeeded by: Western Roman Empire

name: Great Xia
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Great Xia, known in Chinese chronicles as Hu Xia, was a formidable northern dynasty established by the Tiefu-Xiongnu chieftain Helian Bobo in the Ordos Desert. Claiming descent from China's ancient Xia dynasty, the regime constructed the virtually impregnable white-walled capital of Tongwancheng in modern Shaanxi. Xia horsemen captured Chang'an and dominated the Guanzhong plains through mobile shock warfare until internal family discord and relentless assaults by the Northern Wei brought the empire to an end in 431. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Tongwancheng; Common languages: Xiongnu and Middle Chinese; Religion: Steppe shamanism and Buddhism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Helian; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 407; Disestablished: 431; Succeeded by: Northern Wei

name: Yan
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Yan, designated as the Northern Yan in historiography, was a northern Chinese realm that inherited the rump territories of the Later Yan across western Liaoning and north-eastern Hebei. Founded by the Han Chinese official Feng Ba after the assassination of Emperor Gao Yun, the state governed securely from its mountain-fringed fortress capital at Longcheng. Maintaining tenuous autonomy by paying tribute to southern Chinese dynasties and courting Goguryeo, the realm finally collapsed under an all-out invasion launched by the Northern Wei in 436. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Longcheng; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Xianbei; Religion: Buddhism and Confucianism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Feng; Ruler title: Heavenly King; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 407; Disestablished: 436; Succeeded by: Northern Wei and Goguryeo

name: Kingdom of the Alans
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of the Alans was an ephemeral post-Roman realm established in south-western Hispania by Iranic nomadic pastoralists who crossed the frozen Rhine in 406. Settling across the Roman provinces of Lusitania and Carthaginensis, Alan warriors established their administrative centre at Mérida and imposed tribute over the local Hispano-Roman population. Their independent kingdom was crushed in 418 during a campaign conducted by the Visigoths under imperial Roman mandate, forcing surviving Alans to unite with the Hasdingi Vandals. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal kingdom; Capital: Mérida; Common languages: Alanic and Vulgar Latin; Religion: Paganism and Arian Christianity; Government: Tribal military monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Migration Period; Established: 1 November 409; Disestablished: 415; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Vandals and Alans

name: Kingdom of the Suebi
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Suebi was an early post-Roman Germanic realm established across the Atlantic provinces of Gallaecia and northern Lusitania in north-western Hispania. Centred upon the episcopal city of Braga, the kingdom organised a resilient monarchy that adapted Roman provincial administration and alternately embraced Arian and Chalcedonian Christianity. Maintaining independence for nearly two centuries despite periodic conflicts with neighbouring Visigoths, the Suebic realm was annexed by King Leovigild into the Visigothic Kingdom in 585. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Braga; Common languages: Suebic and Vulgar Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity and Arian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 1 November 409; Disestablished: 585; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Visigoths

name: Kingdom of the Vandals
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Vandals in Baetica was founded by Silingi Vandal warbands following the grand barbarian crossing of the Pyrenees into the Iberian Peninsula in 409. Occupying fertile lands across southern Spain with their royal headquarters around Córdoba, the Silingi extracted resources from Roman provincial estates and defied imperial authority. Visigothic federate armies acting under Western Roman orders launched devastating campaigns between 416 and 418 that shattered Silingi resistance, driving the survivors to seek refuge among the northern Hasdingi. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal kingdom; Capital: Córdoba; Common languages: Vandalic and Vulgar Latin; Religion: Germanic paganism and Arian Christianity; Government: Tribal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Migration Period; Established: 1 November 409; Disestablished: 415; Succeeded by: Western Roman Empire

name: Kingdom of the Vandals
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Vandals in Gallaecia was established by the Hasdingi branch of the Vandal people who settled in north-western Hispania alongside the Suebi in 409. Operating from fortified settlements around Braga, Hasdingi chieftains defended their mountain redoubts while absorbing Alan refugees who fled Visigothic attacks. After clashing with the neighbouring Suebi and Roman provincial forces, King Gunderic led his Hasdingi and Alan confederates southward into Baetica in 421, opening a new phase of conquest. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal kingdom; Capital: Braga; Common languages: Vandalic and Vulgar Latin; Religion: Arian Christianity and Germanic paganism; Government: Tribal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hasdingi; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Migration Period; Established: 1 November 409; Disestablished: 421; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Vandals and Alans

name: Roman Empire
description: The Roman Empire under Maximus comprised a rebel regime proclaimed in north-eastern Hispania during the western civil wars that destabilised late imperial Gaul and Spain. Elevated to the purple at Tarraco by the disgruntled general Gerontius, Maximus ruled briefly over portions of the Tarraconensis province without securing wider dynastic legitimacy. Following the defeat and suicide of his military patron, Maximus was deposed, pardoned into monastic obscurity and later executed after attempting a second insurrection. \n\n Status: Contested imperial regime; Capital: Trier; Common languages: Latin; Religion: Nicene Christianity; Government: Military autocracy; Head of state: Maximus of Hispania; Ruler title: Augustus; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 410; Disestablished: 413; Succeeded by: Western Roman Empire

name: Shu
label: sixteen kingdoms (chinese history)
description: Shu, designated in Chinese historiography as Western Shu or Qiao Shu, was an autonomous regional state founded in the Sichuan Basin by the military commander Qiao Zong. Capitalising on peasant unrest and mutinies within the Eastern Jin provincial garrison, Qiao proclaimed himself Prince of Chengdu and governed from that historic city. Aligning with the northern Later Qin regime for military backing, Western Shu defended the upper Yangtze River gorges until southern forces commanded by Liu Yu launched a riverine invasion that crushed the state in 413. \n\n Status: Autonomous principality; Capital: Chengdu; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Qiao; Ruler title: Prince of Shu; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 405; Disestablished: 413; Succeeded by: Jin Dynasty

name: Kingdom of Dumnonia
label: celtic polities in britain;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Dumnonia was a Brittonic realm that emerged across south-western Britain, encompassing present-day Devon, Cornwall and parts of western Somerset following the collapse of Roman administration. Governing initially from the ancient civitas centre at Isca Dumnoniorum and later from the cliff-top coastal citadel at Tintagel, the kingdom maintained maritime trade connections with the Mediterranean. Dumnonia tenaciously preserved Celtic culture, Brittonic speech and monastic Christianity until steady westward encroachment by the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Wessex absorbed its territory. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Exeter and Tintagel; Common languages: Brittonic, Cornish and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 411; Disestablished: 826; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Wessex

name: Kingdom of Dyfed
label: celtic polities in britain;welsh polities;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Dyfed was an early medieval Welsh petty kingdom situated in south-western Wales, rooted in the ancient tribal territory of the Demetae. Founded during the post-Roman withdrawal by Déisi Irish settlers who intermarried with indigenous Romano-British elites, the realm was administered from Carmarthen. Dyfed's princes successfully defended their cantrefi against coastal raids and neighbouring Welsh dynasties for centuries before dynastic marriage united the realm with Seisyllwg in 920 to create the Kingdom of Deheubarth. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Carmarthen; Common languages: Old Welsh, Primitive Irish and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 410; Disestablished: 920; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Deheubarth

name: Kingdom of Strathclyde
label: celtic polities in britain;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Strathclyde was an early medieval Brittonic realm in the Hen Ogledd, spanning the Clyde basin of south-western Scotland and northern Cumbria. Governing from their formidable volcanic stronghold at Dumbarton Rock, known natively as Alt Clud, the kings of Strathclyde maintained Cumbric speech and resisted Northumbrian, Pictish and Norse aggression. Although Dublin Vikings sacked the rock fortress in 870, the dynasty transferred its principal seat to Govan and expanded southward before peaceful assimilation into the emerging Kingdom of Scotland. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Dumbarton and Govan; Common languages: Cumbric and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 411; Disestablished: 1035; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Scotland

name: Kingdom of the Burgundians
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Burgundians in the Rhineland was established when the Germanic Gibichung dynasty led their warrior followers across the Rhine and concluded a treaty of federation with the Western Roman Empire. Centred around Borbetomagus, modern Worms, these federates defended the Rhine limes in exchange for Roman agricultural allotments and imperial recognition. Following an ill-fated Burgundian attempt to expand westward into Belgica, the Roman general Flavius Aetius deployed allied Hunnic horsemen in 436, devastating the kingdom and slaying King Gundahar. \n\n Status: Roman federate client kingdom; Capital: Worms; Common languages: Burgundian and Vulgar Latin; Religion: Arian Christianity; Government: Tribal client monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Gibichung; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Migration Period; Established: 411; Disestablished: 436; Reorganised: 443

name: Kingdom of the Visigoths
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Visigoths was a major post-Roman realm founded when King Wallia negotiated an imperial treaty that settled Gothic federates in the fertile valleys of Gallia Aquitania. Initially governing from Toulouse, the Visigothic kings expanded southward into the Iberian Peninsula, subduing rival barbarian tribes and eventually establishing their royal court at Toledo. Despite suffering defeat against the Franks at Vouillé in 507, the kingdom unified all of Hispania under King Leovigild before its catastrophic collapse during the Umayyad invasion of 711. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Toulouse and Toledo; Common languages: Gothic, Vulgar Latin and Iberian Romance; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity and Arian Christianity; Government: Elective monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Antiquity to Early Middle Ages; Established: 418; Disestablished: 721; Succeeded by: Umayyad Caliphate and Kingdom of Asturias

name: Song
label: northern and southern dynasties (chinese history)
description: Song, designated as the Liu Song dynasty in Chinese historiography, was the first of the four Southern dynasties that ruled southern China from their imperial capital at Jiankang. Founded by the formidable general Liu Yu after he deposed the final Eastern Jin monarch, the dynasty secured the southern interior and maintained control over the Yangtze and Huai river valleys. Although celebrated for administrative centralisation and literary achievement under Emperor Wen, internal dynastic bloodletting and military rebellions hastened its replacement by the Southern Qi in 479. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Jiankang; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism, Confucianism and Taoism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Liu; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Northern and Southern Dynasties; Established: 420; Disestablished: 31 May 479; Succeeded by: Southern Qi

name: Kingdom of the Vandals and Alans
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Vandals and Alans in southern Hispania was established when King Gunderic consolidated Hasdingi, surviving Silingi and Alan warrior contingents across the fertile province of Baetica. Establishing royal headquarters at Seville, the unified confederation defeated Roman field armies, sacked regional ports and assembled an agile maritime fleet along the Mediterranean coast. Under Gunderic and his brother Gaiseric, the confederates exploited the vulnerability of Roman Spain until launching their historic naval migration across the Strait of Gibraltar to North Africa in 429. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Seville; Common languages: Vandalic, Alanic and Vulgar Latin; Religion: Arian Christianity; Government: Tribal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hasdingi; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Migration Period; Established: 421; Disestablished: 430; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Vandals and Alans

name: Vishnukundina Dynasty
description: The Vishnukundina Dynasty was an important royal family that governed coastal Andhra, Telangana and adjoining sections of the Deccan plateau from its capitals at Vinukonda and Denduluru. Emerging during the reign of Madhava Varma following the collapse of the Salankayanas, the rulers performed classical Vedic sacrifices while generously sponsoring elaborate cave architecture at Mogalarajapuram and Undavalli. The dynasty maintained regional power for two centuries until the aggressive western Deccan campaigns of Chalukya king Pulakeshin II dismantled their statehood. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Vinukonda and Denduluru; Common languages: Sanskrit and Old Telugu; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Vishnukundina; Ruler title: Janasraya; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 420; Disestablished: 624; Succeeded by: Eastern Chalukyas

name: Salankayana Dynasty
description: The Salankayana Dynasty was a regional Indian governing family that controlled the coastal Andhra plain situated between the Krishna and Godavari rivers from their capital at Pedavegi. Subordinated as faithful vassals under the suzerainty of the Pallavas of Kanchi, its monarchs oversaw flourishing maritime trade and administered their territories through classical Sanskrit and Prakrit edicts. Royal patrons dedicated monuments to Shiva and the sun while supporting Buddhist monasteries until the expanding Vishnukundina dynasty extinguished their vassal principality. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom; Capital: Pedavegi; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Salankayana; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 426; Disestablished: 501; Succeeded by: Vishnukundina dynasty

name: Kingdom of the Vandals and Alans
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Vandals and Alans in North Africa was established under the charismatic warlord Gaiseric following the seaborne migration of eighty thousand Germanic and Alan warriors from Hispania. Capturing the great metropolitan centre of Carthage in 439, the kingdom wrested North Africa and western Mediterranean islands including Sardinia and Corsica from Roman control. The Vandals created a formidable pirate navy, famously sacked Rome in 455 and maintained an Arian ruling aristocracy until Byzantine general Belisarius destroyed their realm during the Vandalic War of 534. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Carthage; Common languages: Vandalic, Latin and African Romance; Religion: Arian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hasdingi; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 435; Disestablished: 534; Succeeded by: Praetorian Prefecture of Africa

name: Mauro-Roman Kingdom
label: roman-maurian kingdoms;berber kingdoms
description: The Mauro-Roman Kingdom was an independent Christian realm established across the former Roman province of Mauretania Caesariensis in modern northern Algeria. Operating from its fortified upland capital at Altava, the state blended classical Roman administrative titles with indigenous Berber tribal alliances under rulers such as King Masuna. The kingdom fiercely resisted Vandal encroachment from the east and aided Byzantine forces during their North African reconquests before fragmenting into smaller Berber principalities in the late sixth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Altava; Common languages: Berber and African Romance; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Rex gentium Maurorum et Romanorum; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 429; Disestablished: 579; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Altava and Byzantine Empire

name: Kingdom of Gwent
label: celtic polities in britain;welsh polities;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Gwent was an early medieval Welsh successor state established in south-eastern Wales between the lower Wye and Usk rivers. Administered initially from the former Roman civitas of Caerwent and later from Porth-is-Coed, the kingdom maintained strong cultural and institutional continuity with the ancient Silures. Gwent preserved an independent bishopric, resisted Anglo-Saxon encroachment across the Severn estuary and frequently united with neighbouring Glywysing until Norman marcher lords overran the realm in the late eleventh century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Caerwent; Common languages: Old Welsh and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 431; Disestablished: 1070; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Morgannwg and Welsh Marches

name: Hastinapur Kingdom
description: Hastinapur Kingdom was a regional monarchical entity established across the upper Ganges Doab in northern India, centred upon the venerable ancient settlement of Hastinapur. Occupying fertile alluvial plains in present-day Meerut district, the local dynasty maintained autonomy amid the fluctuating authority of the Gupta imperial court. The realm derived sustained prestige from Hastinapur's deep roots in epic Puranic traditions and Jain sacred history before consolidating into larger regional hegemonies during the classical period. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Hastinapur; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 434; Disestablished: 460; Succeeded by: Gupta Empire

name: Principality of Ushrusana
description: The Principality of Ushrusana was an autonomous Iranian mountain principality situated in the rugged highlands of modern northern Tajikistan south of the Syr Darya. Governed by hereditary dynasties bearing the indigenous title of Afshin from their fortified citadel at Bunjikat, the realm maintained Sogdian language, culture and commercial contacts with the Silk Road. Ushrusana preserved its Zoroastrian heritage against early Muslim expansion before converting to Islam in the ninth century and submitting to the Samanid Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Bunjikat; Common languages: Sogdian and Persian; Religion: Zoroastrianism and Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Afshin; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 436; Disestablished: 893; Succeeded by: Samanid Empire

name: Liang
description: Liang, known in Chinese historiography as the Northern Liang of Gaochang, was a remnant state established in the Turpan Basin by surviving members of the Juqu royal family after their expulsion from Gansu. Governing from the oasis city of Gaochang, the court preserved Chinese administrative traditions, patronised flourishing Buddhist monastic institutions and promoted Silk Road caravan traffic. The isolated regime maintained tenuous autonomy against steppe neighbours until the aggressive expansion of the Rouran Khaganate crushed the settlement in 460. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Gaochang; Common languages: Middle Chinese, Sogdian and Tocharian; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Juqu; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Sixteen Kingdoms; Established: 442; Disestablished: 460; Succeeded by: Gaochang and Rouran Khaganate

name: Kingdom of the Burgundians
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Burgundians in Sapaudia was re-established under Roman sponsorship when imperial authorities resettled surviving Burgundian federates in the lands around Lake Geneva and the upper Rhone. Ruling as Roman military officers and kings from Lyon, Burgundian monarchs provided crucial military assistance against Attila the Hun at the Catalaunian Plains while expanding across south-eastern Gaul. This federate relationship gradually transitioned into full territorial sovereignty as Western Roman imperial authority withered during the late fifth century. \n\n Status: Roman federate client kingdom; Capital: Lyon; Common languages: Burgundian, Vulgar Latin and Ecclesiastical Latin; Religion: Arian Christianity and Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Gibichung; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 443; Disestablished: 487; Reorganised: 487

name: Kingdom of Powys
label: celtic polities in britain;welsh polities;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Powys was an influential Welsh successor state established in east-central Wales and parts of the modern English West Midlands following the departure of Roman legions. Governing originally from royal residences along the Severn Valley and later from the fortified stronghold of Mathrafal, the kingdom incorporated the ancient tribal territories of the Ordovices and Cornovii. Powys defended its fertile river lowlands against aggressive Northumbrian and Mercian invasions, preserving its Celtic legal codes and poetic traditions throughout the Early Middle Ages. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Mathrafal; Common languages: Old Welsh and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 448; Disestablished: 1160; Succeeded by: Powys Wenwynwyn and Powys Fadog

name: Wudu Kingdom
description: Wudu Kingdom was an autonomous mountain realm founded in the southern Gansu borderlands by members of the Yang clan of Di ethnicity following the fragmentation of Chouchi. Operating from their fortified upland base at Wudu, its chieftains utilised rugged alpine terrain to preserve political independence while adroitly offering nominal tribute to rival northern and southern Chinese courts. The kingdom served as a strategic buffer between the Northern Wei and southern regimes until Northern Zhou armies incorporated the territory in 580. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Wudu; Common languages: Di and Middle Chinese; Religion: Traditional animism, Buddhism and Daoism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Yang; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Northern and Southern Dynasties; Established: 449; Disestablished: 580; Succeeded by: Northern Zhou

name: Wuxing Kingdom
description: Wuxing Kingdom was a regional Di realm that arose as one of the three splinter dynasties of Chouchi in the mountainous border country of modern southern Shaanxi. Governed from its fortified administrative seat at Wuxing, the state maintained a militarised tribal society that controlled strategic passes connecting the Han River valley with the northern plains. The ruling Yang clan preserved local autonomy through flexible diplomacy with the Northern Wei and southern courts until Northern Zhou expansion brought about its annexation. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Wuxing; Common languages: Di and Middle Chinese; Religion: Traditional animism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Yang; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Northern and Southern Dynasties; Established: 449; Disestablished: 580; Succeeded by: Northern Zhou

name: Yinping Kingdom
description: Yinping Kingdom was a Di mountainous principality established along the rugged river valleys of southern Gansu following the dissolution of the Chouchi state. Centred at Yinping, the kingdom was defended by difficult mountain passes that protected local communities from external aggression and facilitated control over regional trading trails. Its hereditary Yang rulers preserved distinct ethnic traditions and maintained shifting vassal arrangements with neighbouring Chinese empires until Northern Zhou forces extinguished the realm in the late sixth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Yinping; Common languages: Di and Middle Chinese; Religion: Traditional animism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Yang; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Northern and Southern Dynasties; Established: 449; Disestablished: 580; Succeeded by: Northern Zhou

name: Ailech
label: irish medieval kingdoms;celtic polities
description: Ailech was an influential Gaelic over-kingdom in north-western Ireland established by the Cenél nEógain branch of the Northern Uí Néill. Inaugurated at the monumental prehistoric stone hillfort of Grianan of Aileach overlooking Lough Foyle and Lough Swilly, the kings exercised paramount authority over regional tuatha across western Ulster. The dynasty fiercely contested the high kingship of Tara and preserved Gaelic legal traditions until Anglo-Norman campaigns dismembered the over-kingdom in the late twelfth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign over-kingdom; Capital: Grianan of Aileach; Common languages: Old Irish and Middle Irish; Religion: Gaelic Christianity; Government: Tanistry monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Northern Uí Néill; Ruler title: Rí; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 451; Disestablished: 1186; Succeeded by: Lordship of Ireland

name: Airgialla
label: irish medieval kingdoms;celtic polities
description: Airgialla was a prominent Gaelic confederation of nine autonomous petty kingdoms that controlled central Ulster across modern Armagh, Monaghan and Tyrone. Formally meeting under an overking at Clogher, the confederates preserved ancient tributary liberties while providing military contingents across northern Ireland. Although legendary accounts attributed its foundation to the Three Collas, the realm gradually experienced territorial encroachment from the expanding Northern Uí Néill until transforming into the MacMahon lordship of Oriel in the late sixteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign confederation; Capital: Clogher; Common languages: Middle Irish and Early Modern Irish; Religion: Gaelic Christianity and Catholicism; Government: Tanistry confederation; Ruler title: Rí; Historical era: Early Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 451; Disestablished: 1585; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Ireland

name: Copán
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Copán was a prominent Classic Maya kingdom situated in a fertile mountain valley of western Honduras along the Copán River. Operating as a critical commercial and cultural gateway between the Maya lowlands and non-Maya societies of lower Central America, the city flourished under a dynastic line founded by Kʼinich Yax Kʼukʼ Moʼ. Renowned for its extraordinarily detailed high-relief stelae, hieroglyphic stairway and sacred acropolis, Copán suffered demographic collapse and dynastic breakdown during the early ninth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Copán; Common languages: Classic Maya; Religion: Maya polytheism; Government: Sacral city-state monarchy; Ruler title: Kʼuhul Ajaw; Historical era: Classic Mesoamerica; Established: 451; Disestablished: 831

name: Hephthalite Empire
description: The Hephthalite Empire was a powerful Central Asian confederation of White Huns that dominated Bactria, Sogdiana and adjacent Afghan tablelands during the fifth and sixth centuries. Governing from major urban centres including Balkh and Kunduz, the empire subjugated the Kidarites, exacted heavy silver tribute from the Sasanian Persian monarchy and controlled prosperous Silk Road trade stations. Their formidable pastoralist empire collapsed around 560 when a coordinated alliance between the First Turkic Khaganate and the Sasanian Empire overwhelmed their armies. \n\n Status: Nomadic empire; Capital: Balkh and Kunduz; Common languages: Bactrian, Sogdian and Turkic; Religion: Zoroastrianism, Buddhism and Manichaeism; Government: Nomadic confederation; Ruler title: Khagan; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 450; Disestablished: 560; Succeeded by: First Turkic Khaganate and Sasanian Empire

name: Kingdom of Brycheiniog
label: celtic polities in britain;welsh polities;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Brycheiniog was an early medieval Welsh realm situated in the rugged upper basin of the River Usk in south Wales. Established according to Welsh tradition by the legendary prince Brychan, the kingdom was administered from its royal court at Talgarth and acted as a crucial geopolitical buffer between Anglo-Saxon England and western Welsh kingdoms. Despite enduring continuous border raids and dynastic mergers with neighbouring Dyfed, Brycheiniog preserved its Brittonic identity until Norman marcher barons conquered the valley in the late eleventh century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Talgarth; Common languages: Old Welsh, Brittonic and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 450; Disestablished: 1046; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Deheubarth and Lordship of Brecon

name: Kingdom of Deira
label: anglian polities in britain
description: The Kingdom of Deira was an early Anglian realm established in northern England between the Humber estuary and the River Tees. Centred upon the former Roman legionary stronghold of Eoforwic, modern York, Anglian warbands colonised the fertile Vale of York and subordinated indigenous Brittonic settlements. Frequently embroiled in territorial conflicts and dynastic unions with its northern neighbour Bernicia, Deira formed the southern constituent of the unified Kingdom of Northumbria during the seventh century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: York; Common languages: Northumbrian Old English and Common Brittonic; Religion: Anglo-Saxon paganism and Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 450; Disestablished: 635; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Northumbria

name: Kingdom of Gwynedd
label: celtic polities in britain;welsh polities;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Gwynedd was a powerful Brittonic realm established across the mountainous landscapes of north-western Wales and the fertile isle of Anglesey. Founded by Cunedda and his followers following their migration from Manaw Gododdin, the kingdom operated from coastal strongholds such as Deganwy and Aberffraw. Its monarchs tenaciously resisted Anglo-Saxon, Viking and Norman invasions, asserting regional hegemony across Wales until the English conquests of Edward I extinguished native governance in 1283. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Deganwy and Aberffraw; Common languages: Old Welsh, Middle Welsh and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity and Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King of the Britons; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 451; Disestablished: 1217; Reorganised: 1216

name: Lavo Kingdom
description: Lavo Kingdom was a prominent Mon mandala polity established in the lower Chao Phraya river basin of central Thailand, representing a major cultural centre of the Dvaravati civilisation. Governing from the historic city of Lavapura, modern Lopburi, the realm flourished as a vital hub of Theravada and Mahayana Buddhist learning and maritime riverine commerce. The kingdom maintained extensive diplomatic contacts with imperial China and sustained autonomy until increasing political integration into the Angkorian Khmer Empire and the emergent Ayutthaya Kingdom. \n\n Status: Sovereign mandala kingdom; Capital: Lopburi; Common languages: Old Mon, Old Khmer and Old Thai; Religion: Buddhism and Hinduism; Government: Mandala monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Post-classical Southeast Asia; Established: 451; Disestablished: 1409; Succeeded by: Ayutthaya Kingdom and Khmer Empire

name: Middle Nazca Culture
description: The Middle Nazca Culture was an advanced pre-Columbian society that flourished along the hyper-arid southern coastal desert of Peru throughout the Ica and Nazca river drainages. Operating around the great ceremonial pilgrimage centre of Cahuachi, this society constructed elaborate underground aqueducts known as puquios to support desert agriculture and urban gatherings. Middle Nazca artisans achieved outstanding aesthetic renown through intricate polychrome slipware ceramics, complex cotton textiles and monumental geoglyphs etched across the arid desert pampa. \n\n Status: Sovereign ceremonial society; Capital: Cahuachi; Common languages: Proto-Quechuan or Proto-Aymaran; Religion: Andean polytheism; Government: Theocratic tribal chiefdom; Historical era: Early Intermediate Period; Established: 451; Disestablished: 551; Succeeded by: Late Nazca and Wari culture

name: Kingdom of the Gepids
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Gepids in the Middle Danube was reconstituted following the historic Battle of Nedao in 454, where Gepid warriors under King Ardaric led the alliance that shattered Hunnic hegemony. Establishing their royal capital at the strategic Roman fortress city of Sirmium, the Gepids controlled expansive territories across the Hungarian Plain and former Dacia. The kingdom maintained a proud warrior monarchy and resisted imperial Byzantine pressure until a combined invasion by the Lombards and Pannonian Avars destroyed the realm in 567. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Sirmium; Common languages: East Germanic and Latin; Religion: Arian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ardaric; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Migration Period; Established: 455; Disestablished: 567; Succeeded by: Avar Khaganate and Kingdom of the Lombards

name: Kingdom of the Heruls
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Heruls was an East Germanic realm established north of the Middle Danube in Lower Austria and northern Pannonia following the collapse of the Hunnic Empire. Emerging as victorious participants at the Battle of Nedao, Herulian warrior retinues commanded river trade routes and maintained fluctuating diplomatic ties with the Eastern Roman Empire. Persistent territorial friction with neighbouring Germanic realms eventually provoked a disastrous war against the Lombards around 508, which crushed Herulian statehood and dispersed their surviving warriors. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal kingdom; Capital: Belgrade; Common languages: East Germanic and Latin; Religion: Germanic paganism and Arian Christianity; Government: Tribal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Migration Period; Established: 455; Disestablished: 509; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Lombards

name: Kingdom of the Rugii
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Rugii, known historically as Rugiland, was an East Germanic realm founded in modern Lower Austria north of the Danube in the wake of Attila's demise. Ruling from their fortified riverine settlements near Krems, the Rugian kings maintained political independence, extracted grain supplies from Roman Danubian communities and adhered to Arian Christianity. Following hostile diplomatic intrigues between King Feletheus and the Eastern court, Germanic general Odoacer invaded Rugiland in 487, annihilating the monarchy and deporting surviving populations into Italy. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Krems; Common languages: East Germanic and Latin; Religion: Arian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Migration Period; Established: 455; Disestablished: 488; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Italy

name: Kingdom of the Scirii
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Scirii was an ephemeral East Germanic tribal realm established across the Tisza basin and the Great Hungarian Plain after the dissolution of Hunnic supremacy. Led by chieftains such as Edeko, former counsellor to Attila, the Scirii asserted local dominion from encampments near Szeged while seeking federate alliances with Roman authorities. Deep-seated territorial rivalries with the neighbouring Ostrogoths culminated in the Battle of Bolia in 469, where Scirian forces suffered catastrophic defeats that dissolved their sovereign kingdom. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal kingdom; Capital: Szeged; Common languages: East Germanic and Latin; Religion: Germanic paganism; Government: Tribal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Migration Period; Established: 455; Disestablished: 468; Succeeded by: Ostrogothic Kingdom

name: Kingdom of the Suebi
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Suebi in the Danube was a short-lived Germanic realm established in modern Austria and western Slovakia by Danubian Suebi who broke free from Hunnic vassalage at Nedao. Governed by King Hunimund from regional strongholds near Carnuntum, these warriors raided across the Roman frontier and engaged in bitter feuds with the neighbouring Ostrogoths. After suffering heavy defeats against Theodemir's Goths around Lake Balaton and along the Bolia River, the realm lost its political coherence and dissolved into surrounding tribal groups. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal kingdom; Capital: Carnuntum; Common languages: Suebic Germanic and Latin; Religion: Germanic paganism; Government: Tribal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Migration Period; Established: 455; Disestablished: 468; Succeeded by: Ostrogothic Kingdom

name: Kingdom of Kent
label: saxon polities in britain
description: The Kingdom of Kent was an early Anglo-Saxon realm established in south-eastern Britain by Jutish and Saxon settlers following the termination of Roman provincial rule. Governed from its royal and ecclesiastical capital at Canterbury, the kingdom became the pioneer of English Christianity when King Æthelberht received the Roman mission of Saint Augustine in 597. Kent developed prominent legal codes, extensive maritime trade across the Channel and thriving agricultural estates before dynastic subordination incorporated the realm into the expanding Kingdom of Wessex. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Canterbury; Common languages: Kentish Old English and Latin; Religion: Anglo-Saxon paganism and Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Heptarchy; Established: 456; Disestablished: 825; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Wessex

name: Domain of Soissons
description: The Domain of Soissons was the last major Gallo-Roman enclave in northern Gaul, surviving the collapse of the central Western Roman government in Italy. Administered from Soissons by the magister militum Aegidius and later his son Syagrius, the state preserved Roman administrative institutions, coinage and Roman legionary forces between the Somme and Loire rivers. Surrounded by encroaching Germanic polities, the enclave was conquered in 486 when Clovis I led the Salian Franks to victory at the Battle of Soissons. \n\n Status: Autonomous Gallo-Roman enclave; Capital: Soissons; Common languages: Vulgar Latin and Gallo-Romance; Religion: Nicene Christianity; Government: Military magistracy; Ruler title: Rex Romanorum; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 1 September 461; Disestablished: 487; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Franks

name: Kingdom of Licchavi
label: nepal petty kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Licchavi was an influential classical dynasty that governed the Kathmandu Valley and adjoining Himalayan foothills in modern Nepal. Tracing ancestral connections to the ancient Licchavis of northern Bihar, its rulers governed from Kathmandu, erecting Sanskrit stone inscriptions and introducing refined Gupta artistic styles to the valley. The Licchavi era is widely remembered as a golden age of Nepalese administration, trade and religious harmony between Shaivite Hinduism and Mahayana Buddhism before giving way to the Thakuri dynasty. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kathmandu; Common languages: Sanskrit and Proto-Newar; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Licchavi; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Classical South Asia; Established: 465; Disestablished: 1201; Succeeded by: Thakuri dynasty

name: Kingdom of Thuringia
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Thuringia was a prominent Germanic realm established across central Germany between the Harz Mountains and the Thuringian Forest following the retreat of Hunnic dominion. Operating from royal courts around Erfurt, Thuringian kings commanded powerful cavalry retinues and extended their influence southward toward northern Bavaria and eastward along the Elbe. Bitter dynastic rivalries in the early sixth century invited military interventions by the Merovingian Franks, who shattered the Thuringian army at the Unstrut River in 531 and incorporated the territory. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Erfurt; Common languages: Old High German and Thuringian; Religion: Germanic paganism and Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Migration Period to Early Middle Ages; Established: 470; Disestablished: 720; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Franks

name: Kingdom of Ceredigion
label: celtic polities in britain;welsh polities;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Ceredigion was an early medieval Welsh petty kingdom situated along the scenic curve of Cardigan Bay on the western coast of Wales. Established according to tradition by Ceredig, son of Cunedda, the realm relied on rugged mountain ridges to deter foreign invaders and sustain an independent Brittonic society. Ceredigion developed vibrant monastic communities and preserved native Celtic laws until the late ninth century, when dynastic union integrated its territory into the enlarged southern kingdom of Seisyllwg. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Cardigan; Common languages: Old Welsh and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 471; Disestablished: 681; Succeeded by: Seisyllwg

name: Kingdom of Gododdin
label: celtic polities in britain;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Gododdin was an early Brittonic realm established across south-eastern Scotland and north-eastern England in the region celebrated in Welsh literature as the Hen Ogledd. Descended from the Iron Age Votadini tribe, the people of Gododdin defended their kingdom from the volcanic crag of Din Eidyn, modern Edinburgh. The tragic northern military expedition to Catraeth, immortalised in the classical heroic poem attributed to Aneirin, weakened native defences and facilitated the gradual conquest of Gododdin by the expanding Anglian kingdom of Bernicia. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Edinburgh; Common languages: Cumbric, Brythonic and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 471; Disestablished: 639; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Northumbria

name: Roman Empire
description: The Roman Empire under Julius Nepos was the legitimate continuation of the Western Roman state preserved in the Adriatic province of Dalmatia. Retaining imperial recognition from the Eastern Roman court at Constantinople, Nepos governed from the fortified palace at Salona after being expelled from Ravenna by his rebellious military commander Orestes. He continued to claim legitimate authority as Western Augustus, minting imperial coinage and directing provincial administration until his assassination by mutinous retainers in 480. \n\n Status: Legitimate Western Roman imperial court; Capital: Ravenna; Common languages: Latin and Greek; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Imperial autocracy; Ruling dynasty: Leonid; Head of state: Julius Nepos; Ruler title: Augustus; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 1 September 475; Disestablished: 9 December 480; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Italy

name: Maitraka Kingdom
description: The Maitraka Kingdom was a prosperous regional dynasty that governed the Saurashtra peninsula and southern Gujarat in western India from its bustling capital at Vallabhi. Founded by General Bhatarka amid the political fragmentation of the Gupta Empire, the Maitraka monarchs presided over an internationally celebrated commercial seaport and monastic university that attracted scholars across Asia. The dynasty sponsored Shaivite temples alongside extensive Buddhist institutions until devastating naval raids launched by Arab forces from Sindh overthrew the kingdom in the late eighth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Vallabhi; Common languages: Sanskrit and Western Prakrit; Religion: Shaivism, Jainism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Maitraka; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 476; Disestablished: 784; Succeeded by: Gurjara-Pratihara Empire

name: Kingdom of Italy
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Italy under Odoacer was established when Germanic federate troops mutinied, deposed Romulus Augustulus and acclaimed their commander as king in 476. Ruling from Ravenna while acknowledging formal suzerainty under the Eastern Roman emperor in Constantinople, Odoacer maintained the Roman Senate, preserved the civil administrative bureaucracy and protected Italian agriculture. His regime maintained territorial stability across Italy, Sicily and Dalmatia until Theodoric the Great led an Ostrogothic invasion sanctioned by the Eastern court that culminated in Odoacer's death in 493. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ravenna; Common languages: Latin, Vulgar Latin and Gothic; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity and Arian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Head of state: Odoacer; Ruler title: Rex; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 4 September 476; Disestablished: 5 March 493; Succeeded by: Ostrogothic Kingdom

name: Cantabria
description: Cantabria was an autonomous mountainous realm in northern Hispania where the indigenous Cantabrian people preserved political independence following the collapse of Roman provincial authority. Operating from fortified upland settlements such as Amaya along the southern slopes of the Cantabrian Mountains, local leaders resisted Visigothic expansion across the meseta. Cantabrian warriors defended their alpine valleys and traditional pastoral lifestyle until the energetic Visigothic monarch Leovigild stormed Amaya in 574, incorporating the highland region into the Visigothic Kingdom. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal kingdom; Capital: Amaya; Common languages: Cantabrian Latin and Proto-Basque; Religion: Roman paganism and Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Tribal chieftaincy; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 477; Disestablished: 575; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Visigoths

name: Tamna
description: Tamna was an insular maritime kingdom established on Jeju Island off the southern coast of the Korean Peninsula. Originating from ancient indigenous island lineages, the realm conducted seafaring trade and entered into a formal tributary vassal relationship with the mainland kingdom of Baekje in 476. Tamna provided marine products, horses and tribute goods to Baekje while maintaining domestic self-governance under native lords until its eventual incorporation into Silla and later the Goryeo dynasty. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom; Capital: Jeju City; Common languages: Tamna and Old Korean; Religion: Korean shamanism and Buddhism; Government: Insular monarchy; Ruler title: Seongju; Historical era: Three Kingdoms of Korea; Established: 477; Reorganised: 18 July 660; Succeeded by: Silla

name: Kingdom of Sussex
label: saxon polities in britain
description: The Kingdom of Sussex was an early Anglo-Saxon kingdom established along the English Channel coast in southern Britain by Saxon settlers under the legendary war leader Ælle. Administered from Chichester, the realm remained geographically isolated from northern neighbours by the dense woodland of the Weald. Although Ælle was recorded as the first Bretwalda wielding overlordship across southern England, Sussex experienced persistent border skirmishes with Wessex and Mercia before being permanently absorbed into the Kingdom of Wessex during the ninth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Chichester; Common languages: Old English; Religion: Anglo-Saxon paganism and Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Heptarchy; Established: 478; Disestablished: 828; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Wessex

name: Qi
label: northern and southern dynasties (chinese history)
description: Qi, designated as the Southern Qi in Chinese historiography, was the second of the four Southern dynasties that governed southern China from the imperial metropolis of Jiankang. Founded by the military commander Xiao Daocheng after displacing the Liu Song dynasty, the state held sway over the fertile Yangtze basin and defended its northern frontier along the Huai River. Despite domestic economic prosperity and cultural patronage, violent court intrigues among rival imperial princes weakened the regime and led to its replacement by the Liang dynasty in 502. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Jiankang; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Xiao; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Northern and Southern Dynasties; Established: 31 May 479; Disestablished: 30 April 502; Succeeded by: Liang dynasty

name: Arbe
label: dalmatian city-states
description: Arbe was a Romanised maritime city-state established on the Adriatic island of Rab, where Latin urban communities maintained self-governance following the collapse of Western Roman authority in Dalmatia. Protected by island geography and fortified harbour walls, Arbe preserved Roman municipal law, civic assemblies and Latin Christian church traditions during waves of barbarian migrations. The commune developed extensive fishing and maritime trade networks across the Kvarner Gulf while accommodating loose Byzantine and Venetian naval protection throughout the early medieval era. \n\n Status: Autonomous maritime city-state; Capital: Rab; Common languages: Dalmatian Latin and Vulgar Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Municipal commune; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 481; Disestablished: 1001; Succeeded by: Republic of Venice

name: Cattaro
label: dalmatian city-states
description: Cattaro was an ancient fortified coastal city-state situated in a sheltered fjord of the Bay of Kotor beneath the steep cliffs of the Lovćen massif. Originally established as the Roman municipium of Acruvium, the Latin-speaking citizenry fortified their maritime harbour against invading Slavs and Avars following the retreat of Western Roman rule. The city preserved Roman civil statutes, maintained an independent bishopric and developed skilled seafaring trade while navigating protectorate relations under the Byzantine Empire and Venetian maritime influence. \n\n Status: Autonomous maritime city-state; Capital: Cattaro; Common languages: Dalmatian Latin and Vulgar Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Municipal commune; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 481; Disestablished: 1155; Succeeded by: Byzantine Empire and Republic of Venice

name: Cres
label: dalmatian city-states
description: Cres was an autonomous Latin insular city-state situated on the long, rocky island of Cres in the northern Adriatic Sea. Originating as a Roman municipal settlement that weathered the barbarian invasions of Late Antiquity, the urban commune maintained ancient administrative institutions and maritime fishing rights across the Kvarner Gulf. Cres sustained its Latinate civic culture and ecclesiastical hierarchy for centuries, establishing mutual trade pacts with neighbouring island communities before formally entering the Venetian maritime commonwealth. \n\n Status: Autonomous maritime city-state; Capital: Cres; Common languages: Dalmatian Latin and Vulgar Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Municipal commune; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 481; Disestablished: 1001; Succeeded by: Republic of Venice

name: Kingdom of the Aurès
label: roman-maurian kingdoms;berber kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Aurès was an independent Christian Berber realm established in the rugged Aurès Mountains of modern north-eastern Algeria. Founded by King Masties following successful Berber insurrections against the Vandal Kingdom, the state combined Roman administrative titles with indigenous tribal authority, with its monarch styling himself Imperator. The kingdom maintained fierce independence, clashed with Byzantine armies during their North African campaigns and preserved its autonomy until Queen Dihya died fighting against the Umayyad Arab conquest in 703. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Arris; Common languages: Berber, African Romance and Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Imperator; Historical era: Late Antiquity to Early Middle Ages; Established: 481; Disestablished: 704; Succeeded by: Umayyad Caliphate

name: Ragusa
label: dalmatian city-states
description: Ragusa was a resilient Latin maritime city-state established on a rocky promontory along the southern Dalmatian coast by Roman citizens fleeing the destruction of Epidaurum. Developing formidable stone fortifications, the city governed itself through merchant councils and civic magistracies that safeguarded ancient Roman urban liberties. Ragusa built an agile commercial fleet, fostered diplomacy across the Adriatic and Mediterranean seas and laid the enduring foundations for its later emergence as the prosperous maritime Republic of Ragusa. \n\n Status: Autonomous maritime city-state; Capital: Ragusa; Common languages: Dalmatian Latin, Vulgar Latin and Old Croatian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Oligarchic merchant republic; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 481; Disestablished: 1001; Succeeded by: Republic of Ragusa and Republic of Venice

name: Spalato
label: dalmatian city-states
description: Spalato was an autonomous post-Roman urban commune established within the monumental stone ramparts of Diocletian's Palace on the Dalmatian coastline. Populated by Latin-speaking refugees following the devastating Slavic and Avar sack of nearby Salona, the community transformed the imperial palace into a fortified medieval city. Spalato preserved Roman civic administration, established an archiepiscopal see and flourished through coastal commerce while maintaining strategic autonomy between the Byzantine Empire, Croatian duchies and Venice. \n\n Status: Autonomous maritime city-state; Capital: Spalato; Common languages: Dalmatian Latin, Vulgar Latin and Croatian; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Municipal commune; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 481; Disestablished: 999; Succeeded by: Republic of Venice

name: Trau
label: dalmatian city-states
description: Trau was a fortified Dalmatian island city-state situated in a protected maritime channel between the Croatian mainland and the island of Čiovo. Emerging from the ancient Greek and Roman settlement of Tragurium, the Latin community maintained municipal self-government and maritime shipping following the collapse of imperial Roman control in the western provinces. Trau preserved its distinctive Romanic culture, defended its harbour against mainland incursions and engaged in vibrant coastal trade before accepting Venetian naval hegemony around the turn of the millennium. \n\n Status: Autonomous maritime city-state; Capital: Trau; Common languages: Dalmatian Latin and Vulgar Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Municipal commune; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 481; Disestablished: 1001; Succeeded by: Republic of Venice

name: Veglia
label: dalmatian city-states
description: Veglia was an insular Latin city-state situated on the northern Adriatic island of Krk in the Bay of Kvarner. Originating as the Roman municipium of Curicta, the urban community preserved its Latin language, municipal councils and bishopric through the tumultuous migrations that followed the fall of the Western Roman Empire. Veglia flourished through olive cultivation, seafaring commerce and salt harvesting, maintaining regional autonomy alongside fellow Dalmatian city-states before swearing fealty to the Doge of Venice. \n\n Status: Autonomous maritime city-state; Capital: Veglia; Common languages: Dalmatian Latin and Vulgar Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Municipal commune; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 481; Disestablished: 1002; Succeeded by: Republic of Venice

name: Zara
label: dalmatian city-states
description: Zara was an ancient Roman maritime city-state and the pre-eminent urban centre of northern Dalmatia, situated on an easily defended coastal peninsula. Preserving its classical street grid, municipal forum and civic administration after the disintegration of the Western Roman Empire, the Latin city served as the administrative capital of the Byzantine Theme of Dalmatia. Zara maintained vital Adriatic merchant fleets and defended its communal independence against neighbouring Slavic principalities before acknowledging Venetian suzerainty in 998. \n\n Status: Autonomous maritime city-state; Capital: Zara; Common languages: Dalmatian Latin, Vulgar Latin and Greek; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Municipal commune; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 481; Disestablished: 999; Succeeded by: Republic of Venice

name: Nezak Huns
description: The Nezak Huns were an important Huna principality established in the mountain valleys south of the Hindu Kush across modern eastern Afghanistan following the defeat of the Sasanian Empire by the Hephthalites. Governing from royal centres at Kapisa and Ghazna, its monarchs issued distinctive silver coinage displaying a bull-headed crown and Middle Persian inscriptions. The realm maintained flourishing Buddhist and Hindu sanctuaries while resisting early Islamic incursions from the west until being supplanted by the Turk Shahi dynasty in the mid-seventh century. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Kapisa; Common languages: Middle Persian and Bactrian; Religion: Buddhism, Hinduism and Zoroastrianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Nezak Shah; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 485; Disestablished: 666; Succeeded by: Turk Shahis

name: Kingdom of the Burgundians
description: The Kingdom of the Burgundians in its sovereign phase emerged when Burgundian monarchs consolidated complete territorial independence across south-eastern Gaul and western Switzerland following the collapse of Western Roman imperial authority. Governing from their prestigious royal capital at Lyon, kings such as Gundobad codified the renowned Lex Burgundionum and fostered reconciliation between Germanic warriors and Gallo-Roman landholders. The wealthy kingdom maintained regional prominence until the combined armies of the Merovingian Franks invaded and annexed Burgundy in 534. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Lyon; Common languages: Burgundian, Vulgar Latin and Ecclesiastical Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity and Arian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Gibichung; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 487; Disestablished: 535; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Franks

name: Kingdom of the Lombards
label: lombard polities
description: The Kingdom of the Lombards in the Danubian basin was established when the Germanic Langobards moved south from the Elbe and occupied Rugiland and northern Noricum in the late fifth century. Establishing encampments along the Danube frontier in modern Lower Austria, the Lombards developed disciplined cavalry forces and absorbed neighbouring Germanic warrior contingents. After defeating the Heruls and concluding alliances with the Eastern Roman Empire, King Alboin led the Lombard host across the Alps in 568 to conquer northern Italy. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal kingdom; Capital: Rugiland; Common languages: Lombardic and Vulgar Latin; Religion: Germanic paganism and Arian Christianity; Government: Elective tribal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Migration Period; Established: 488; Disestablished: 569; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Lombards

name: Rai Dynasty
description: The Rai Dynasty was a prominent regional royal house that governed the fertile lower Indus Valley across modern Sindh, extending its authority to Makran and the port of Debal. Ruling from their capital at Alor near modern Rohri, the monarchs patronised Buddhism alongside Shaivite Hinduism and accumulated considerable wealth through Indian Ocean maritime commerce. The dynasty maintained independent sovereignty for over a century until internal court succession crises led to the usurpation of the throne by the Brahmin dynasty under Chach of Alor. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Alor; Common languages: Sindhi Prakrit and Sanskrit; Religion: Buddhism and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rai; Ruler title: Rai; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 490; Disestablished: 633; Succeeded by: Brahmin dynasty of Sindh

name: Bro Waroc'h
label: celtic polities of brittany;celtic polities
description: Bro Waroc'h was an early medieval Brittonic realm established in south-western Brittany around the Gulf of Morbihan by Christian Britons migrating across the Channel from Britain.
