Centred upon the ancient Roman civitas of Darioritum, modern Vannes, the kingdom was organised by chieftain Waroch I and his successors, who defended their territory against Frankish incursions. Bro Waroc'h preserved Celtic Brittonic speech, customs and monastic institutions until Frankish expansion and inter-Breton dynastic politics incorporated the county into the Breton March and the Duchy of Brittany. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Vannes; Common languages: Breton, Brittonic and Vulgar Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 491; Disestablished: 579; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Franks

name: Kingdom of Glywysing
label: celtic polities in britain;welsh polities;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Glywysing was an early medieval Welsh petty kingdom situated in south-eastern Wales between the River Tawe and the River Usk. Named after its founder Glywys and administered from Cardiff, the kingdom was populated by descendants of the ancient Silures who maintained strong institutional and Christian ecclesiastical traditions. Glywysing defended its fertile coastal lowlands against Anglo-Saxon border pressure and frequently entered into dynastic unions with neighbouring Gwent, eventually merging in the tenth century to form the Kingdom of Morgannwg. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Cardiff; Common languages: Old Welsh and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 491; Disestablished: 1056; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Morgannwg

name: Tiele Confederation
description: The Tiele Confederation was a pastoral union of Turkic tribes that coalesced across the steppes of eastern Kazakhstan and the northern Altai during the late fifth century. Emerging in the wake of the Xiongnu collapse, the tribes asserted independence from the encroaching Rouran Khaganate through mobile equestrian warfare. The confederacy dominated vital Central Asian trade trails until intertribal conflict and the rapid rise of the Göktürks absorbed its constituent clans in the mid-sixth century. \n\n Status: Nomadic tribal confederation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Old Turkic; Religion: Tengrism; Government: Tribal confederation; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 491; Disestablished: 541; Succeeded by: First Turkic Khaganate

name: Jewish Kingdom of Mar-Zutra II
description: The Jewish Kingdom of Mar-Zutra II was an autonomous insurgent realm established around Mahoza and Ctesiphon following a revolt against the Sasanian Empire in 496. Led by the young Jewish Exilarch Mar-Zutra II, the community exploited internal Persian strife and Mazdakite unrest to secure self-governance and field its own defence militia. Sasanian imperial forces eventually suppressed the insurrection after seven years of independence, executing the Exilarch and reintegrating the territory. \n\n Status: Insurgent state; Capital: Mahoza; Common languages: Jewish Babylonian Aramaic and Middle Persian; Religion: Judaism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Established: 496; Disestablished: 503; Succeeded by: Sasanian Empire

name: Kingdom of the Alemanni
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of the Alemanni was a Germanic realm in south-western Germany that fell under Frankish suzerainty following its defeat by King Clovis I in the late fifth century. Governed by native dukes who owed military allegiance to Merovingian overlords, the polity maintained substantial internal autonomy across the Upper Rhine and Black Forest. Alemannic resistance to centralised Frankish administration persisted until the realm was formally dismantled and converted into a direct duchy during the mid-eighth century. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Frankish Empire; Capital: Augsburg; Common languages: Old High German and Latin; Religion: Germanic paganism and Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Subordinate monarchy; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 497; Disestablished: 747; Preceded by: Germania superior; Succeeded by: Duchy of Swabia

name: Corcu Duibne
label: irish medieval kingdoms;celtic polities
description: Corcu Duibne was an autonomous Gaelic petty kingdom that dominated the Dingle and Iveragh peninsulas in south-western Ireland throughout the early medieval era. Affiliated with the wider Erainn lineage, its ruling dynasties controlled vital coastal harbours and sustained maritime trade across the North Atlantic seaways. The polity preserved its distinct territorial integrity and ancestral legal customs for five centuries before being gradually integrated into the emergent regional overkingdoms of Munster. \n\n Status: Petty kingdom; Capital: Dingle; Common languages: Old Irish; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 501; Disestablished: 1001; Historical region: Munster

name: Cornouaille
label: celtic polities of brittany;celtic polities
description: Cornouaille was an independent Celtic realm established along the south-western coast of Armorica by Brythonic migrants from south-western Britain during the early sixth century. Centred on the fortified see of Quimper, the principality fostered distinctive maritime traditions and insular Christian institutions across the peninsula. Its dynastic rulers successfully maintained sovereignty against neighbouring Armorican lords until escalating Frankish expansion compelled the principality to accept Merovingian tributary status in the late 570s. \n\n Status: Independent principality; Administrative seat: Quimper; Common languages: Early Breton, Old Cornish and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 501; Disestablished: 579; Succeeded by: Cornouaille (Frankish vassal)

name: Domnonia
label: celtic polities of brittany;celtic polities
description: Domnonia was a prominent Brythonic kingdom in northern Armorica established by British settlers fleeing Saxon incursions during the early post-Roman era. Governing the littoral zones from Saint-Brieuc to the western reaches of the Breton peninsula, the monarchy preserved intimate cultural, dynastic and religious links with Dumnonia in south-western Britain. The realm exercised total sovereignty over its maritime territories until Frankish military incursions forced its monarch to submit as a Merovingian tributary in the late 570s. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Carhaix; Common languages: Early Breton, Brittonic and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 501; Disestablished: 579; Preceded by: Sub-Roman Britain; Succeeded by: Domnonia (Frankish vassal)

name: Jaintia Kingdom
description: The Jaintia Kingdom was an enduring monarchy located in the hill tracts of Meghalaya and the plains of north-eastern Bengal. Governed by the matrilineal Syiem Sutnga dynasty of the Pnar people, the realm balanced upland traditional authority with agrarian revenue administration across the lowlands. The state maintained strategic autonomy through flexible diplomacy with neighbouring Ahom and Mughal authorities until British imperial forces annexed its plains and hill domains in March 1835. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Jaintiapur; Common languages: Pnar, Khasi and Bengali; Religion: Niamtre and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Syiem Sutnga; Historical era: Early Middle Ages to Modern era; Established: 501; Disestablished: 15 March 1835; Succeeded by: Company rule in India

name: Kingdom of Elmet
label: celtic polities in britain;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Elmet was a resilient Brythonic enclave in northern Britain that preserved Celtic political independence long after neighbouring lowland territories succumbed to Anglo-Saxon settlement. Centred around the Pennine foothills and modern Yorkshire, the realm relied upon dense woodlands and strategic hillforts for defence against encroaching eastern Angle kingdoms. Its sovereign autonomy came to an end in 618 when King Edwin of Northumbria invaded, expelled King Ceretic and annexed the territory into his expanding northern empire. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Leeds; Common languages: Cumbric, Brittonic and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 501; Disestablished: 618; Preceded by: Sub-Roman Britain; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Northumbria

name: Kingdom of Lindsey
label: anglian polities in britain
description: The Kingdom of Lindsey was an early Anglo-Saxon petty realm founded by Anglian settlers across the coastal marshes and limestone ridges of modern north Lincolnshire. Centred upon the ancient Roman administrative hub of Lincoln, the kingdom developed distinct dynastic traditions alongside a mixed agrarian and maritime economy. Squeezed between larger neighbours during the seventh century, Lindsey repeatedly changed allegiance before being definitively absorbed into the hegemonies of Northumbria and Mercia. \n\n Status: Petty kingdom; Capital: Lincoln; Common languages: Old English; Religion: Anglo-Saxon paganism and Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 501; Disestablished: 631; Preceded by: Sub-Roman Britain; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Northumbria

name: Kingdom of Rheged
label: celtic polities in britain;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Rheged was an influential Brythonic realm of the Hen Ogledd that spanned the territories bordering the Solway Firth, north-western England and south-western Scotland. Achieving its greatest political and military power under King Urien, the polity mounted formidable resistance against Anglian expansion from Bernicia. Following decades of shifting alliances and territorial erosion, the kingdom was peacefully integrated into Northumbria during the mid-seventh century through dynastic intermarriage. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Carlisle; Common languages: Cumbric and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 501; Disestablished: 639; Preceded by: Hen Ogledd; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Northumbria

name: Old Pahang Kingdom
description: The Old Pahang Kingdom was an ancient maritime polity centred along the Pahang River basin on the eastern coast of the Malay Peninsula. Functioning as an important trading hub for aromatic woods, tin and gold, the realm participated in wide-ranging mandala networks linking regional Southeast Asian empires. Governed by a lineage of Hindu-Buddhist monarchs styled as maharajas, Pahang retained autonomy until the mid-fifteenth century, when forces of the expansionist Malacca Sultanate conquered the realm and replaced it with a vassal sultanate. \n\n Status: Mandala kingdom; Capital: Pekan; Common languages: Old Malay and Sanskrit; Religion: Mahayana Buddhism and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Post-classical; Established: 501; Disestablished: 1455; Succeeded by: Pahang Sultanate

name: Pitrbhakta Dynasty
description: The Pitrbhakta Dynasty was a regional monarchical line that governed the Kalinga territory across northern Andhra Pradesh and southern Odisha during the sixth century. Establishing their seat at Simhapura, the rulers issued royal copper-plate charters declaring their filial piety and patronage of Shaivite religious establishments. The dynasty maintained regional trade and agrarian administration along the eastern seaboard until political competition with neighbouring powers culminated in the ascent of the Early Eastern Gangas. \n\n Status: Regional kingdom; Capital: Singupuram; Common languages: Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 501; Disestablished: 601; Preceded by: Mathara dynasty; Succeeded by: Eastern Ganga dynasty

name: Sarir
description: Sarir was a medieval Christian highland state established across the mountainous valleys of modern Dagestan in the north-eastern Caucasus. Named in Arabic records after the ceremonial golden throne that served as its dynastic emblem, the kingdom commanded vital trans-Caucasian mountain passes from its fortified redoubt at Khunzakh. The realm fiercely defended its political autonomy against successive invasions by the Khazars and the early Islamic Caliphate before internal fragmentation led to the emergence of the Avar Khanate. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Khunzakh; Common languages: Avar and Caucasian languages; Religion: Orthodox Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Early to High Middle Ages; Established: 501; Disestablished: 1101; Succeeded by: Avar Khanate

name: Srivijaya Empire
description: The Srivijaya Empire was a powerful Buddhist thalassocracy centred at Palembang on the island of Sumatra that dominated maritime trade across western Maritime Southeast Asia. Controlling the vital sea corridors of the Malacca and Sunda straits, the empire amassed vast wealth by levying transit tariffs and directing commerce between China, India and the Islamic world. Srivijaya also flourished as an international focal point of Mahayana scholarship until naval incursions by the Chola Empire eroded its regional hegemony. \n\n Status: Thalassocratic empire; Capital: Palembang; Common languages: Old Malay and Sanskrit; Religion: Mahayana Buddhism and Hinduism; Government: Mandala monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 501; Disestablished: 1401; Succeeded by: Melayu Kingdom

name: Liang
label: northern and southern dynasties (chinese history)
description: The Liang dynasty was the third of the Southern dynasties of China, ruling the fertile middle and lower Yangtze valleys from its imperial seat at Jiankang. Established by Xiao Yan, later canonised as Emperor Wu, the dynasty experienced an extended era of cultural flowering, commercial prosperity and enthusiastic imperial patronage of Buddhism. This stability was shattered by the devastating Hou Jing rebellion in the late 540s, which crippled the state and precipitated its replacement by the Chen dynasty. \n\n Status: Imperial dynasty; Capital: Nanjing; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Imperial autocracy; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Northern and Southern dynasties; Established: 30 April 502; Disestablished: 16 November 557; Preceded by: Southern Qi; Succeeded by: Chen dynasty

name: Kingdom of Uí Failghe
label: irish medieval kingdoms;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Uí Failghe was a durable Gaelic polity located in the Irish midlands, encompassing territory across present-day counties Offaly, Kildare and Laois. Governed by native dynasties that traced descent from Failge Berraide, the kingdom defended its bogland borders against neighbouring Leinster septs and Anglo-Norman settlers. It retained traditional brehon legal structures and political sovereignty until the mid-sixteenth century, when Tudor military campaigns subdued the region and shired it into County Offaly. \n\n Status: Gaelic kingdom; Capital: Rathangan; Common languages: Old Irish, Middle Irish and Early Modern Irish; Religion: Celtic Christianity and Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Early Middle Ages to Early Modern; Established: 508; Disestablished: 1551; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Ireland

name: Kingdom of the Visigoths
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Visigoths entered a distinct phase of Ostrogothic tutelage between 511 and 527 following disastrous territorial losses to the Franks in Gaul. Ruling in the name of his infant grandson King Amalaric, Theodoric the Great exercised direct regency and administrative oversight from Ravenna over the Iberian domains. This arrangement stabilised the Visigothic realm and defended its frontiers against Frankish expansion until Theodoric died in 526, enabling Amalaric to assume sovereign personal governance. \n\n Status: Protectorate under Ostrogothic Kingdom; Capital: Toledo; Common languages: Gothic, Latin and Vulgar Latin; Religion: Arian Christianity; Government: Monarchy under regency; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 511; Disestablished: 527; Preceded by: Visigothic Kingdom; Succeeded by: Visigothic Kingdom

name: Kingdom of the Franks
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of the Franks centred at Orléans was one of four Merovingian partition realms created following the death of King Clovis I in November 511. Assigned to his second son Chlodomer, the kingdom encompassed territories across the Loire Valley and portions of northern Aquitaine. Chlodomer actively pursued aggressive foreign policy against the Burgundians until he was killed at the Battle of Vézeronce in 524, after which his brothers murdered his heirs and partitioned his lands. \n\n Status: Partition kingdom; Capital: Orléans; Common languages: Frankish and Gallo-Romance Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Merovingian; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 27 November 511; Disestablished: 525; Preceded by: Kingdom of the Franks; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Franks

name: Kingdom of the Franks
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of the Franks centred at Metz comprised the eastern Austrasian core of the Merovingian realm established during the imperial division of November 511. Allocated to Clovis's eldest son Theuderic I, the state bordered the Rhine frontier, governing both Romanised Gaul and subjugated Germanic territories eastwards into Thuringia. Successive kings defended the realm against nomadic raids and Gothic conflicts until the childless death of King Theudebald in 555 enabled Chlothar I to annex the territory. \n\n Status: Partition kingdom; Capital: Metz; Common languages: Frankish, Old High German and Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Merovingian; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 27 November 511; Disestablished: 556; Preceded by: Kingdom of the Franks; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Franks

name: Kingdom of the Franks
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of the Franks centred at Paris was established under the partition of 511 for Childebert I, the third son of King Clovis I. Spanning the Île-de-France, the lower Seine basin and coastal Normandy, the realm expanded southwards into Aquitaine and incorporated parts of Orléans following joint Frankish military campaigns. Childebert governed this prosperous western domain for nearly five decades until his death without male heirs in December 558, allowing his brother Chlothar I to reunite all Frankish territories. \n\n Status: Partition kingdom; Capital: Paris; Common languages: Frankish and Gallo-Romance Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Merovingian; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 27 November 511; Disestablished: 23 December 558; Preceded by: Kingdom of the Franks; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Franks

name: Kingdom of the Franks
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of the Franks centred at Soissons formed the north-western territorial share inherited by King Chlothar I upon the death of Clovis I in November 511. Anchored in the Salian Frankish homelands between the Meuse and Somme rivers, the monarchy conducted relentless campaigns against neighbouring rivals and annexed adjacent lands after dynastic assassinations. Through longevity, strategic alliances and brutal civil warfare, Chlothar outlived his brothers to absorb their dominions in late 558, briefly uniting the Frankish realm. \n\n Status: Partition kingdom; Capital: Soissons; Common languages: Frankish and Gallo-Romance Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Merovingian; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 27 November 511; Disestablished: 23 December 558; Preceded by: Kingdom of the Franks; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Franks

name: Kingdom of Wihtwara
label: saxon polities in britain
description: The Kingdom of Wihtwara was an independent early medieval insular realm established by Jutish migrants on the Isle of Wight off the southern English coast. Operating from fortified earthworks at Carisbrooke, the islanders sustained a maritime society that stubbornly preserved Germanic pagan practices long after surrounding mainland peoples adopted Christianity. The kingdom came to a violent end in the late 680s when King Cædwalla of Wessex launched a devastating invasion, killed King Arwald and incorporated the island. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Carisbrooke; Common languages: Old English; Religion: Anglo-Saxon paganism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 513; Disestablished: 687; Preceded by: Sub-Roman Britain; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Wessex

name: Antes Confederation
description: The Antes Confederation was an early Slavic political and military union that occupied the forest-steppe zones between the Dniester, Dnieper and Don rivers during the sixth century. Associated archaeologically with the Penkovka culture, the confederacy initially raided the Danubian frontier before entering formal treaty alliances as Byzantine foederati guarding against nomadic incursions. Antean military power flourished across Eastern Europe until punitive campaigns by the Pannonian Avars in the early seventh century shattered the tribal league. \n\n Status: Tribal confederation; Capital: Kyiv; Common languages: Proto-Slavic; Religion: Slavic paganism; Government: Tribal union; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 519; Disestablished: 603; Succeeded by: Pannonian Avars

name: Kingdom of Wessex
label: saxon polities in britain
description: The Kingdom of Wessex was an Anglo-Saxon monarchy established across southern Britain that gradually expanded from the Hampshire lowlands to encompass all southern England. Governed by the House of Cerdic from its royal capital at Winchester, the kingdom successfully reorganised its military and naval defences to withstand extensive Viking incursions during the ninth century. Under King Alfred the Great and his successors, Wessex launched concerted counter-offensives that conquered Danish territories, culminating in the unification of England in 927. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Winchester; Common languages: Old English and Latin; Religion: Anglo-Saxon paganism and Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Wessex; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 520; Disestablished: 928; Succeeded by: Kingdom of England

name: Kingdom of the Franks (Military Occupation)
description: The Kingdom of the Franks under joint military occupation functioned as a temporary condominium administered across disputed Burgundian frontier lands during the fraternal campaigns of 524 and 525. Following concerted invasions orchestrated by Kings Childebert I, Chlodomer and Chlothar I, the territory was garrisoned directly by allied Frankish royal retinues without establishing a permanent provincial capital. This wartime administration maintained military control and extracted tribute until Chlodomer fell in battle and his brothers partitioned regional spheres of influence. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Frankish and Gallo-Romance Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Military condominium; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 524; Disestablished: 525; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Franks

name: Rano
label: hausa states
description: Rano was an ancient Hausa city-state and autonomous kingdom founded in the fertile savannah plains of modern northern Nigeria. Counted by indigenous historical tradition among the foundational Hausa Bakwai realms, the state developed extensive ironworking, agricultural terracing and trans-Saharan trading connections. Governed by hereditary chieftains and later kings from their walled capital, Rano preserved political sovereignty for centuries before the rising power of neighbouring Kano gradually overshadowed and incorporated its domain. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Rano; Common languages: Hausa; Religion: Traditional Hausa religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Early to High Middle Ages; Established: 524; Disestablished: 1351; Historical region: Hausaland

name: Kingdom of Essex
label: saxon polities in britain
description: The Kingdom of Essex was an early medieval Anglo-Saxon realm established in south-eastern Britain across modern Essex, Middlesex and eastern Hertfordshire. Centred initially upon ancient Colchester and London, the monarchy controlled commercial river trade along the Thames estuary while balancing the conflicting political influences of Kent and Mercia. Although the kingdom maintained its own royal line and converted to Christianity during the seventh century, persistent Mercian hegemony eventually eroded its autonomy, leading to annexation by Wessex in 825. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Colchester; Common languages: Old English; Religion: Anglo-Saxon paganism and Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 528; Disestablished: 826; Preceded by: Sub-Roman Britain; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Wessex

name: Kingdom of Mercia
label: anglian polities in britain
description: The Kingdom of Mercia was a major Anglo-Saxon state centred on the River Trent and the fertile river valleys of the English Midlands. Rising from a borderland petty realm, Mercia expanded rapidly through formidable military leadership, achieving south-English hegemony during the eighth-century Mercian Supremacy under King Offa. The kingdom maintained flourishing administrative networks, issued sophisticated coinage and constructed extensive frontier earthworks along the Welsh border before internal instability and Viking incursions brought about its partition and absorption by Wessex. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Tamworth; Common languages: Mercian Old English and Latin; Religion: Anglo-Saxon paganism and Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 528; Disestablished: 880; Preceded by: Sub-Roman Britain; Succeeded by: Kingdom of England

name: Champa Kingdom
description: The Champa Kingdom was a confederation of seafaring Austronesian city-states that stretched along the central and southern coastline of modern Vietnam. Flourishing upon maritime trade routes across the South China Sea, the Cham realms developed rich temple complexes and sophisticated irrigated agriculture under monarchs devoted to syncretic Hinduism and Buddhism. Despite enduring recurrent invasions from Chinese dynasties, the Khmer Empire and expanding Vietnamese states, Champa preserved its maritime mercantile culture and political autonomy for over a millennium. \n\n Status: Maritime kingdom; Capital: Kandapurpura; Common languages: Old Cham, Old Malay and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King of Champa; Historical era: Early Middle Ages to Modern era; Established: 530; Disestablished: 1833; Succeeded by: Nguyen dynasty

name: Tribal Confederation of the Saxons
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Tribal Confederation of the Saxons comprised a loose defensive union of pagan Germanic pagi occupying the plains between the Rhine and Elbe rivers. Following early Merovingian campaigns, the confederacy owed nominal tribute to Frankish monarchs while jealously maintaining customary pagan religion and decentralised self-governance. Devoid of a single urban capital, local chieftains coordinated regional affairs through an annual general assembly at Marklo until Charlemagne's protracted Saxon Wars forced their baptism and political incorporation into the Frankish Empire. \n\n Status: Vassal tribal confederation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Old Saxon; Religion: Germanic paganism; Government: Tribal confederation; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 532; Disestablished: 783; Succeeded by: Duchy of Saxony

name: Kingdom of the Franks (Military Occupation)
description: The Kingdom of the Franks under joint military occupation constituted an expeditionary wartime regime established in 534 during the final Frankish conquest of the Burgundian kingdom. Led jointly by the Merovingian brothers Childebert I and Chlothar I, allied armies overran the Rhône and Saône valleys, bringing an end to the reign of King Godomar. Operating without a permanent municipal seat, the occupying monarchs maintained garrison outposts to pacify Burgundian strongholds before partitioning the territory into their respective Frankish realms. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Frankish and Gallo-Romance Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Military condominium; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 534; Disestablished: 534; Preceded by: Kingdom of the Burgundians; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Franks

name: Wei
label: northern and southern dynasties (chinese history)
description: The Eastern Wei dynasty was a northern Chinese imperial realm established in 534 following the internal disintegration and partition of the Northern Wei Empire. Controlled politically and militarily by the paramount general Gao Huan, the dynasty ruled eastern northern China from its capital at Yecheng under the figurehead monarch Emperor Xiaojing. The state waged protracted warfare against the rival Western Wei along the Yellow River before Gao Huan's son deposed the emperor in 550 to establish the Northern Qi dynasty. \n\n Status: Imperial dynasty; Capital: Handan; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Xianbei; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Imperial autocracy; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Northern and Southern dynasties; Established: 8 November 534; Disestablished: 551; Preceded by: Northern Wei; Succeeded by: Northern Qi

name: Provence
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: Provence was an autonomous Mediterranean territory in south-eastern Gaul governed under Frankish overlordship between 538 and 561. Ceded by the Ostrogothic king Witiges to secure Frankish neutrality during the Byzantine-Gothic War, the province retained its distinctive Roman legal traditions, ecclesiastical metropolitanate at Arles and lucrative maritime commerce. Merovingian rulers administered the region through patricians who balanced regional municipal autonomy with Frankish fiscal obligations until the death of King Chlothar I prompted further administrative reorganisation. \n\n Status: Vassal territory of the Frankish Empire; Capital: Arles; Common languages: Vulgar Latin, Gallo-Romance and Frankish; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Principality under patricians; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 538; Disestablished: 29 November 561; Preceded by: Ostrogothic Kingdom; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Franks

name: Vạn Xuân
description: Vạn Xuân was an early independent Vietnamese monarchy established in the Red River Delta following a successful uprising against the southern Chinese Liang dynasty in 542. Proclaimed by its founder Lý Bí, who adopted the imperial title of Southern Emperor, the state established its administrative capital at Long Biên and promoted indigenous administrative autonomy. Despite persistent military pressure from Chinese imperial commanders, the realm defended its sovereignty for six decades until the reunified Sui dynasty invaded and reconquered northern Vietnam in 603. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Hanoi; Common languages: Proto-Vietnamese and Classical Chinese; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and indigenous Vietnamese religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Medieval Asia; Established: 542; Disestablished: 603; Preceded by: Liang dynasty; Succeeded by: Sui dynasty

name: Chalukya Dynasty
description: The Chalukya Dynasty was a prominent imperial power that emerged in the western Deccan during the mid-sixth century under King Pulakeshin I. Establishing their fortified capital at Vatapi, the Badami Chalukyas rapidly subdued neighbouring Kadamba feudatories and consolidated hegemony across the plateau between the Narmada and Kaveri rivers. Renowned for constructing spectacular rock-cut and structural temples at Aihole and Pattadakal, the dynasty dominated southern Indian politics until the rival Rashtrakutas eclipsed their authority in the mid-eighth century. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Badami; Common languages: Kannada and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism, Jainism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Chalukya; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 544; Disestablished: 758; Preceded by: Kadamba dynasty; Succeeded by: Rashtrakuta Empire

name: Calakmul
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Calakmul was a dominant Classic Maya superpower located in the tropical forests of the Petén Basin within the modern Mexican state of Campeche. Known in contemporary hieroglyphic inscriptions as the seat of the Kaan or Snake dynasty, the city-state exerted political and tributary hegemony over an extensive confederation of allied lowland centres. Calakmul engaged in prolonged geopolitical rivalries with its southern competitor Tikal, maintaining regional supremacy until disastrous military defeats in the late seventh century curtailed its imperial dominance. \n\n Status: Maya city-state; Capital: Calakmul; Common languages: Classic Maya; Religion: Maya religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Divine King (Ajaw); Historical era: Classic Maya; Established: 547; Disestablished: 696; Historical region: Mesoamerica

name: Kingdom of Bernicia
label: anglian polities in britain
description: The Kingdom of Bernicia was an Anglian realm established in north-eastern Britain during the sixth century, spanning coastal lands between the Firth of Forth and the River Tees. Operating from the formidable coastal citadel of Bamburgh, its founding rulers steadily expanded inland at the expense of native Brythonic kingdoms such as Gododdin. Under King Æthelfrith in the early seventh century, Bernicia absorbed its southern neighbour Deira, forming the united overkingdom of Northumbria and establishing northern Anglian supremacy. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Bamburgh; Common languages: Northumbrian Old English; Religion: Anglo-Saxon paganism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 548; Disestablished: 605; Preceded by: Sub-Roman Britain; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Northumbria

name: Cañari
description: The Cañari was an independent pre-Columbian tribal confederation that inhabited the inter-Andean valleys of modern southern Ecuador across Azuay and Cañar. Organised under a diarchical governance model, the federation maintained sophisticated metalworking, irrigated agriculture and fortified hill settlements centred around the sacred city of Tomebamba. The Cañari fiercely defended their mountain territories against multiple invading armies before the expanding Inca Empire under Huayna Capac subjugated the region in the late fifteenth century, heavily influencing its subsequent architectural landscape. \n\n Status: Tribal confederation; Capital: Tomebamba; Common languages: Cañari and Kichwa; Religion: Polytheism; Government: Diarchy; Historical era: Integration Period; Established: 551; Disestablished: 1439; Succeeded by: Inca Empire

name: Chamba State
description: Chamba State was an enduring Himalayan principality established in the upper Ravi River basin in modern Himachal Pradesh. Founded during the mid-sixth century by Raja Maru, the hill state governed secluded mountain valleys from its original seat at Bharmour before transferring the royal capital to Chamba in the tenth century. Protected by rugged alpine topography, the dynasty preserved ancient Hindu cultural institutions, copperplate charters and temple art while retaining uninterrupted local sovereignty until British colonial paramountcy was formalised in 1846. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Chamba; Common languages: Chambeali, Pahari and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early Middle Ages to Modern era; Established: 551; Disestablished: 3 September 1846; Succeeded by: British Empire

name: Chenla Kingdom
description: The Chenla Kingdom was an early Khmer political formation that emerged along the middle Mekong basin in Cambodia and southern Laos as the maritime kingdom of Funan declined. Governing a mandala network of regional aristocratic principalities, the state established its primary urban and religious capital at Isanapura under King Isanavarman. The realm patronised Shaivite state cults and sophisticated reservoir irrigation until dynastic rivalries fragmented the territory into northern Land Chenla and southern Water Chenla during the early eighth century. \n\n Status: Mandala kingdom; Capital: Isanapura; Common languages: Old Khmer and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 551; Disestablished: 708; Preceded by: Kingdom of Funan; Succeeded by: Khmer Empire

name: Comalcalco
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Comalcalco was an autonomous Classic Maya city-state located on the alluvial coastal plains of modern Tabasco in southern Mexico. Serving as the westernmost urban centre of the Maya world, the settlement developed a unique architectural style utilising kiln-fired clay bricks cemented with oyster-shell mortar due to the local scarcity of building limestone. Comalcalco functioned as a vital commercial nexus controlling cacao trade and riverine transport routes before regional societal collapse led to its abandonment in the mid-ninth century. \n\n Status: Maya city-state; Capital: Comalcalco; Common languages: Classic Maya; Religion: Maya religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Ajaw; Historical era: Classic Maya; Established: 551; Disestablished: 851; Historical region: Mesoamerica

name: Kalachuris of Mahishmati
description: The Kalachuris of Mahishmati were an early medieval Indian ruling dynasty that controlled west-central India, encompassing modern Maharashtra, southern Madhya Pradesh and mainland Gujarat. Ruling from their capital on the Narmada at Mahishmati, the monarchs issued extensive silver coinage and patronised magnificent rock-cut cave shrines, including early monuments at Elephanta and Ellora. The dynasty maintained regional supremacy for nearly a century before being decisively defeated and supplanted by the expanding Badami Chalukyas during the early seventh century. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Maheshwar; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 551; Disestablished: 643; Preceded by: Vakataka dynasty; Succeeded by: Chalukya dynasty

name: Kingdom of Cochin
description: The Kingdom of Cochin was an ancient South Indian principality established across the backwaters and fertile coastal lowlands of modern central Kerala. Known traditionally as the Perumpadappu Swaroopam, the polity prospered through extensive maritime spice trade with foreign merchants calling at its Malabar ports. While balancing relations with neighbouring Chera rulers and local Brahmin oligarchies, the monarchy preserved its hereditary lineage and regional autonomy until broader political reorganisation culminated in its formal sixteenth-century interactions with European naval powers. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Kochi; Common languages: Malayalam and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 551; Disestablished: 1501; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Cochin (Portuguese protectorate)

name: Late Nazca Culture
description: The Late Nazca Culture was an advanced Andean coastal society that occupied the arid river valleys of southern Peru along the Ica and Rio Grande drainages. Based ceremonially around the monumental adobe mounds of Cahuachi, the population constructed sophisticated underground aqueducts known as puquios to support desert agriculture. As prolonged environmental desiccation strained regional resources during the late sixth century, the culture underwent political decentralisation before being absorbed into the expanding Wari imperial sphere. \n\n Status: Archaeological culture; Capital: Cahuachi; Religion: Andean polytheism; Government: Theocratic confederation; Historical era: Early Intermediate; Established: 551; Disestablished: 601; Preceded by: Paracas culture; Succeeded by: Wari Empire

name: Later Gupta Dynasty
description: The Later Gupta Dynasty of Magadha functioned as a subordinate regional monarchy in northern India, governing the central Gangetic plains under Pushyabhuti imperial suzerainty. Operating from the historic metropolis of Pataliputra, the dynasty supplied military contingents and paid tribute to Emperor Harsha while retaining internal administrative governance over local estates. Following Harsha's death without an heir in 648, the Later Guptas reasserted independent authority across Bihar and parts of Bengal. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Pushyabhuti Empire; Capital: Patna; Common languages: Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Subordinate monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Later Gupta; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 551; Disestablished: 648; Succeeded by: Later Gupta Dynasty

name: Maukhari Kingdom
description: The Maukhari Kingdom was a powerful post-Gupta realm that established its political and military supremacy across the fertile Ganga-Yamuna doab from its fortified capital at Kannauj. Under monarchs such as Ishanavarman, the dynasty defended northern India against Hunnic incursions and consolidated extensive agrarian territories across Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. The state maintained close dynastic alliances with the Pushyabhutis of Thanesar until military conflict with the rulers of Malwa and Gauda culminated in its absorption into Harsha's empire. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Kannauj; Common languages: Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Maukhari; Ruler title: Maharajadhiraja; Historical era: Medieval India; Established: 551; Disestablished: 607; Succeeded by: Pushyabhuti Dynasty

name: Mutharaiyar Dynasty
description: The Mutharaiyar Dynasty was a notable regional ruling lineage that governed the fertile Kaveri delta in southern India, controlling territories across modern Thanjavur, Tiruchirappalli and Pudukkottai. Maintaining their capital at Thanjavur, the monarchs patronised classical Tamil literature, commissioned elegant cave shrines and sponsored both Shaivite and Jain institutions. The dynasty effectively balanced power between the competing Pallava and Pandya realms until the resurgent Chola chieftain Vijayalaya captured Thanjavur in the mid-ninth century, extinguishing their independence. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Thanjavur; Official languages: Tamil; Religion: Shaivism, Vaishnavism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Mutharaiyar; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 551; Disestablished: 852; Preceded by: Kalabhra dynasty; Succeeded by: Chola dynasty

name: Nala Dynasty
description: The Nala Dynasty was an early medieval Indian royal house that ruled the forested plateau regions of Bastar and Koraput across modern Chhattisgarh and Odisha. Operating from their fortified administrative centre at Pushkari, the kings issued gold coinage and successfully contested regional dominion against the neighbouring Vakatakas. Persistent military pressure from the expanding Badami Chalukyas and northern Sharabhapuriya rivals steadily weakened the dynasty, leading to its eventual displacement by the Panduvamshi lineage around the opening of the seventh century. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Pushkari; Common languages: Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 551; Disestablished: 601; Preceded by: Gupta Empire; Succeeded by: Panduvamshis of Dakshina Kosala

name: Osraighe
label: irish medieval kingdoms;celtic polities
description: Osraighe was an independent Gaelic kingdom in south-eastern Ireland that encompassed the fertile river valleys of modern County Kilkenny and western County Laois. Governed by the hereditary Dál Birn dynasty, the kingdom frequently acted as a pivotal buffer state between the overkingdoms of Munster and Leinster. Osraighe asserted complete political autonomy under King Cerball mac Dúnlainge and maintained sovereign institutions for centuries until Anglo-Norman forces under Richard de Clare and William Marshal overran the realm in the late twelfth century. \n\n Status: Gaelic kingdom; Capital: Kilkenny; Common languages: Old Irish and Middle Irish; Religion: Celtic Christianity and Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Dál Birn; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early to High Middle Ages; Established: 551; Disestablished: 1177; Succeeded by: Lordship of Ireland

name: Pushyabhuti Dynasty
description: The Pushyabhuti Dynasty was a dominant imperial house that originated in eastern Punjab at Sthanveshvara before extending its authority across northern India during the sixth and seventh centuries. Under its most renowned sovereign Harsha Vardhana, the realm incorporated disparate post-Gupta principalities from the Punjab to the Bengal delta, establishing a grand imperial court at Kannauj. The dynasty supported international Buddhist learning at Nalanda and conducted diplomatic exchanges with Tang China before disintegrating rapidly following Harsha's death in 648. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Thanesar; Common languages: Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Pushyabhuti; Ruler title: Maharajadhiraja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 551; Disestablished: 648; Succeeded by: Later Gupta Dynasty

name: Qi
description: The Northern Qi dynasty was an imperial Chinese realm that governed the prosperous north-eastern plains from its capital at Yecheng following the displacement of Eastern Wei in 550. Established by Emperor Wenxuan of the Gao family, the state fielded formidable Xianbei cavalry forces and sponsored remarkable achievements in Buddhist sculpture and ceramic arts. Despite its substantial economic wealth and military strength, political purges and dynastic instability undermined imperial governance, culminating in conquest by the rival Northern Zhou in February 577. \n\n Status: Imperial dynasty; Capital: Anyang; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Xianbei; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Imperial autocracy; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Northern and Southern dynasties; Established: 551; Disestablished: 28 February 577; Preceded by: Eastern Wei; Succeeded by: Northern Zhou

name: Rajarsitulyakula Dynasty
description: The Rajarsitulyakula Dynasty was an ancient royal lineage that held sway over the fertile plains of Dakshina Kosala in modern Chhattisgarh during the sixth century. Ruling from their administrative seat at Arang, the monarchs maintained classical Sanskrit administrative traditions and patronised Vedic Brahmanical rituals across the upper Mahanadi basin. The dynasty secured regional stability following the retreat of imperial Gupta influence, providing a crucial administrative foundation until competing local houses, notably the Parvatadvarakas and Nalas, supplanted its authority around 601. \n\n Status: Regional kingdom; Capital: Arang; Common languages: Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rajarsitulyakula; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 551; Disestablished: 601; Preceded by: Gupta Empire; Succeeded by: Parvatadvaraka Dynasty

name: Sharabhapuriya Dynasty
description: The Sharabhapuriya Dynasty was a prominent royal house that governed Dakshina Kosala across modern Chhattisgarh and western Odisha during the later sixth century. Issuing distinctive repoussé gold coinage and copper charters embossed with the image of Gaja-Lakshmi, the rulers administered their realm from capitals at Sharabhapura and Shripura. The kings patronised Vaishnavite shrines and oversaw substantial agricultural development along the Mahanadi River until internal dynastic shifts enabled the related Panduvamshi family to seize control of the territory in 591. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Malhar; Common languages: Sanskrit; Religion: Vaishnavism and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 551; Disestablished: 591; Preceded by: Gupta Empire; Succeeded by: Panduvamshis of Dakshina Kosala

name: Duchy of Bavaria
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Duchy of Bavaria was an early medieval Germanic principality established across the Alpine foreland and Danube basin by Bavarian tribes under the Agilolfing dynasty. Operating from their ancient ducal seat at Regensburg, the dukes enacted the Lex Baiuvariorum, promoted monastic Christianisation and maintained substantial diplomatic autonomy between the Frankish and Lombard realms. This sovereign status endured until Charlemagne accused Duke Tassilo III of treason, deposing the native dynasty in 788 and absorbing Bavaria directly into the Carolingian Empire. \n\n Status: Stem duchy; Capital: Regensburg; Common languages: Old High German and Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Agilolfing; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 552; Disestablished: 789; Succeeded by: Carolingian Empire

name: Turkic Khaganate
description: The Turkic Khaganate was a vast nomadic transcontinental empire established across the Eurasian steppe in 552 by Bumin Qaghan and the Ashina clan of the Göktürks. Overthrowing the Rouran Khaganate, the Göktürks rapidly expanded from the sacred Orkhon forest of Ötüken westwards to the Black Sea, dominating the northern Silk Road through Sogdian diplomatic and mercantile networks. After three decades of unified steppe hegemony, internal succession disputes and Chinese diplomatic manipulation splintered the khaganate into separate eastern and western realms in 582. \n\n Status: Nomadic empire; Capital: Otukan; Common languages: Old Turkic and Sogdian; Religion: Tengrism and Buddhism; Government: Khaganate; Ruling dynasty: Ashina; Ruler title: Khagan; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 552; Disestablished: 582; Preceded by: Rouran Khaganate; Succeeded by: Eastern Turkic Khaganate

name: Liang
label: northern and southern dynasties (chinese history)
description: The Western Liang dynasty was a client buffer state established in the middle Yangtze valley in 556 under the imperial sponsorship of the Xianbei-led Western Wei dynasty. Governed from the fortified city of Jiangling by Xiao Cha, a grandson of the Liang founder, the rump realm preserved Southern court rituals and administrative institutions while depending upon Western Wei garrisons for military survival. This initial puppet arrangement lasted until Western Wei political transitions transferred regional suzerainty to the emergent Northern Zhou court in 558. \n\n Status: Puppet state under Western Wei; Capital: Jiangling; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Imperial autocracy; Ruling dynasty: Xiao clan of Lanling; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Northern and Southern dynasties; Established: 556; Disestablished: 558; Preceded by: Liang dynasty; Succeeded by: Western Liang (under Northern Zhou)

name: Chen
label: northern and southern dynasties (chinese history)
description: The Chen dynasty was the fourth and final imperial regime of the Southern dynasties period, governing southern China from its capital at Jiankang between 557 and 589. Founded by General Chen Baxian amidst the wreckage of the Liang dynasty, the state restored fiscal stability, rebuilt agricultural productivity and successfully repelled multiple northern military invasions. Despite vigorous efforts to modernise river defences along the Yangtze, the realm was overwhelmed and annexed by the reunified Sui dynasty in February 589, concluding centuries of southern dynastic separation. \n\n Status: Imperial dynasty; Capital: Jiankang; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Imperial autocracy; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Northern and Southern dynasties; Established: 16 November 557; Disestablished: 10 February 589; Preceded by: Liang dynasty; Succeeded by: Sui dynasty

name: Liang
label: northern and southern dynasties (chinese history)
description: The Western Liang dynasty functioned as a subordinate client state under the suzerainty of the Northern Zhou dynasty across central Hubei from 558 to 582. Preserving the dynastic continuity of the southern Xiao clan at Jiangling, Emperor Ming governed local civil administration while relying upon Northern Zhou military detachments for frontier security against the Chen dynasty. This delicate balance of imperial diplomacy and domestic governance ended when the newly proclaimed Sui dynasty usurped Northern Zhou authority in 582. \n\n Status: Puppet state under Northern Zhou; Capital: Jiangling; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Imperial autocracy; Ruling dynasty: Xiao clan of Lanling; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Northern and Southern dynasties; Established: 558; Disestablished: 582; Preceded by: Western Liang (under Western Wei); Succeeded by: Western Liang (under Sui dynasty)

name: Zhou
label: northern and southern dynasties (chinese history)
description: The Northern Zhou dynasty was a powerful Xianbei-led imperial state that dominated northern China from its capital at Chang'an between 558 and 582. Governed by the Yuwen clan, the regime instituted the Fubing military system, revitalised ancient Zhou institutional titles and systematically consolidated its control across the Guanzhong region and Sichuan. Under Emperor Wu, the dynasty conquered the rival Northern Qi realm in 577 to unify northern China, before imperial minister Yang Jian seized the throne in 581 to establish the Sui dynasty. \n\n Status: Imperial dynasty; Capital: Chang'an; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Xianbei; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Imperial autocracy; Ruling dynasty: Yuwen clan; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Northern and Southern dynasties; Established: 558; Disestablished: 582; Preceded by: Western Wei; Succeeded by: Sui dynasty

name: Kingdom of Dál Riata
label: celtic polities in britain;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Dál Riata was a maritime Gaelic realm that spanned the sea lanes between western Scotland and north-eastern Ireland, incorporating Argyll and County Antrim. Governed from the formidable royal hillfort of Dunadd, the monarchy flourished through extensive maritime commerce, naval expeditions and monastic networks centred upon Saint Columba's abbey on Iona. Although the kingdom exerted widespread cultural and political influence across northern Britain, persistent Pictish counter-offensives eventually constrained its borders prior to the ninth-century dynastic unification of Scotland. \n\n Status: Gaelic kingdom; Capital: Dunadd; Common languages: Old Gaelic and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 561; Disestablished: 742; Preceded by: Ulaid; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Scotland

name: Principality of Chaghaniyan
label: tarim basin
description: The Principality of Chaghaniyan was an autonomous Iranian petty state located in the fertile Surkhan Darya valley north of the Oxus River. Governed by hereditary monarchs titled Chaghan Khudah, the principality asserted political independence following the collapse of the Hephthalite Empire in the 560s. The realm prospered through irrigated agriculture and overland Silk Road trade, fostering a syncretic cultural environment of Buddhism and Zoroastrianism until the Umayyad Caliphate subjugated the region during the Muslim conquest of Transoxiana in the early eighth century. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Denov; Common languages: Bactrian, Sogdian and Middle Persian; Religion: Buddhism and Zoroastrianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Chaghan Khudah; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 561; Disestablished: 706; Preceded by: Hephthalite Empire; Succeeded by: Umayyad Caliphate

name: Qarinvand Dynasty
description: The Qarinvand Dynasty was an indigenous Iranian noble house that ruled the rugged highlands of Tabaristan along the southern Caspian shore from the 560s onwards. Descended from the prestigious Parthian House of Karen, its dynastic princes bore the traditional military title of Ispahbadh and operated from mountain redoubts such as Lafur. The dynasty preserved Zoroastrian religious culture and fierce political autonomy against repeated Arab caliphal invasions for centuries before internal strife and regional Islamic dynasties extinguished their highland realm. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Lafur; Common languages: Tabari, Middle Persian and Persian; Religion: Zoroastrianism and Islam; Government: Hereditary military regime; Ruling dynasty: House of Karen; Ruler title: Ispahbadh; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 561; Disestablished: 1043; Preceded by: Sasanian Empire

name: Kingdom of the Franks
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of the Franks centred at Paris was formed under the Merovingian imperial partition of November 561 following the death of King Chlothar I. Allotted to his second surviving son Charibert I, the state comprised the lower Seine basin, western Armorican borderlands and expansive territories across Aquitaine. Charibert's reign was marked by turbulent relations with the Gallic episcopate and complex fiscal administration until his untimely death in late 567 prompted his three surviving brothers to divide his vast western domains among themselves. \n\n Status: Partition kingdom; Capital: Paris; Common languages: Frankish and Gallo-Romance Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Merovingian; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 29 November 561; Disestablished: 568; Preceded by: Kingdom of the Franks; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Franks

name: Kingdom of the Franks
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of the Franks centred at Orléans was a major Merovingian realm governed by King Guntram following the territorial partition of November 561. Encompassing the historic Burgundian lands, the Rhône Valley and southern urban centres, the kingdom maintained a reputation for judicial stability, ecclesiastical synods and diplomatic moderation amidst bitter dynastic civil wars. Guntram secured the realm's long-term continuity through the Treaty of Andelot in 587, bequeathing his territory upon his death in 592 to his nephew Childebert II of Austrasia. \n\n Status: Partition kingdom; Capital: Orléans; Common languages: Frankish and Gallo-Romance Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Merovingian; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 29 November 561; Disestablished: 593; Preceded by: Kingdom of the Franks; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Franks

name: Kingdom of the Franks
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of the Franks centred at Metz comprised the north-eastern Austrasian portion of the Merovingian monarchy created upon the partition of 561. Allocated to King Sigebert I, the realm repelled eastern Avar invasions along the Danube frontier and engaged in decades of bitter dynastic warfare against Neustrian rivals. Following Sigebert's assassination in 575, his queen Brunhilda and son Childebert II maintained central governance, eventually absorbing the Burgundian inheritance of King Guntram before further dynastic divisions reshaped the Frankish state. \n\n Status: Partition kingdom; Capital: Metz; Common languages: Frankish, Old High German and Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Merovingian; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 29 November 561; Disestablished: 594; Preceded by: Kingdom of the Franks; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Franks

name: Kingdom of the Franks
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of the Franks centred at Soissons formed the western Neustrian realm inherited by King Chilperic I upon the partition of 561. Anchored in the Salian heartlands between the Scheldt and the Seine, the state expanded through ruthless dynastic warfare against Austrasian and Burgundian relatives. Following Chilperic's assassination in 584, Queen Fredegund defended the infant king Chlothar II against aggressive external rivals until Chlothar attained adulthood, crushed his dynastic opponents and reunified the entire Frankish kingdom in 613. \n\n Status: Partition kingdom; Capital: Soissons; Common languages: Frankish and Gallo-Romance Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Merovingian; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 29 November 561; Disestablished: 614; Preceded by: Kingdom of the Franks; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Franks

name: Avar Khaganate
description: The Avar Khaganate was a formidable nomadic empire established in the Carpathian Basin during the late sixth century under the leadership of Khagan Bayan. Operating from their fortified ring encampments and the strategic Danubian stronghold of Sirmium, the Avars dominated subject Slavic, Germanic and Romanised populations across Central and South-Eastern Europe. The khaganate mounted massive military campaigns against the Byzantine Empire before internal fragmentation and Charlemagne's decisive Carolingian campaigns in the late 790s extinguished their nomadic hegemony. \n\n Status: Nomadic empire; Capital: Sirmium; Common languages: Turkic, Mongolic and Proto-Slavic; Religion: Tengrism, Slavic paganism and Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Khaganate; Ruler title: Khagan; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 563; Disestablished: 797; Preceded by: Kingdom of the Gepids; Succeeded by: Carolingian Empire

name: Tokhara Yabghus
description: The Tokhara Yabghus were a ruling dynasty of Western Turk princes who governed the historic region of Tokharistan on both banks of the Oxus River. Establishing their administrative and spiritual centres around Balkh and Kunduz, these yabghus ruled over local Bactrian and Hephthalite populations, issuing distinctive coinage and providing generous patronage to Mahayana Buddhist monastic sanctuaries. The dynasty maintained regional trade and mountain frontier defences until Arab Muslim incursions and Tang Chinese imperial expansion dismantled their authority in the mid-seventh century. \n\n Status: Subordinate kingdom; Capital: Balkh; Common languages: Bactrian and Old Turkic; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Yabghu; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 566; Disestablished: 654; Preceded by: Hephthalite Empire; Succeeded by: Tang dynasty

name: Kingdom of the Lombards
label: lombard polities;barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Lombards was an early medieval Germanic state established across the Italian peninsula following King Alboin's invasion in May 568. Governed from its royal capital at Pavia, the monarchy divided northern Italy into autonomous duchies while contesting control over central and southern territories against the Byzantine Exarchate of Ravenna. Over two centuries, the Lombards codified written laws, converted from Arianism to Roman Catholicism and assimilated Latin administrative customs before Charlemagne conquered Pavia in 774, annexing the kingdom into the Frankish realm. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Pavia; Common languages: Lombardic, Vulgar Latin and Medieval Latin; Religion: Arianism and Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Elective monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 1 May 568; Disestablished: 775; Preceded by: Byzantine Empire; Succeeded by: Carolingian Empire

name: Alodia
label: christian kingdoms of nubia
description: Alodia was a flourishing medieval Christian kingdom established in central Sudan following the dissolution of the Kingdom of Kush. Centred upon its opulent capital of Soba near the confluence of the Blue and White Niles, the realm developed extensive riverine trade networks connecting Egypt, the Red Sea and sub-Saharan Africa. The monarchy sustained Greek and Old Nubian literacy alongside vibrant Coptic monastic traditions for nearly a millennium before nomadic Arab migrations and the rising Funj Sultanate dismantled the state around 1505. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Soba; Common languages: Old Nubian and Greek; Religion: Coptic Orthodox Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 570; Disestablished: 1505; Preceded by: Kingdom of Kush; Succeeded by: Funj Sultanate

name: Duchy of Spoleto
label: lombard polities
description: The Duchy of Spoleto was an influential Lombard principality founded in the mountainous interior of central Italy by Duke Faroald I in 571. Controlling vital transit arteries along the Via Flaminia, the dukes exercised broad political and military autonomy, maintaining independent diplomatic relations and frequently challenging the authority of the Lombard royal court in Pavia. The duchy defended its borders against Byzantine Rome and Ravenna until the Carolingian conquest of 774 transformed it into a subordinate imperial fief within the Western Empire. \n\n Status: Duchy; Capital: Spoleto; Common languages: Lombardic and Vulgar Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 571; Disestablished: 777; Preceded by: Byzantine Empire; Succeeded by: Carolingian Empire

name: Kingdom of East Anglia
label: anglian polities in britain
description: The Kingdom of East Anglia was an early medieval Anglo-Saxon monarchy established across modern Norfolk and Suffolk by Anglian settlers during the sixth century. Governed by the illustrious Wuffingas dynasty, the realm attained paramount prestige across Britain under King Rædwald, whose affluent court culture was preserved in the magnificent ship burials at Sutton Hoo. The kingdom navigated complex rivalries with neighbouring Mercia before the Danish Great Heathen Army invaded in 869, executing King Edmund the Martyr and establishing the Danelaw. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Norwich; Common languages: Old English; Religion: Anglo-Saxon paganism and Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Wuffingas; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 572; Disestablished: 1 December 869; Preceded by: Sub-Roman Britain; Succeeded by: Danelaw

name: Duchy of Benevento
label: lombard polities
description: The Duchy of Benevento was the premier Lombard state in southern Italy, established across the mountainous Samnite uplands by Duke Zotto in 577. Separated geographically from the northern kingdom by the Byzantine and Papal corridors, Benevento governed with near-total political sovereignty and repelled repeated imperial offensives from Naples and Byzantine Apulia. The duchy developed distinctive Lombard legal and religious traditions, enduring well beyond the Frankish conquest of northern Italy in 774 to evolve into an independent southern principality. \n\n Status: Duchy; Capital: Benevento; Common languages: Lombardic and Vulgar Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 577; Disestablished: 730; Preceded by: Byzantine Empire; Succeeded by: Principality of Benevento

name: Kingdom of the Hwicce
label: celtic polities in britain;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of the Hwicce was an early Anglo-Saxon tribal polity established in the lower Severn basin and Cotswolds following the pivotal Battle of Deorham in 577. Centred upon the ancient Roman river crossing at Worcester, the realm incorporated mixed Saxon and native Brythonic populations into a prosperous agricultural and pastoral territory. The monarchy maintained political independence for half a century until the ambitious King Penda of Mercia secured victory at the Battle of Cirencester in 628, reducing Hwicce to a subordinate sub-kingdom. \n\n Status: Tribal kingdom; Capital: Worcester; Common languages: Old English and Brittonic; Religion: Anglo-Saxon paganism and Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 578; Disestablished: 629; Preceded by: Sub-Roman Britain; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Mercia

name: Bro Waroc'h
label: celtic polities of brittany;celtic polities
description: Bro Waroc'h was an early medieval Brythonic realm in south-eastern Armorica that entered tributary vassalage to King Chilperic I of Soissons between 579 and 588. Governed from the fortified episcopal see of Vannes by the resolute Breton ruler Waroch II, the territory balanced Celtic legal customs with the payment of tribute to the Neustrian Frankish court. Despite acknowledging formal Merovingian suzerainty, Waroch regularly launched retaliatory border raids against Frankish garrisons until Chilperic's death enabled the principality to renegotiate its political allegiance. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of Soissons; Capital: Vannes; Common languages: Early Breton and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Subordinate monarchy; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 579; Disestablished: 588; Preceded by: Bro Waroc'h; Succeeded by: Bro Waroc'h (vassal under Orleans)

name: Chalukyas of Badami
description: The Chalukyas of Badami were an illustrious imperial dynasty that exercised supreme authority across central and southern India from 579 until the mid-eighth century. Ruling from the cliff-fortress of Vatapi, the emperors subdued neighbouring peninsular realms and famously halted the southward imperial advance of Emperor Harsha at the Narmada River under Pulakeshin II. name: Cornouaille
label: celtic polities of brittany;celtic polities
description: Cornouaille functioned as a subordinate Celtic principality on the western Armorican peninsula under the suzerainty of King Chilperic I of Soissons from 579 to 588. Centred upon Quimper, the Breton countship maintained native administrative and ecclesiastical authority while providing annual tribute to the Neustrian royal court following Frankish military expeditions. name: Domnonia
label: celtic polities of brittany;celtic polities
description: Domnonia was a Brythonic coastal kingdom in northern Brittany that accepted Frankish suzerainty under King Chilperic I of Soissons between 579 and 588. Administered from Saint-Brieuc, the monarchy maintained customary Celtic legal codes and sea trade across the English Channel while fulfilling diplomatic and tribute obligations imposed by the Neustrian Merovingians. name: Kingdom of Altava
label: roman-maurian kingdoms;berber kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Altava was an independent Christian Berber realm that emerged in modern north-western Algeria following the collapse of the Mauro-Roman Kingdom in 578. Centred upon the fortified Roman city of Altava, the state unified disparate Moorish tribes and Gallo-Roman communities across the former province of Mauretania Caesariensis. Under legendary monarchs such as Aksel, the kingdom spearheaded regional military resistance against incoming Islamic armies before final conquest by the Umayyad Caliphate brought an end to Berber sovereignty in 709. \n\n Status: Berber kingdom; Capital: Altava; Common languages: Berber, African Romance and Latin; Religion: Nicene Christianity and Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 579; Disestablished: 709; Preceded by: Mauro-Roman Kingdom; Succeeded by: Umayyad Caliphate

name: Kingdom of Cabaon
label: roman-maurian kingdoms;berber kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Cabaon was a semi-autonomous Romano-Berber polity established along the arid coastline and desert hinterlands of Tripolitania around modern Tripoli. Emerging from tribal confederacies that resisted both Vandal rule and Byzantine encroachment through mobile camel warfare, the state preserved regional pastoral independence and Romano-African commercial contacts. The kingdom maintained its traditional territorial autonomy across the coastal oases for more than a century until expanding Arab Muslim armies under the Umayyad Caliphate absorbed Tripolitania during the late seventh century. \n\n Status: Tribal kingdom; Capital: Tripoli; Common languages: Berber and African Romance; Religion: Traditional Berber religion and Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Chieftain; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 579; Disestablished: 709; Preceded by: Mauro-Roman Kingdom; Succeeded by: Umayyad Caliphate

name: Kingdom of Capsus
label: roman-maurian kingdoms;berber kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Capsus was an autonomous Romano-Berber state located around the strategic oasis settlement of Capsa in modern southern Tunisia. Established during the political fragmentation of the post-Vandal North African interior, the realm commanded overland caravan routes connecting the Mediterranean coast with the Saharan trade networks. The polity retained distinct Berber tribal traditions alongside lingering Latin municipal customs until the eastward campaigns of the Umayyad Caliphate integrated the oasis region into the wider Islamic empire in the early eighth century. \n\n Status: Oasis kingdom; Administrative seat: Capsa; Common languages: Berber and African Romance; Religion: Christianity and traditional Berber religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 579; Disestablished: 709; Preceded by: Mauro-Roman Kingdom; Succeeded by: Umayyad Caliphate

name: Kingdom of the Dorsale
label: roman-maurian kingdoms;berber kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Dorsale was a robust Romano-Berber confederation established by the Frexes and Naffur tribes across the mountainous dorsal ridges of modern Tunisia and eastern Algeria. Centred near the fortified border hub of Tébessa, the kingdom rose to military prominence under King Antalas, defeating Vandal forces and later mounting fierce insurrections against Byzantine imperial garrisons. The warrior confederation maintained its upland independence through guerrilla warfare until final subjugation by the Umayyad Caliphate in the opening decade of the eighth century. \n\n Status: Tribal confederation; Capital: Tébessa; Common languages: Berber, African Romance and Latin; Religion: Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 579; Disestablished: 709; Preceded by: Vandal Kingdom; Succeeded by: Umayyad Caliphate

name: Kingdom of the Hodna
label: roman-maurian kingdoms;berber kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Hodna was an autonomous Romano-Berber highland realm located around the Hodna Mountains and the surrounding salt flats of north-central Algeria. Arising from the fragmentation of earlier Moorish confederacies, the state maintained strategic alliances and periodic conflicts with Byzantine authorities under native kings such as Ortaias. Operating from mountain redoubts without a fixed metropolitan capital, the kingdom defended its upland pastures and agrarian communities until Umayyad armies conquered the Algerian interior during the early eighth century. \n\n Status: Highland kingdom; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Berber and African Romance; Religion: Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 579; Disestablished: 709; Preceded by: Mauro-Roman Kingdom; Succeeded by: Umayyad Caliphate

name: Kingdom of the Nemencha
label: roman-maurian kingdoms;berber kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Nemencha was a resilient Berber highland state established across the rugged Nemencha Mountains of modern eastern Algeria. Formed in the wake of imperial Roman withdrawal and the fracturing of the Mauro-Roman Kingdom, the polity relied upon fortified mountain passes and pastoral pastoralism to sustain its independence. The mountain clans fiercely resisted Byzantine administrative control and avoided lowland entanglements until sweeping Umayyad military expeditions incorporated the eastern Maghreb into the Islamic Caliphate during the late seventh century. \n\n Status: Highland kingdom; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Berber and African Romance; Religion: Traditional Berber religion and Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 579; Disestablished: 709; Preceded by: Mauro-Roman Kingdom; Succeeded by: Umayyad Caliphate

name: Kingdom of the Ouarsenis
label: roman-maurian kingdoms;berber kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of the Ouarsenis was an independent Romano-Berber principality established across the rugged Ouarsenis mountain massif and the high plateau of Tiaret in western Algeria. Renowned for constructing the monumental Jedars royal tumuli, the realm blended late Roman administrative titles with traditional Berber clan governance.
