name: Kingdom of Ulaid
label: irish medieval kingdoms;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Ulaid was an ancient Gaelic overkingdom in north-eastern Ireland that encompassed territories east of the River Bann across modern counties Down and Antrim. Governed primarily by the Dál Fiatach dynasty from their royal hill seat at Downpatrick, the kingdom reached an apex of martial ambition under King Báetán mac Cairill, who extended suzerainty across the Irish Sea to the Isle of Man. Following Báetán's death, external counter-attacks by neighbouring northern Uí Néill kingdoms curtailed Ulaid's maritime expansion and restored its regional borders. \n\n Status: Gaelic overkingdom; Capital: Downpatrick; Common languages: Old Irish; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Dál Fiatach; Ruler title: King of Ulaid; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 579; Disestablished: 583; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Ulaid

name: Principality of Iberia
description: The Principality of Iberia was an early medieval Georgian aristocratic realm established in the central region of Kartli under the suzerainty of the Eastern Roman Empire. Created following the collapse of the indigenous royal monarchy, the principality was led by presiding princes such as Guaram I, who received Byzantine patrician honours in exchange for guarding Caucasian mountain passes against Sasanian Persian forces. The regime fostered the development of early Georgian ecclesiastical literature and Christian monumental architecture while serving as a strategic Byzantine buffer state. \n\n Status: Client principality of the Eastern Roman Empire; Capital: Tbilisi; Common languages: Georgian; Religion: Georgian Orthodox Christianity; Government: Aristocratic principate; Ruler title: Presiding Prince; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 581; Disestablished: 738; Preceded by: Kingdom of Iberia; Succeeded by: Principality of Kakheti

name: Eastern Turkic Khaganate
description: The Eastern Turkic Khaganate was a nomadic steppe empire that controlled the Mongolian Plateau following the partition of the original Göktürk realm in 582. Anchored politically around the sacred forest mountain of Ötüken, the khagans commanded vast mobile cavalry formations and extracted heavy tributary concessions from northern Chinese borders during the late Sui period. However, internal factional disputes and severe steppe blizzards weakened the polity, allowing the Tang Empire under Emperor Taizong to crush their forces and capture their last ruler in 630. \n\n Status: Nomadic empire; Capital: Otukan; Common languages: Old Turkic and Middle Chinese; Religion: Tengrism and Buddhism; Government: Khaganate; Ruling dynasty: Ashina; Ruler title: Khagan; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 582; Disestablished: 646; Preceded by: First Turkic Khaganate; Succeeded by: Tang dynasty

name: Liang
label: northern and southern dynasties (chinese history)
description: The Western Liang dynasty entered its final political phase as a client principality under the newly established Sui dynasty between 582 and 588. Operating from Jiangling along the middle Yangtze, the regime retained formal Southern imperial court rituals and administrative offices under Emperor Ming and his successor Emperor Jing. name: Northern Turkic Khaganate
description: The Northern Turkic Khaganate was an ephemeral nomadic splinter state that arose on the northern Mongolian steppe during the chaotic Göktürk civil war of the 580s. Formed by dissident Ashina princes seeking to carve out an independent dominion away from the primary Eastern and Western khaganates, the faction established its base of operations around the Orkhon River basin. Lacking broad tribal consensus and targeted by concerted diplomatic sabotage from the Sui dynasty, the northern confederacy rapidly collapsed and was partitioned between rival steppe factions by 585. \n\n Status: Nomadic khaganate; Capital: Ordu-Baliq; Common languages: Old Turkic; Religion: Tengrism; Government: Khaganate; Ruling dynasty: Ashina; Ruler title: Khagan; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 582; Disestablished: 585; Preceded by: First Turkic Khaganate; Succeeded by: Eastern Turkic Khaganate

name: Sui
description: The Sui dynasty was a transformative imperial power that brought an end to nearly three centuries of Chinese political division by conquering the southern Chen dynasty in 589. Established by Emperor Wen from the northern capital of Chang'an, the dynasty implemented far-reaching administrative centralisation, instituted the equal-field agricultural system and commenced construction of the Grand Canal. However, exorbitant taxation, forced labour and catastrophic military expeditions against the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo under Emperor Yang triggered widespread rebellions, leading to the dynasty's collapse in 618. \n\n Status: Imperial dynasty; Capital: Chang'an; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Imperial autocracy; Ruling dynasty: House of Yang; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Medieval China; Established: 582; Disestablished: 18 June 618; Preceded by: Northern Zhou; Succeeded by: Tang dynasty

name: Western Turkic Khaganate
description: The Western Turkic Khaganate was an expansive nomadic confederation, known historically as the Onoq or Ten Arrows, that dominated Central Asia from the Altai Mountains to the Aral and Caspian shores. Administered from its primary capital at Suyab in the Chui River valley, the khaganate prospered by securing Silk Road caravan oasis cities and taxing trans-Eurasian commerce. The empire reached its cultural and military height under Tong Yabghu Khagan before internal succession conflicts enabled the Tang Empire to launch a decisive invasion and subjugate the Western Turks in 658. \n\n Status: Nomadic empire; Capital: Suyab; Common languages: Old Turkic and Sogdian; Religion: Tengrism, Buddhism and Zoroastrianism; Government: Khaganate; Ruling dynasty: Ashina; Ruler title: Khagan; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 582; Disestablished: 658; Preceded by: First Turkic Khaganate; Succeeded by: Tang dynasty

name: Chiefdom of Sizhou

description: The Chiefdom of Sizhou was an autonomous indigenous polity established in the rugged karst river valleys of modern eastern Guizhou. Founded by Tian Zongxian during the late sixth century and recognised by the Sui imperial court, the realm was governed as a hereditary tusi lordship by the influential Tian clan. name: Kingdom of the Picts
label: celtic polities in britain;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of the Picts was an early medieval realm that encompassed the highlands and north-eastern plains of Scotland north of the River Forth. Dominated by the powerful regional hegemony of Fortriu and governed from assemblies at Scone, the Pictish confederacy successfully defended its borders, decisively halting Anglian Northumbrian expansion at the Battle of Nechtansmere in 685. The kingdom fostered distinctive monumental stone art and insular monastic scholarship until dynastic intermarriage and Viking pressures precipitated its formal merger with Dál Riata to establish the unified Kingdom of Alba in 844. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Scone; Common languages: Pictish, Old Gaelic and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King of the Picts; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 585; Disestablished: 844; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Scotland

label: celtic polities of brittany;celtic polities
description: Cornouaille was a maritime Celtic lordship in south-western Brittany that operated as a tributary dependency of King Guntram of Orléans from 588 to 593. label: celtic polities of brittany;celtic polities
description: Domnonia was a Brythonic kingdom across northern Armorica that adhered to the suzerainty of King Guntram of Orléans between 588 and 593. Although compelled to render formal submission, the Breton nobility guarded their customary regional autonomy until the death of Childebert prompted a repartition of Frankish royal authority across western Gaul. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of Metz; Capital: Vannes; Common languages: Early Breton and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Subordinate monarchy; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 593; Disestablished: 594; Preceded by: Bro Waroc'h (vassal under Orleans); Succeeded by: Bro Waroc'h (vassal under Theuderic II)

name: Cornouaille
label: celtic polities of brittany;celtic polities
description: Cornouaille was a Celtic principality located along the western Breton coast that passed into tributary vassalage to the Merovingian court of Metz during 593 and 594. Administered from Quimper, the countship maintained local civil traditions and Atlantic maritime shipping while acknowledging the nominal suzerainty of King Childebert II of Austrasia. This transitory phase of eastern Frankish overlordship concluded swiftly when Childebert's death led to the division of his territories and the realignment of Breton dependencies under the realm of Orléans. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of Metz; Administrative seat: Quimper; Common languages: Early Breton and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Subordinate monarchy; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 593; Disestablished: 594; Preceded by: Cornouaille (vassal under Orleans); Succeeded by: Cornouaille (vassal under Theuderic II)

description: Domnonia was a Brythonic monarchy in northern Armorica that recognised the overlordship of the Austrasian court at Metz from 593 to 594. The brief period of Austrasian vassalage came to an end with the untimely death of the king, prompting Domnonia to renegotiate its subordinate tributary status with the neighbouring Frankish kingdom of Orléans. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of Metz; Capital: Saint-Brieuc; Common languages: Early Breton, Brittonic and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Subordinate monarchy; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 593; Disestablished: 594; Preceded by: Domnonia (vassal under Orleans); Succeeded by: Domnonia (vassal under Theuderic II)

name: Bro Waroc'h
label: celtic polities of brittany;celtic polities
description: Bro Waroc'h was a south-eastern Breton principality that remained subject to the suzerainty of King Theuderic II of Orléans between 594 and 614. label: celtic polities of brittany;celtic polities
description: Cornouaille was a maritime Celtic realm in south-western Armorica that functioned as a vassal territory under King Theuderic II of Orléans between 594 and 614. Administered from its traditional ecclesiastical see at Quimper, the countship retained its native legal practices and insular cultural life while providing regular diplomatic submission and tribute to the Burgundian royal court. This extended period of regional vassalage concluded in 614 when King Chlothar II reunified Francia, bringing all Breton territories under direct pan-Frankish imperial oversight. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of Orléans; Administrative seat: Quimper; Common languages: Early Breton and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Subordinate monarchy; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 594; Disestablished: 614; Preceded by: Cornouaille (vassal under Metz); Succeeded by: Cornouaille (Frankish vassal)

description: Domnonia was a Brythonic kingdom on the northern Armorican coast that owed feudal vassalage to King Theuderic II of Orléans from 594 to 614. Centred administratively at Saint-Brieuc, the realm preserved its traditional dynastic governance and cross-Channel shipping networks while complying with the tributary obligations imposed by the Burgundian court. The kingdom successfully protected its borders against regional Frankish encroachment until Chlothar II deposed Queen Brunhilda and reunited the Frankish kingdoms in 614, consolidating Breton tributary relations under a unified crown. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of Orléans; Capital: Saint-Brieuc; Common languages: Early Breton, Brittonic and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Subordinate monarchy; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 594; Disestablished: 614; Preceded by: Domnonia (vassal under Metz); Succeeded by: Domnonia (Frankish vassal)

name: Kingdom of the Franks
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of the Franks centred at Metz comprised the eastern Austrasian realm ruled by King Theudebert II between 594 and 613. Governing territories from the Meuse across the Rhine into Alemannia, the kingdom faced substantial aristocratic pressure and constant dynastic rivalry against the king's brother Theuderic II of Burgundy. After expelling Queen Brunhilda from his court, Theudebert engaged in bitter civil conflicts that culminated in his catastrophic defeat at Tolbiac in 612, leading to his execution and the absorption of Austrasia by his brother. \n\n Status: Partition kingdom; Capital: Metz; Common languages: Frankish, Old High German and Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Merovingian; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 594; Disestablished: 613; Preceded by: Kingdom of the Franks; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Franks

name: Kingdom of the Franks
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: The Kingdom of the Franks centred at Orléans constituted the Burgundian realm governed by King Theuderic II under the formidable regency of his grandmother Queen Brunhilda from 594 to 614. Controlling the strategic Rhône Valley, southern Aquitanian civitates and the Loire basin, the monarchy successfully waged warfare against Austrasia, culminating in Theudebert II's downfall in 612. However, Theuderic's sudden death in 613 precipitated an aristocratic revolt by Austrasian nobles who invited King Chlothar II of Neustria to seize the throne and execute Brunhilda. \n\n Status: Partition kingdom; Capital: Orléans; Common languages: Frankish and Gallo-Romance Latin; Religion: Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Merovingian; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 594; Disestablished: 614; Preceded by: Kingdom of the Franks; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Franks

name: Cahokia
description: Cahokia was the pre-eminent urban centre and proto-state of the Mississippian culture, established across the fertile bottomlands of the Mississippi River in modern south-western Illinois. Peaking as the largest pre-Columbian city north of the Rio Grande, the metropolis constructed immense earthen platform mounds, notably the colossal Monks Mound, alongside astronomical woodhenges and ceremonial plazas. The polity orchestrated vast continental trading networks and agricultural surplus distribution before environmental degradation, resource depletion and regional unrest precipitated its gradual abandonment by the early fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Mississippian city-state; Capital: Cahokia; Religion: Mississippian religion; Government: Theocratic chiefdom; Historical era: Post-classical; Established: 601; Disestablished: 1301; Historical region: North America

name: Connacht

description: The Kingdom of Connacht was a powerful Gaelic realm established across the western province of Ireland, centred upon the ancient ceremonial inauguration complex of Rathcroghan. Dominated by the Uí Briúin Aí dynasty and their descendants of the Ó Conchobair sept, the kingdom established extensive hegemony across the Irish midlands during the eleventh and twelfth centuries. Kings such as Tairrdelbach and Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair attained the High Kingship of Ireland before bitter dynastic civil wars allowed Anglo-Norman forces under Richard de Burgh to colonise the territory. \n\n Status: Gaelic kingdom; Capital: Cruachan; Common languages: Old Irish, Middle Irish and Early Modern Irish; Religion: Celtic Christianity and Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Uí Briúin; Ruler title: King of Connacht; Historical era: Early to High Middle Ages; Established: 601; Disestablished: 1462; Succeeded by: Lordship of Ireland

name: Eastern Ganga Dynasty
description: The Eastern Ganga Dynasty was a major imperial power that ruled the historic Kalinga region encompassing modern Odisha, northern Andhra Pradesh and parts of West Bengal. Administering their realm from Kalinganagara and later Cuttack, the monarchs constructed iconic architectural wonders, including the Jagannath Temple at Puri and the Sun Temple at Konark. The dynasty vigorously repelled repeated invasions by Delhi Sultanate armies and fostered classical Odia literature until internal political shifts led to the establishment of the Suryavamsa Gajapati Empire in 1435. \n\n Status: Imperial dynasty; Capital: Kalinganagara; Common languages: Odia and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Eastern Ganga; Ruler title: Tri-Kalingadhipati; Historical era: Classical India to Middle Ages; Established: 601; Disestablished: 1435; Preceded by: Pitrbhakta dynasty; Succeeded by: Gajapati Empire

name: El Tajín
label: mesoamerican polities
description: El Tajín was a prominent pre-Columbian ceremonial city-state that flourished amidst the tropical lowlands of modern Veracruz as the capital of the Classic Veracruz culture. Famous for its distinctive architectural mastery of decorative niches, stepped pyramids and over twenty ceremonial ballcourts, the urban complex functioned as a focal point for the worship of the rain deity. The city-state commanded vital trade routes between the Gulf Coast and the Mexican central highlands until violent destruction and fire led to its abandonment around 1200. \n\n Status: Mesoamerican city-state; Capital: El Tajin; Common languages: Totonac; Religion: Mesoamerican polytheism; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Historical era: Classic to Postclassic Mesoamerica; Established: 601; Disestablished: 1201; Historical region: Mesoamerica

name: Gurjaradesa
description: Gurjaradesa was an influential regional polity that emerged across southern Rajasthan and northern Gujarat during the early seventh century under the leadership of Harichandra Rohilladhi. Operating from fortified strongholds around Mandore and Bhinmal, the early Gurjara monarchs defended western India's desert frontiers against regional competitors and expanding Arab incursions from Sindh. The state fostered martial Rajput traditions and prosperous overland trade networks, providing the political and military foundation that enabled its dynastic scions, the Gurjara-Pratiharas, to establish imperial dominance over northern India. \n\n Status: Regional kingdom; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Gurjara; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 601; Disestablished: 751; Succeeded by: Gurjara-Pratihara Empire

name: Igodomigodo
description: Igodomigodo was the foundational Edo monarchy established across the tropical rainforests of modern southern Nigeria, serving as the direct predecessor to the renowned Benin Empire. Governed by a succession of semi-legendary divine monarchs styled as the Ogiso, the realm developed sophisticated bronze-casting traditions, municipal earthworks and structured guild organisations from its capital at modern Benin City. Centuries of aristocratic governance ended in the late twelfth century following domestic administrative crises and the banishment of Prince Ekaladerhan, leading to the establishment of the Oba dynasty. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Benin City; Common languages: Edo; Religion: Edo traditional religion; Government: Divine monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ogiso; Ruler title: Ogiso; Historical era: Early to High Middle Ages; Established: 601; Disestablished: 1181; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Benin

name: Kingdom of Bumthang
description: The Kingdom of Bumthang was an ancient highland monarchy located across the fertile alpine valleys of central Bhutan. Governed by indigenous kings styled as Chogyal from fortified strongholds at Chakhar and Jakar Dzong, the realm served as the historic gateway through which Tantric Buddhism first took root in the Himalayas following the visit of Guru Rinpoche. The kingdom maintained flourishing monastic estates and localised feudal independence until theocratic unification under Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal incorporated Bumthang into the state of Bhutan in the seventeenth century. \n\n Status: Highland kingdom; Capital: Jakar; Common languages: Bumthang and Chöke; Religion: Bön and Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Chogyal; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 601; Disestablished: 1641; Succeeded by: Bhutan

name: Kingdom of Frisia
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Frisia was an independent maritime realm that dominated the coastal wetlands and river estuaries of modern Netherlands and north-western Germany. Operating from major mercantile emporia at Utrecht and Dorestad, the Frisians established a flourishing North Sea trading network, issued extensive silver sceat coinage and stubbornly resisted Christianisation. Under renowned monarchs such as King Redbad, the kingdom repeatedly repelled Frankish armies until Charles Martel secured a decisive victory at the Battle of the Boarn in 734, annexing Frisia into the Frankish realm. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Utrecht; Common languages: Old Frisian; Religion: Germanic paganism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 601; Disestablished: 735; Preceded by: Magna Frisia; Succeeded by: Frankish Empire

name: Kingdom of Kalingga
description: The Kingdom of Kalingga was an early Indianised Buddhist realm established along the northern coast of Central Java around modern Jepara. Documented in contemporary Chinese Tang chronicles as Heling, the kingdom flourished through maritime trade, agricultural cultivation and Buddhist scholarly institutions. Most celebrated under the rigorous legal administration of Queen Shima during the late seventh century, Kalingga maintained harmonious relations with regional principalities before political leadership shifted towards the interior of the island, culminating in the rise of the Mataram Kingdom. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Jepara; Common languages: Old Javanese and Sanskrit; Religion: Buddhism and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Queen; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 601; Disestablished: 756; Succeeded by: Mataram Kingdom

name: Panduvamshis of Dakshina Kosala
description: The Panduvamshis of Dakshina Kosala were a prominent medieval Indian dynasty that ruled the upper Mahanadi basin across present-day Chhattisgarh throughout the seventh and eighth centuries. Governing from their grand capital at Shripura, modern Sirpur, the dynasty achieved imperial prominence during the long reign of Mahashivagupta Balarjuna, who constructed magnificent brick temple complexes including the Lakshmana Temple. The monarchs fostered religious tolerance by patronising Shaivism, Vaishnavism and Buddhism simultaneously until regional instability led to their displacement by the related Somavamshi dynasty. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Sirpur; Common languages: Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Panduvamshi; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Medieval India; Established: 601; Disestablished: 801; Preceded by: Sharabhapuriya dynasty; Succeeded by: Somavamshi dynasty

name: Panduvamshis of Mekala
description: The Panduvamshis of Mekala were a regional ruling lineage that governed the rugged hill country of the Maikal Range across modern eastern Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh. Establishing their administrative centre at the ancient hill-fortress of Bandhavgarh, the monarchs claimed descent from the legendary lunar heroes of the Mahabharata. The dynasty patronised Shaivite worship, issued royal copperplate grants and defended upland trade routes between northern India and the Deccan before being overshadowed and incorporated by expanding neighbouring powers during the early eighth century. \n\n Status: Regional kingdom; Capital: Bandhavgarh; Common languages: Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Panduvamshi; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 601; Disestablished: 701; Preceded by: Gupta Empire; Succeeded by: Panduvamshis of Dakshina Kosala

name: Parvatadvaraka Dynasty
description: The Parvatadvaraka Dynasty was an early medieval royal house that governed the fertile Tel River valley within the modern Kalahandi district of western Odisha. Establishing their administrative seat at Belkhandi, the monarchs issued royal copper-plate charters and dedicated their sovereignty to the tutelary goddess Stambhesvari. The dynasty maintained local agrarian security and hill-pass trade following the decline of the Rajarsitulyakula family, sustaining independent authority for half a century until the expanding Sharabhapuriya and Nala polities absorbed their riverside territories around 651. \n\n Status: Regional kingdom; Capital: Belkhandi; Common languages: Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Parvatadvaraka; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 601; Disestablished: 651; Preceded by: Rajarsitulyakula Dynasty; Succeeded by: Sharabhapuriya dynasty

name: Wari Empire
description: The Wari Empire was an expansive pre-Columbian state that originated in the Ayacucho Basin and consolidated imperial authority across the central highlands and Pacific coast of modern Peru. Governed from their vast stone-walled metropolis at Huari, the imperial elite engineered advanced hillside terracing, maintained administrative quipu record-keeping and established orthogonal planned provincial centres like Pikillacta. The empire unified diverse regional populations through the shared religious iconography of the Staff God before climatic shifts and internal revolts brought about its collapse around 1101. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Huari; Common languages: Early Aymaran and Quechuan; Religion: Andean religion; Government: Imperial monarchy; Historical era: Middle Horizon; Established: 601; Disestablished: 1101; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Chimor

name: Xcaret
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Xcaret was a flourishing Classic and Postclassic Maya maritime city-state located on the Caribbean coastline of the Yucatán Peninsula in modern Quintana Roo. Functioning as a premier trading port and harbour, the city served as the principal embarkation terminal for sacred pilgrimages to the island shrine of Ixchel on Cozumel. The merchant elite constructed coastal watchtowers, defensive walls and limestone ceremonial temples, maintaining vibrant canoe-based commercial networks across Mesoamerica until Spanish colonial campaigns subdued the eastern coast in the mid-sixteenth century. \n\n Status: Maya city-state; Capital: Xcaret; Common languages: Yucatec Maya; Religion: Maya religion; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Batab; Historical era: Classic to Postclassic Mesoamerica; Established: 601; Disestablished: 1551; Succeeded by: New Spain

name: Kingdom of Northumbria
label: saxon polities in britain
description: The Kingdom of Northumbria was a dominant Anglo-Saxon realm formed in 605 through the political unification of Bernicia and Deira, encompassing northern England and south-eastern Scotland. Governed from the coastal citadel of Bamburgh and the ancient city of York, the kingdom achieved paramount authority across Britain under powerful kings such as Edwin and Oswald. Northumbria fostered an illustrious Golden Age of Christian scholarship and insular illumination before internal dynastic factionalism left the realm vulnerable to the Great Heathen Army, which captured York in 867. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Bamburgh; Common languages: Northumbrian Old English and Latin; Religion: Anglo-Saxon paganism and Chalcedonian Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King of Northumbria; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 605; Disestablished: 21 March 867; Preceded by: Kingdom of Bernicia; Succeeded by: Kingdom of York

name: Roman Empire
description: The Eastern Roman Empire entered a transformative medieval phase upon the accession of Emperor Heraclius in October 610, establishing Greek as its official language and reorganising military governance into provincial themes. Operating from the imperial capital of Constantinople, the state survived catastrophic Persian wars and early Arab sieges to preserve classical Mediterranean civilisation, Roman jurisprudence and Orthodox Christian culture. The empire experienced renewed territorial expansion and cultural renaissance under the Macedonian dynasty before western crusaders sacked Constantinople in 1204, fragmenting imperial authority. \n\n Status: Imperial state; Capital: Constantinople; Official languages: Medieval Greek and Latin; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Imperial autocracy; Ruler title: Basileus; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 5 October 610; Disestablished: 1205; Preceded by: Roman Empire; Succeeded by: Latin Empire

name: Raška
description: Raška was an early medieval Serbian principality established across the mountainous river valleys of south-western Serbia and northern Montenegro around the ancient fortress of Ras. Emerging during the Slavic settlement of the Balkans, the tribal state governed highland pastoral communities while balancing delicate diplomatic relations with the Byzantine Empire and the First Bulgarian Empire. The princes of Raška preserved indigenous Slavic customary law and fortified key mountain corridors, creating the territorial and administrative core that eventually evolved into the unified medieval Grand Principality of Serbia. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Ras; Common languages: Old Church Slavonic and Proto-Slavic; Religion: Slavic paganism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Prince (Knyaz); Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 611; Disestablished: 731; Succeeded by: Principality of Serbia

name: Bro Waroc'h
label: celtic polities of brittany;celtic polities
description: Bro Waroc'h was an autonomous Brythonic principality in south-eastern Brittany that acknowledged the suzerainty of the unified Frankish Empire following the accession of King Chlothar II in 614. Administered from Vannes, the polity preserved traditional Breton legal institutions and ecclesiastical privileges while offering formal fealty to Merovingian and early Carolingian monarchs. Under rulers such as Judicaël, the realm concluded non-aggression pacts with King Dagobert I, maintaining substantial domestic self-governance across the Vannetais until Pepin the Short launched direct campaigns to subjugate Brittany in the 750s. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of the Frankish Empire; Capital: Vannes; Common languages: Early Breton and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Subordinate monarchy; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 614; Disestablished: 754; Preceded by: Bro Waroc'h (vassal under Theuderic II); Succeeded by: Kingdom of Brittany

name: Cornouaille
label: celtic polities of brittany;celtic polities
description: Cornouaille was a maritime Celtic county on the western Armorican peninsula that operated under the overarching suzerainty of the reunified Frankish Empire from 614 onwards. Centred upon the episcopal town of Quimper, the Breton countship maintained insular linguistic heritage, coastal commerce and regional judicial customs while paying periodic tribute to Merovingian overlords. The local nobility retained effective day-to-day autonomy over their rugged coastal territory until mid-eighth-century Carolingian military expeditions imposed tighter royal governance across the Breton borderlands. \n\n Status: Vassal county of the Frankish Empire; Administrative seat: Quimper; Common languages: Early Breton and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Subordinate monarchy; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 614; Disestablished: 754; Preceded by: Cornouaille (vassal under Theuderic II); Succeeded by: Kingdom of Brittany

name: Domnonia
label: celtic polities of brittany;celtic polities
description: Domnonia was a Brythonic kingdom spanning the northern littoral of Brittany that accepted the suzerainty of the unified Frankish monarchy following the re-establishment of royal peace in 614. Headquartered at Saint-Brieuc, the kingdom governed the coastal cantons of Trégor, Goëlo and Penthièvre, sustaining cross-Channel ties with Celtic Britain and preserving its native monastic hierarchy. Although acknowledging formal Frankish imperial supremacy, Domnonia operated with virtual independence until the military campaigns of King Pepin the Short incorporated the territory into the Carolingian realm in the 750s. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Frankish Empire; Capital: Saint-Brieuc; Common languages: Early Breton, Brittonic and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Subordinate monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 614; Disestablished: 754; Preceded by: Domnonia (vassal under Theuderic II); Succeeded by: Kingdom of Brittany

name: Kingdom of Ergyng
label: celtic polities in britain;welsh polities;celtic polities
description: The Kingdom of Ergyng was an early medieval Welsh realm established along the lower River Wye in modern south-eastern Wales and Herefordshire. Known to later Anglo-Saxons as Archenfield, the kingdom flourished upon fertile agricultural plains and controlled crucial river crossings from its administrative focus near Hereford. Governed by native Brythonic dynasts, Ergyng nurtured Celtic monastic institutions and fiercely defended its eastern borders against encroaching Mercian expansion until dynastic alliances and military pressures led to its merger into the Kingdom of Gwent around 621. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Hereford; Common languages: Brittonic, Old Welsh and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 616; Disestablished: 621; Preceded by: Sub-Roman Britain; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Gwent

name: Eastern Chalukyas
description: The Eastern Chalukyas were a durable South Indian ruling dynasty that established sovereign control over the coastal Vengi region of modern Andhra Pradesh. Founded by Prince Kubja Vishnuvardhana after breaking away from the parent Badami Chalukya house, the dynasty governed from successive capitals at Pishtapura, Vengi and Rajahmundry. The monarchs presided over a remarkable cultural flourishing characterised by the patronage of classical Telugu literature, Shaivite temple building and maritime commerce before close matrimonial alliances culminated in their dynastic integration with the Chola Empire. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Vengi; Common languages: Telugu, Sanskrit and Kannada; Religion: Shaivism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Eastern Chalukya; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 617; Disestablished: 1098; Preceded by: Chalukya dynasty; Succeeded by: Chola Empire

name: Tang
description: The Tang dynasty was an illustrious Chinese imperial empire founded on 18 June 618 by Li Yuan following the collapse of the Sui state. Administered from the cosmopolitan world metropolis of Chang'an, the dynasty presided over a golden age of cosmopolitan trade, artistic brilliance, poetry and expansive military conquest across Central Asia. Although interrupted by Empress Wu Zetian's Zhou interregnum and severely shaken by the mid-eighth-century An Lushan Rebellion, the dynasty sustained the civil service examinations and imperial bureaucracy until military warlords precipitated its fall in 907. \n\n Status: Imperial empire; Capital: Chang'an; Official languages: Literary Chinese and Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Imperial autocracy; Ruling dynasty: House of Li; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Medieval China; Established: 18 June 618; Disestablished: 17 October 690; Preceded by: Sui dynasty; Succeeded by: Zhou dynasty (Wu Zetian)

name: Tibetan Empire
description: Tibetan Empire was an expansive Inner Asian power founded by the Yarlung monarch Songtsen Gampo on the high Tibetan Plateau. Operating from its capital at Lhasa, the realm projected military supremacy across Central Asia, clashing repeatedly with the Tang dynasty and extending authority over the Tarim Basin and Himalayan passes. Internal administrative reforms and the adoption of Buddhism fostered a distinct classical imperial culture until factional civil strife dissolved the central state in the mid-ninth century. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Lhasa; Common languages: Old Tibetan; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism and Bon; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Tsenpo; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 618; Disestablished: 842

name: Shailodbhava Dynasty
description: Shailodbhava Dynasty ruled the fertile coastal domain of Kongoda-mandala along the Bay of Bengal in modern Odisha. Initially governing as regional feudatories under imperial overlords, the monarchs assumed full independence under Madhavaraja II following the retreat of Gauda authority. The dynasty maintained patronage of classical Brahmanical learning and Shaivite religious establishments until political dominance was seized by the rising Bhauma-Kara rulers in the late eighth century. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Banpur; Common languages: Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Classical India; Preceded by: Gauda Kingdom; Succeeded by: Bhauma-Kara dynasty

name: State of Medina
description: State of Medina was the initial Islamic commonwealth established in western Arabia under the leadership of the Prophet Muhammad following the migration from Mecca. Governed in accordance with the Constitution of Medina, the polity united diverse tribal factions, Muhajirun and Ansar into a cohesive religious and political confederation. Through active diplomacy and military expeditions across the Hejaz, the nascent state integrated the Arabian Peninsula prior to Muhammad's death and the inauguration of the caliphates. \n\n Status: Islamic state; Capital: Medina; Common languages: Old Arabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Theocratic commonwealth; Ruler title: Prophet and political leader; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Succeeded by: Rashidun Caliphate

name: Karkota Empire
description: Karkota Empire was a formidable northern Indian dynasty centred in the Kashmir Valley that achieved continental prominence under energetic rulers such as Lalitaditya Muktapida. The monarchs maintained an administrative seat at Parihaspur and developed an extensive tributary network extending across the Punjab and parts of Central Asia. Renowned for constructing monumental stone architecture including the Martand Sun Temple, the dynasty fostered both Vaishnavite and Buddhist monastic traditions before being superseded by the Utpala dynasty. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Srinagar; Common languages: Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 625; Succeeded by: Utpala dynasty

name: Khadga Dynasty
description: Khadga Dynasty was a Buddhist royal lineage that held sway across the deltaic tracts of Vanga and Samatata in ancient eastern Bengal. Rising to power in the power vacuum following the fall of Shashanka's Gauda kingdom, the dynasty governed from Karmanta Vasaka near modern Comilla. Their rulers patronised monastic complexes and sponsored epigraphic copperplates recording religious grants until sovereign authority passed to the Buddhist Deva dynasty. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Comilla; Common languages: Sanskrit and Old Bengali; Religion: Mahayana Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Classical period; Established: 625; Succeeded by: Deva dynasty

name: Pala Empire
description: Pala Empire was a major imperial power founded in eastern India when regional chieftains elected Gopala to restore political order across Bengal and Bihar. Operating from royal riverine capitals including Pataliputra and Munger, the realm commanded formidable war elephant divisions and held diplomatic prestige throughout the Buddhist world. Imperial influence extended across northern India during the reigns of Dharmapala and Devapala, maintaining renowned monastic universities such as Nalanda and Vikramashila before fracturing under external pressures. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Patna and Munger; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Mahayana Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharajadhiraja; Historical era: Early Medieval India; Established: 750; Disestablished: 1161

name: Dvaravati
label: mon kingdoms
description: Dvaravati was a flourishing Mon mandala civilisation centred on Nakhon Pathom and Lopburi in the Chao Phraya River basin of central Thailand. Governed through a decentralised network of moated settlements and trading emporia, the realm served as an essential conduit for Theravada Buddhist doctrine and artistic models across Southeast Asia. The polity retained considerable cultural vitality until its independent urban centres were gradually incorporated into the expanding Khmer Empire. \n\n Status: Mon mandala confederation; Capital: Nakhon Pathom; Common languages: Old Mon and Sanskrit; Religion: Theravada Buddhism and Hinduism; Government: Decentralised monarchy; Historical era: Early Southeast Asia; Disestablished: 11th century

name: Old Great Bulgaria
description: Old Great Bulgaria was a short-lived nomad empire organised by Khan Kubrat across the Pontic-Caspian steppe between the Dniester and the lower Volga. Establishing an administrative hub at the former Greek colony of Phanagoria, Kubrat unified various Onogur-Bulgar and Slavic clans into an autonomous federation outside Avar control. Following Kubrat's death, persistent military assaults by Khazar armies fractured the steppe realm, prompting Bulgar migrations towards the Danube and the middle Volga. \n\n Status: Steppe empire; Capital: Phanagoria; Common languages: Bulgar; Religion: Tengrism; Government: Nomadic khaganate; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 632; Succeeded by: First Bulgarian Empire and Volga Bulgaria

name: Duchy of Aquitaine
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: Duchy of Aquitaine functioned as an autonomous southwestern Frankish sub-kingdom and ducal fiefdom south of the Loire River, governed from Toulouse. During this era of intermittent Merovingian and early Carolingian suzerainty, native Aquitanian dukes frequently exercised de facto independence while navigating royal Frankish civil wars. Ducal commanders defended the rich southern territories against Gascon incursions and northern royal armies before mounting centralising campaigns under Charles Martel. \n\n Status: Vassal duchy of the Frankish Empire; Capital: Toulouse; Common languages: Latin, Old Occitan and Basque; Religion: Christianity; Government: Feudal duchy; Ruler title: Duke of Aquitaine; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of France

name: Gour Kingdom
description: Gour Kingdom was a prominent regional principality centred in the Sylhet basin of modern north-eastern Bangladesh following the territorial division of Greater Gour. The dynasty championed Brahminical religious revivalism, patronising Hindu scholarship and constructing defensive forts along the river networks of the Surma Valley. The realm endured until the early fourteenth century, when its final monarch was defeated during the Islamic conquest led by the Delhi Sultanate. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Gaur; Common languages: Sanskrit and Bengali; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Classical period; Established: 630; Disestablished: 1303

name: Kingdom of Morgannwg
label: celtic polities in britain;welsh polities;celtic polities
description: Kingdom of Morgannwg was a Welsh realm in south-eastern Wales created through dynastic associations between the ancient kingdoms of Glywysing and Gwent. Centred around defensible strongholds near modern Cardiff, its native rulers defended Celtic legal traditions and monastic foundations against encroaching Mercian and Saxon neighbours. The realm retained stubborn autonomy through early medieval conflicts until falling to Anglo-Norman Marcher barons in the late eleventh century. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Cardiff; Common languages: Old Welsh and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King of Morgannwg; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1091; Succeeded by: Norman March of Glamorgan

name: Laur Kingdom
description: Laur Kingdom was a semi-autonomous riverine principality situated in the northern wetland tracts of the Sylhet region near the modern border of Bangladesh and Meghalaya. Emerging from ancient territorial partitions, the state maintained a secluded mountain-fringe capital at Nabagram and defended its trade routes against rival neighbours. Local Hindu rulers preserved hereditary sovereignty for several centuries until their mountain domain was finally integrated into the Mughal Empire. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Laur; Common languages: Sanskrit and Bengali; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Classical period; Established: 630; Disestablished: 1565; Succeeded by: Mughal Empire

name: Principality of Travunia
description: Principality of Travunia was an early medieval South Slavic polity established in the karst hinterland and coastal valleys around modern Trebinje in Herzegovina. Originating with Slavic settlements sanctioned by the Byzantine Empire to defend imperial borders against Avars, the principality was governed by hereditary zupans linked to the Belojevic clan. Its chieftains navigated shifting allegiances between Byzantine authorities, Serbian grand princes and Bulgarian forces until the realm became subordinated to Duklja. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Trebinje; Common languages: Proto-Slavic and Old Serbian; Religion: Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Duklja

name: Principality of Zachlumia
description: Principality of Zachlumia was a South Slavic maritime state situated between the Neretva River and the Peljesac Peninsula in modern Herzegovina and southern Dalmatia. Centred upon the fortified coastal town of Ston, the principality maintained lucrative Adriatic trade and sea salt production while asserting strategic autonomy. Its rulers balanced diplomatic relations between the Byzantine court, early Croatian monarchs and Bulgarian sovereigns until undergoing political absorption into regional successor realms. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Ston; Common languages: Proto-Slavic and Old Serbian; Religion: Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Preceded by: Byzantine Empire; Succeeded by: Duklja

name: Toquz Oghuz
description: Toquz Oghuz was a powerful confederation of nine Turkic-speaking Tiele tribes inhabiting the extensive grasslands of the northern Mongolian steppe. Initially united within the broader framework of the First Turkic Khaganate, the alliance maintained nomadic autonomy following the collapse of eastern Gokturk power. Relying on seasonal mobile camps and equestrian warfare rather than fixed urban settlements, the tribal coalition influenced inner steppe diplomacy until its absorption into the Second Turkic Khaganate. \n\n Status: Nomadic tribal confederation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Old Turkic; Religion: Tengrism; Government: Confederal tribal alliance; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Preceded by: First Turkic Khaganate; Succeeded by: Second Turkic Khaganate

name: Xueyantuo Khaganate
description: Xueyantuo Khaganate was a dominant Tiele nomadic empire that established hegemony over the Orkhon and Tuul river valleys following the fall of the Eastern Gokturks. Governed by their own supreme khagans without a static capital city, the Xueyantuo initially allied with Tang China to secure dominion over rival steppe confederations. Escalating frontier friction and military confrontations with Tang imperial armies culminated in the destruction of their ruling dynasty in 646. \n\n Status: Steppe khaganate; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Old Turkic; Religion: Tengrism; Government: Nomadic confederation; Ruler title: Khagan; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 628; Disestablished: 646; Succeeded by: Tang dynasty

name: Samo's Empire
description: Samo's Empire was the earliest recorded political union of Slavic tribes in Central Europe, established under the leadership of the Frankish merchant Samo. Centred along the middle Danube and Morava valleys, the confederation arose from a successful rebellion by local Slavic populations against Avar overlordship. King Samo successfully repulsed punitive Frankish incursions at the Battle of Wogastisburg in 631, preserving regional independence until the loose confederacy dissolved following his death. \n\n Status: Tribal confederation; Capital: Devín; Common languages: Proto-Slavic; Religion: Slavic paganism; Government: Elective tribal kingship; Ruler title: King of the Slavs; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 623; Disestablished: 658

name: Rashidun Caliphate
description: Rashidun Caliphate was the foundational Islamic imperial state established after the death of the Prophet Muhammad, guided in succession by Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali. Operating initially from Medina and later transferring administrative headquarters to Kufa, the caliphate achieved extraordinary territorial expansion across the Levant, Mesopotamia, Egypt and Persia. Its consultative governance and disciplined military armies dismantled the Sasanian Empire and severely reduced Byzantine territory before internal strife culminated in the First Fitna. \n\n Status: Caliphate; Capital: Medina and Kufa; Official languages: Arabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Consultative caliphate; Ruler title: Caliph; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Preceded by: State of Medina; Succeeded by: Umayyad Caliphate

name: Brahman Dynasty
description: Brahman Dynasty was a Hindu royal lineage established in the lower Indus valley following the overthrow of the Buddhist Rai dynasty by the royal minister Chach of Alor. Governing from the fortified city of Aror, the dynasty controlled an extensive commercial realm spanning Sindh, Makran and southern Punjab. Internal religious tensions and dynastic fractures left the kingdom vulnerable to external campaigns, resulting in its conquest by Umayyad armies led by Muhammad ibn al-Qasim in 712. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Alor; Common languages: Sanskrit and Old Sindhi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 632; Disestablished: 712; Succeeded by: Umayyad Caliphate

name: Tuyuhun Kingdom
description: Tuyuhun Kingdom was an Inner Asian realm established by Xianbei nomadic clans along the pasturelands of the Qilian Mountains and upper Yellow River in modern Qinghai. Following extensive Tang military campaigns in 635, the kingdom was compelled to submit as an imperial Chinese tributary and buffer state under King Murong Nuohebo. Despite Tang diplomatic backing, the polity faced relentless pressure from the expanding Tibetan Empire, which overran and absorbed its heartland in the late 660s. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of China; Capital: Fusi; Common languages: Tuyuhun and Middle Chinese; Religion: Traditional animism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Khagan; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Disestablished: 670; Succeeded by: Tibetan Empire

name: Kingdom of Ngoenyang
description: Kingdom of Ngoenyang was an early northern Tai kingdom centred in the upper Mekong basin around Chiang Saen in modern northern Thailand. Known in regional chronicles as Hiran Nakhon, the mandala state established agricultural settlements and defensive city fortifications across the surrounding valleys. The dynasty preserved enduring sovereign authority through flexible local alliances until King Mangrai unified the region in the late thirteenth century to establish the Lan Na Kingdom. \n\n Status: Mandala kingdom; Capital: Chiang Saen; Common languages: Northern Thai; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Mandala monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Post-classical era; Established: 638; Succeeded by: Lan Na

name: Bro Waroc'h
label: celtic polities of brittany;celtic polities
description: Bro Waroc'h was an early medieval Breton realm centred upon the ancient city of Vannes in south-western Armorica. Inhabited by Brittonic emigrants who blended with local populations, the principality frequently recognised the nominal suzerainty of the Merovingian sub-kingdom of Neustria while jealously maintaining territorial autonomy. Its rulers resisted Frankish assimilation and retained customary legal authority across modern Morbihan until being integrated into the unified Breton state. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of Neustria; Capital: Vannes; Common languages: Old Breton, Latin and Gallo-Romance; Religion: Christianity; Government: Feudal principality; Ruler title: Count of Vannes; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Brittany

name: Cornouaille
label: celtic polities of brittany;celtic polities
description: Cornouaille was a historical Celtic realm established along the rugged western coastline of Brittany by migrant princes and clerics from south-western Britain. Governed from its episcopal and administrative centre at Quimper, the county maintained intermittent vassal ties with the Frankish crown of Neustria while preserving its native language and legal customs. The territory played an important role in coastal trade and monastic reform before becoming an integral fief of the medieval Duchy of Brittany. \n\n Status: Vassal county of Neustria; Administrative seat: Quimper; Common languages: Old Breton and Latin; Religion: Christianity; Government: Feudal county; Ruler title: Count of Cornouaille; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Brittany

name: Domnonia
label: celtic polities of brittany;celtic polities
description: Domnonia was a prominent Brittonic polity in northern Armorica extending from Saint-Brieuc to Dol-de-Bretagne, established by Celtic settlers fleeing post-Roman Britain. Subject to fluctuating Merovingian overlordship under Neustria, the realm maintained close seafaring connections with insular Dumnonia across the English Channel. Local princes and missionary bishops fortified the northern coast against piratical raids until the region was merged into the wider Kingdom of Brittany during the ninth century. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of Neustria; Capital: Saint-Brieuc; Common languages: Old Breton and Latin; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Brittany

name: Kingdom of Austrasia
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: Kingdom of Austrasia formed the north-eastern core of the Merovingian Frankish realm, encompassing the Meuse, Moselle and middle Rhine river valleys with its royal court at Metz. As an autonomous Frankish sub-kingdom, it preserved Germanic linguistic traditions and served as the political cradle for the rising Carolingian dynasty under powerful mayors of the palace. Austrasian monarchs and nobles repeatedly clashed with neighbouring Neustria before the Frankish lands were consolidated under Charlemagne. \n\n Status: Sub-kingdom of the Franks; Capital: Metz; Common languages: Old Frankish, Latin and Old High German; Religion: Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King of Austrasia; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 481; Succeeded by: Carolingian Empire

name: Kingdom of Neustria
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: Kingdom of Neustria formed the western component of the Merovingian Frankish kingdom, stretching between the Loire and the northern borderlands with Paris as a primary royal seat. More thoroughly Romanised than its eastern neighbour Austrasia, the realm developed sophisticated administrative institutions and urban bishoprics across northern Gaul. Persistent civil conflicts between Neustrian and Austrasian factions defined early Frankish history until Carolingian supremacy integrated the western territories into the wider empire. \n\n Status: Sub-kingdom of the Franks; Capital: Paris; Common languages: Old Gallo-Romance, Latin and Old Frankish; Religion: Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King of Neustria; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 486; Succeeded by: Kingdom of France

name: Kingdom of Thuringia
label: barbarian kingdoms
description: Kingdom of Thuringia was an early Germanic realm situated between the Harz Mountains and the Thuringian Forest in central Germany. Following severe Merovingian military defeats in the sixth century, the territory was reduced to a dependent Frankish marcher duchy governed from Erfurt. Local noble lineages struggled repeatedly against Frankish governors and encroaching Slavic confederacies until the duchy was fully reorganised into the eastern marches of the Carolingian Empire. \n\n Status: Vassal duchy of the Frankish Empire; Capital: Erfurt; Common languages: Old High German and Latin; Religion: Germanic paganism and Christianity; Government: Stem duchy; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Carolingian Empire

name: Dabuyid Dynasty
description: Dabuyid Dynasty was a Zoroastrian Iranian princely house that ruled the mountainous Caspian littoral of Tabaristan and western Khorasan following the collapse of the Sasanian Empire. Operating from regional strongholds such as Sari and Fuman, its rulers took the ancient military title of Ispahbadh and successfully resisted early Arab Caliphate incursions into the Alborz mountain passes. The realm preserved ancient Sasanian courtly traditions and religious institutions until Abbasid armies finally overran the region in 761. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Sari; Common languages: Middle Persian, Tabari and Caspian dialects; Religion: Zoroastrianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Ispahbadh; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 642; Disestablished: 761; Succeeded by: Abbasid Caliphate

name: Principality of Farghana
description: Principality of Farghana was an autonomous Iranian dynasty of Sogdian cultural descent that governed the fertile Ferghana Valley along the upper Syr Darya. Ruled by monarchs holding the indigenous title of Ikhshid from their administrative seat at Akhsikath, the state controlled vital Silk Road transit trade and oasis agriculture. The principality skilfully balanced tributary ties with the Tang dynasty, the Turgesh and early Arab armies before being incorporated into the Samanid realm. \n\n Status: Autonomous principality; Capital: Akhsikath; Common languages: Sogdian and Middle Persian; Religion: Zoroastrianism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Ikhshid; Historical era: Middle Ages; Disestablished: 819; Succeeded by: Samanid Empire

name: Principality of Iberia
description: Principality of Iberia functioned as an aristocratic Georgian buffer state in Kartli during a brief period of submission to the expanding Arab Caliphate. Guided by presiding princes seated at Tbilisi, the Georgian nobles agreed to tributary terms to protect Christian religious autonomy and regional administration from destructive military raids. This precarious arrangement shifted frequently as local eristavis leveraged Byzantine and Arab rivalries across Transcaucasia to restore internal independence. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of the Arab Caliphate; Capital: Tbilisi; Common languages: Old Georgian; Religion: Georgian Orthodox Christianity; Government: Principate; Ruler title: Presiding Prince; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Preceded by: Sasanian Iberia; Succeeded by: Principality of Kakheti and Emirate of Tbilisi

name: Gurjara-Pratihara Kingdom
description: Gurjara-Pratihara Kingdom was a dominant imperial dynasty in northern India that rose to prominence by repelling early Arab Caliphate invasions from Sindh. After establishing their capital at the prestigious imperial city of Kannauj, the monarchs engaged in the prolonged Tripartite Struggle against the Rashtrakutas and the Palas for paramountcy across the Gangetic Plains. Renowned for their ornate stone temples and military prowess, the dynasty maintained widespread authority before declining under regional challenges in the eleventh century. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Kannauj; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharajadhiraja; Historical era: Early Medieval India; Established: 730; Disestablished: 1036

name: Later Gupta Dynasty
description: Later Gupta Dynasty was a regional royal house of Magadha and Malwa that asserted local sovereignty in eastern northern India during the political vacuum following the collapse of Harsha's empire. Seated at the historic capital of Pataliputra, the dynasty revived classical Gupta imperial titles and sought to re-establish administrative stability across the central Gangetic plains. Their brief independent resurgence faced immediate opposition from rival powers, leading to subjugation by the Varman rulers of Kannauj. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Patna; Common languages: Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharajadhiraja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 490; Disestablished: 750; Succeeded by: Varman dynasty of Kannauj

name: Great Meng
description: Great Meng was an early Bai-dominated kingdom established by chieftain Xinuluo in the fertile basin of Lake Erhai in south-western China. Centred at Mengshe, the realm formed the leading polity among the Six Zhao confederations of Yunnan before acquiring imperial Chinese diplomatic support. Through systematic consolidation of neighbouring tribal valleys, the Meng house laid the territorial and military foundations for the unified kingdom of Nanzhao. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Mengshe; Common languages: Bai, Nuosu and Middle Chinese; Religion: Traditional animism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Chieftain and King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 649; Succeeded by: Nanzhao

name: Khazar Khaganate
description: Khazar Khaganate was a semi-nomadic Turkic empire that dominated the vast steppe expanse between the lower Volga, the Don and the northern Caucasus. Governed successively from Balanjar, Samandar and the river metropolis of Atil, the khaganate commanded crucial Eurasian transit routes linking China, the Caliphate and Byzantium. Famed for the ruling elite's adoption of Rabbinic Judaism alongside widespread religious pluralism, the state functioned as a regional superpower until falling to Kievan Rus' in the late tenth century. \n\n Status: Khaganate; Capital: Balanjar, Samandar and Atil; Common languages: Oghuric Turkic and Alanic; Religion: Judaism, Tengrism, Islam and Christianity; Government: Nomadic khaganate; Ruler title: Khagan; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 650; Disestablished: 969; Succeeded by: Kievan Rus'

name: Melayu Kingdom
description: Melayu Kingdom was a classical Buddhist maritime realm situated along the Batang Hari River on the eastern coast of Sumatra, centred at Jambi. Flourishing as an active commercial hub for camphor, gold and spice trade across the Malacca Strait, the kingdom attracted international Buddhist pilgrims and Chinese emissaries. Although temporarily absorbed by the neighbouring thalassocracy of Srivijaya in the late seventh century, Melayu retained distinct regional autonomy and re-emerged as an independent power in later centuries. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Jambi; Common languages: Old Malay and Sanskrit; Religion: Buddhism and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Early Southeast Asia; Preceded by: Srivijaya; Succeeded by: Pagaruyung Kingdom

name: Tula
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Tula was an influential Mesoamerican urban state located in the Tula River valley of modern Hidalgo in central Mexico. Serving as the primary capital of Toltec civilisation from Tollan-Xicocotitlan, the city developed extensive monumental plazas, colonnades and distinctive warrior statues known as Atlanteans. The polity directed a wide commercial and tributary network across the central Mexican plateau, creating cultural and architectural conventions that deeply influenced later Postclassic civilisations including the Aztecs. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Tollan-Xicocotitlan; Common languages: Nahuatl and Otomi; Religion: Mesoamerican polytheism; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Ruler title: Tlatoani; Historical era: Mesoamerican Postclassic; Established: 650; Disestablished: 1150

name: Varman Dynasty of Kannauj
description: Varman Dynasty of Kannauj was a northern Indian royal house that controlled the strategic doab between the Ganges and Yamuna rivers from their imperial seat at Kannauj. Under the leadership of King Yashovarman, the dynasty mounted ambitious military expeditions across northern India, checking Tibetan southward incursions and asserting hegemony over Magadha. Their court served as an illustrious patron of Sanskrit literature and Brahminical scholarship before succumbing to regional rivalries with Kashmir and the Ayudha dynasty. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Kannauj; Common languages: Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharajadhiraja; Historical era: Early Medieval India; Established: 725; Disestablished: 770; Succeeded by: Ayudha dynasty

name: Bavand Dynasty
description: Bavand Dynasty was an enduring Iranian princely house claiming descent from the Sasanian nobility that governed the mountainous Alborz highlands of Tabaristan. Basing their rule initially in Perim and later at Sari, the princes bore the ancestral title of Ispahbadh and successfully preserved local Persian culture against direct Arab rule. The dynasty maintained unbroken local authority through flexible diplomacy, shifting between staunch independence and formal vassalage until disappearing in the mid-fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Perim and Sari; Common languages: Mazanderani and Persian; Religion: Zoroastrianism and later Shia Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Ispahbadh; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 651; Disestablished: 1349

name: Masmughans of Damavand
description: Masmughans of Damavand was an aristocratic Iranian dynasty of Karenid descent that ruled the high valleys surrounding Mount Damavand in the central Alborz range. Holding the ancient sacerdotal title of Masmughan, signifying the great magian, the rulers preserved Zoroastrian religious orthodoxy and maintained fortified independence following the collapse of the Sasanian state. The principality defended its mountainous territory against Umayyad forces until final Abbasid campaigns in 760 dissolved its autonomy. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Damavand; Common languages: Middle Persian and Caspian dialects; Religion: Zoroastrianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Masmughan; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 651; Disestablished: 760; Succeeded by: Abbasid Caliphate

name: Emirate of Tbilisi
description: Emirate of Tbilisi was a frontier Islamic principality established in eastern Georgia following the Arab subjugation of the South Caucasus. Ruling from the fortified river city of Tbilisi under the suzerainty of the Caliphate, the Muslim emirs managed trade between the Islamic world and the Christian mountain polities. The emirate persisted as an outpost of Islamic power for nearly four centuries until it was reconquered by King David IV of Georgia in 1122. \n\n Status: Vassal emirate of the Arab Caliphate; Capital: Tbilisi; Common languages: Arabic and Georgian; Religion: Islam and Christianity; Government: Emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 736; Disestablished: 1122; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Georgia

name: Kingdom of East Anglia
label: anglian polities in britain
description: Kingdom of East Anglia was an Anglo-Saxon realm comprising the lands of Norfolk and Suffolk, which fell under the hegemony of Mercia during the Mercian Supremacy. Governed from Norwich, local sub-kings paid tribute and provided military contingents to Mercian overlords while preserving native administrative traditions. Despite intermittent rebellions by local rulers seeking independence, Mercian dominance persisted until the West Saxon victory at Ellendun reshaped the English political landscape. \n\n Status: Protectorate of Mercia; Capital: Norwich; Common languages: Old English; Religion: Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Heptarchy; Preceded by: Sub-Roman Britain; Succeeded by: Kingdom of England

name: Paduspanids
description: Paduspanids formed an exceptionally resilient Iranian dynasty of local rulers who held authority over the rugged mountain enclaves of Ruyan and Rostamdar in western Mazandaran. Tracing their lineage to Sasanian royalty, the rulers governed from Kojur and defended their mountain territory against external conquerors for more than nine centuries. The dynasty preserved Caspian cultural autonomy and shifted gradually from Zoroastrianism to Twelver Shiism before falling to the Safavids in 1598. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Kojur; Common languages: Persian and Caspian dialects; Religion: Zoroastrianism and later Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Ispahbadh; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 665; Disestablished: 1598; Succeeded by: Safavid Empire

name: Rashidun Caliphate
description: Rashidun Caliphate experienced a turbulent phase of governance following the assassination of Caliph Uthman in 656, when Ali ibn Abi Talib assumed leadership from his new administrative base at Kufa. This period was characterised by the bitter internal conflict of the First Fitna, pitting Ali's loyalists against opposing factions led by Mu'awiya in Syria and the emerging Kharijites. Despite Ali's efforts to preserve communal integrity, his assassination in 661 brought the Rashidun era to an end and paved the way for the Umayyad dynasty. \n\n Status: Caliphate; Capital: Kufa; Official languages: Arabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Consultative caliphate; Ruler title: Caliph; Historical era: Late Antiquity; Preceded by: State of Medina; Succeeded by: Umayyad Caliphate

name: Umayyad Caliphate
description: Umayyad Caliphate was the second imperial Islamic caliphate, established by Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan following the conclusion of the First Fitna. Administered from its primary capital at Damascus and later Harran, the caliphate expanded rapidly across North Africa, the Iberian Peninsula, Transoxiana and Sindh to become one of the largest empires in world history. Umayyad rulers centralised administrative authority, instituted Arabic as the official language of government and struck standardised Islamic currency before being overthrown by the Abbasid Revolution in 750. \n\n Status: Caliphate; Capital: Damascus and Harran; Official languages: Arabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Caliph; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 661; Disestablished: 750; Succeeded by: Abbasid Caliphate and Emirate of Córdoba

name: Kharijites
description: Kharijites constituted a radical early Islamic faction that seceded from Caliph Ali's coalition following his agreement to arbitration at the Battle of Siffin. Establishing a fortified military base at Nahrawan without a formal urban capital, the dissidents maintained an egalitarian doctrine asserting that leadership belonged solely to the most righteous Muslim. Ali defeated their main force at the Battle of Nahrawan in 658, yet splinter groups continued to mount insurrections and targeted assassinations across Iraq and Arabia for decades. \n\n Status: Insurgent schismatic movement; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Kharijite Islam; Government: Elective theocracy; Ruler title: Imam; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 657; Disestablished: 658

name: Carantania
description: Carantania was an early Slavic principality that took shape across the eastern Alpine valleys of modern southern Austria and north-eastern Slovenia. Centred at the ritual and administrative seat of Krnskigrad, the polity emerged from the fragmentation of Samo's realm and defended its Alpine borders against nomadic Avar raids. The princes gradually allied with the neighbouring Bavarians, entering the Frankish sphere of influence and receiving Christian missionaries before being reorganised into a Carolingian march. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Krnskigrad; Common languages: Proto-Slavic; Religion: Slavic paganism and Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 658; Succeeded by: Carolingian Empire

name: Kangar Union
description: Kangar Union was a Turkic tribal federation that dominated the expansive steppe lands of central and western Kazakhstan following the collapse of the Western Turkic Khaganate. Governed from the Ulytau mountain redoubt with regional centres near Taraz, the union brought together nomadic Kangly clans to control trans-Eurasian trade routes. Under mounting pressure from Oghuz, Karluk and Kimek confederacies, elements of the union migrated westwards to form the historical Pecheneg nation. \n\n Status: Steppe federation; Capital: Taraz; Common languages: Old Turkic; Religion: Tengrism; Government: Tribal confederation; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 659; Disestablished: 750; Succeeded by: Oghuz Yabgu State

name: Tamna
description: Tamna was an ancient maritime island realm situated on Jeju Island off the southern coast of the Korean Peninsula. Following the fall of its former Baekje patrons to allied Tang and Silla forces, the island state submitted as a tributary vassal to the Kingdom of Silla while retaining substantial domestic autonomy. Governed by native lords known as Seongju, the kingdom maintained maritime trade, pastoral horse breeding and distinct cultural customs until its eventual incorporation into Goryeo. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of Silla; Capital: Jeju City; Common languages: Tamna and Old Korean; Religion: Korean shamanism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Three Kingdoms of Korea; Preceded by: Baekje; Succeeded by: Goryeo

name: Chalukyas of Navasarika
description: Chalukyas of Navasarika formed a cadet branch of the Vatapi Chalukya dynasty that governed southern Gujarat and northern Maharashtra. Established by Dharashraya Jayasimhavarman with an administrative centre at modern Navsari, the principality protected the northern marches of the Deccan against aggressive neighbours. The dynasty achieved historic renown under Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin, who decisively repulsed an invading Umayyad Caliphate army before the region was absorbed by the rising Rashtrakutas. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Navsari; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Classical India; Established: 661; Disestablished: 758; Succeeded by: Rashtrakuta dynasty

name: Kingdom of Fortriu
label: celtic polities in britain;celtic polities
description: Kingdom of Fortriu was a powerful Pictish realm centred around the Moray Firth and Easter Ross in northern Scotland. Ruling from fortifications near Inverness, its monarchs consolidated paramount authority over neighbouring northern and central Pictish territories during the seventh and eighth centuries. Fortriu resisted Northumbrian military expansion at the Battle of Nechtansmere and defended against Norse incursions before blending with Gaelic kingdoms to lay the foundations of medieval Scotland. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Inverness; Common languages: Pictish and Old Gaelic; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King of the Picts; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Scotland

name: Sultanate of Bijapur
description: Sultanate of Bijapur was an influential Deccani realm established in south-western India under the rule of the Adil Shahi dynasty following the dissolution of the Bahmani Sultanate. Centred at its fortified capital of Bijapur, the monarchy patronised distinctive Islamic architecture, cultivated Persianate literature and commanded extensive territories across Karnataka and southern Maharashtra. The sultanate maintained strategic commercial ports along the Konkan coast and contested regional dominance with the Vijayanagara Empire and Mughal forces. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Bijapur; Official languages: Persian; Common languages: Deccani, Kannada and Marathi; Religion: Shia and Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1490; Disestablished: 1686; Succeeded by: Mughal Empire

name: Turk Shahi
description: Turk Shahi was a dynasty of Western Turk and Hephthalite heritage that ruled Kabulistan, Kapisa and Gandhara across modern eastern Afghanistan and north-western Pakistan. Governed from royal seats at Kabul and Udabhanda, the monarchs defended their mountain redoubts and strategic passes against early Umayyad and Abbasid Caliphate expansions for more than two centuries. The kingdom patronised a vibrant synthesis of Buddhism and Hinduism along the northern Silk Road before being supplanted by the Hindu Shahis. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Kabul; Common languages: Bactrian and Sanskrit; Religion: Buddhism and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Shahi; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 665; Disestablished: 822; Succeeded by: Hindu Shahi

name: Tang and Silla (Military Occupation)
description: Tang and Silla (Military Occupation) comprised the joint Allied military protectorate established over the conquered territories of Goguryeo and Baekje across the Korean Peninsula. Joint command garrisons administered strategic urban forts without establishing a unified civil capital, focusing instead on quelling widespread local insurgencies and refugee uprisings. Tensions between the two victorious allies over territorial demarcation rapidly escalated, resulting in the Silla-Tang War and the expulsion of Chinese garrisons south of the Taedong River. \n\n Status: Allied military occupation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Middle Chinese and Old Korean; Religion: Buddhism and Confucianism; Government: Military administration; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Preceded by: Goguryeo and Baekje; Succeeded by: Unified Silla

name: Sunda Kingdom
