description: Sunda Kingdom was an enduring Sundanese Hindu-Buddhist state established in western Java following the decline of the Tarumanagara Kingdom. Governing from royal centres including Pakuan Pajajaran and Kawali, the realm dominated maritime trade routes along the Sunda Strait and maintained extensive agricultural river valleys. The kingdom cultivated a sophisticated inland and maritime commerce that resisted external pressures until finally yielding to the expanding Islamic Sultanate of Banten in the late sixteenth century. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Bogor; Common languages: Old Sundanese and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism, Buddhism and Sunda Wiwitan; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Medieval Southeast Asia; Established: 669; Disestablished: 1579; Succeeded by: Banten Sultanate

name: Bulgarian Empire
description: Bulgarian Empire was a formidable Balkan realm founded south of the Danube by Khan Asparuh after defeating the Byzantine army of Constantine IV. Administered from monumental stone capitals at Pliska and Preslav, the empire integrated Bulgar nomadic elites with South Slavic populations, evolving into a dominant power in south-eastern Europe. Following its conversion to Orthodox Christianity and adoption of Old Church Slavonic as the official administrative language, the state flourished culturally before succumbing to Byzantine reconquest under Basil II. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Pliska, Preslav and Ohrid; Official languages: Old Church Slavonic; Common languages: Danubian Bulgar and Common Slavic; Religion: Orthodox Christianity; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: Tsar; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 681; Disestablished: 1018

name: Galuh Kingdom
description: Galuh Kingdom was an ancient Sundanese realm established in eastern Tatar Sunda following the partition of Tarumanagara. Seated at Kawali and Karangkamulyan, the kingdom held territory spanning the Citarum and Serayu rivers across modern West and Central Java. Galuh maintained a dynamic political relationship with the neighbouring Sunda Kingdom, alternating between dynastic competition and cooperative personal unions until both branches permanently reunited under the crown of Pakuan Pajajaran. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Kawali; Common languages: Old Sundanese and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Sunda Wiwitan; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Prabu; Historical era: Medieval Southeast Asia; Established: 669; Disestablished: 1482; Succeeded by: Sunda Kingdom

name: Principality of Khuttal
label: tarim basin
description: Principality of Khuttal was an Iranian highland state situated between the Panj and Vakhsh rivers in modern south-western Tajikistan. Governed by native dynasts bearing the ancient title of Khuttalan Shah from their palace city of Hulbuk, the principality commanded lucrative salt mines and fostered trade in prized Central Asian horses. The principality skilfully preserved its autonomy amidst shifting pressures from the Tang dynasty, the Turgesh and Umayyad governors before falling to Abbasid campaigns in 751. \n\n Status: Autonomous principality; Capital: Hulbuk; Common languages: Sogdian and Middle Persian; Religion: Zoroastrianism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Khuttalan Shah; Historical era: Middle Ages; Disestablished: 751; Succeeded by: Abbasid Caliphate

name: Protectorate General to Pacify the South
description: Protectorate General to Pacify the South was the southernmost imperial administrative division established by Tang China to supervise northern Vietnam and adjacent coastal frontiers. Operating from its headquarters at Songping near modern Hanoi, the protectorate exercised military oversight, collected tribute and governed indigenous Viêt populations through Sino-Vietnamese scholar-officials. Persistent local uprisings and invasions by the neighbouring Kingdom of Nanzhao repeatedly disrupted Chinese authority until the protectorate was reorganised into the Jinghai Military Command. \n\n Status: Imperial protectorate of China; Capital: Hanoi; Common languages: Early Middle Chinese and Austroasiatic dialects; Religion: Mahayana Buddhism and Taoism; Government: Imperial military protectorate; Ruler title: Protector General; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 679; Disestablished: 866; Succeeded by: Jinghai Military Command

name: Domain of Husayn
description: Domain of Husayn was the short-lived revolutionary political movement established by Husayn ibn Ali, the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, during the opening months of the Second Fitna. Rejecting the hereditary succession of the Umayyad caliph Yazid I, Husayn marched from Mecca toward Kufa following invitations from local Alid loyalists seeking legitimate religious leadership. Intercepted in the desert near Karbala by an overwhelming Umayyad army, Husayn and his companions were martyred on 10 October 680, an event that became foundational for Shia Islam. \n\n Status: Revolutionary Alid state; Capital: Karbala; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Theocratic leadership; Ruler title: Imam; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 680; Disestablished: 680; Succeeded by: Umayyad Caliphate

name: Kingdom of Seisyllwg
label: celtic polities in britain;welsh polities;celtic polities
description: Kingdom of Seisyllwg was an early medieval Welsh realm in south-western Wales formed when King Seisyll united the territory of Ceredigion with the Ystrad Tywi basin. Centred near Cardigan and Carmarthen, the kingdom preserved Celtic legal institutions and rural church communities against Viking sea raiders and Mercian expansionists. Under the leadership of Hywel Dda in the early tenth century, Seisyllwg combined with the neighbouring Kingdom of Dyfed to form the unified realm of Deheubarth. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Cardigan; Common languages: Old Welsh; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 680; Disestablished: 920; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Deheubarth

name: Zunbils
description: Zunbils formed a prominent royal dynasty of Hephthalite descent that ruled the southern Afghan highlands of Zabulistan and Zamindawar from their fortified seat at Ghazni. The monarchs patronised the indigenous worship of the solar deity Zhun alongside Buddhist and Zoroastrian traditions, maintaining formidable mountain defences against foreign invaders. The dynasty consistently defeated invading armies from the Umayyad and early Abbasid caliphates for nearly two centuries before finally succumbing to the Persian Saffarids in 870. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Zamindawar; Common languages: Bactrian; Religion: Zunism, Buddhism and Zoroastrianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Rutbil; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 680; Disestablished: 870; Succeeded by: Saffarid dynasty

name: Bukhar Khudahs
description: Bukhar Khudahs was an ancient Sogdian urban dynasty that held sovereign authority over the wealthy Silk Road oasis of Bukhara in modern Uzbekistan. Residing in the fortified citadel of Bukhara, the local rulers managed flourishing trans-continental caravan trade, agricultural irrigation canals and the circulation of distinct local coinage. The dynasts negotiated complex tributary arrangements with Arab conquerors and maintained aristocratic administrative influence until the city was permanently incorporated into the Samanid Empire. \n\n Status: Urban principality; Capital: Bukhara; Common languages: Sogdian and Middle Persian; Religion: Zoroastrianism, Manichaeism and Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Bukhar Khudah; Historical era: Middle Ages; Disestablished: 893; Succeeded by: Samanid Empire

name: Turkic Khaganate
description: Turkic Khaganate, known historically as the Second Turkic Khaganate, was a revitalised steppe empire established across Mongolia by Ilterish Khagan and Tonyukuk of the Ashina clan. Ruling from their ancestral sacred grounds at Otuken and Ordu-Baliq, the Gokturks threw off Tang Chinese domination to restore nomad supremacy over Inner Asia. The khaganate commanded nomadic cavalry that subdued neighbouring steppe tribes and extracted extensive tribute from northern Chinese dynasties before collapsing under an alliance of Uyghurs, Karluks and Basmyls. \n\n Status: Steppe khaganate; Capital: Ordu-Baliq; Official languages: Old Turkic; Religion: Tengrism; Government: Nomadic confederation; Ruler title: Khagan; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 682; Disestablished: 744; Succeeded by: Uyghur Khaganate

name: Ansar and Quraysh Tribes
description: Ansar and Quraysh Tribes constituted a short-lived anti-Umayyad municipal insurrection in the holy city of Medina during the opening stages of the Second Fitna. Denouncing the perceived impiety and hereditary rule of the Umayyad caliph Yazid I, local descendants of the Prophet Muhammad's original companions expelled the imperial governor and established autonomous council rule. The uprising was brutally crushed by an invading Syrian army led by Muslim ibn Uqba following the Battle of al-Harra in 683. \n\n Status: Revolutionary tribal commonwealth; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Tribal council; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 683; Disestablished: 683; Succeeded by: Umayyad Caliphate

name: Domain of Julanda
description: Domain of Julanda was an independent Ibadi state established in south-eastern Arabia by the native Julanda dynasty of Oman during the upheaval of the Second Fitna. Ruling from their interior stronghold at Nizwa, the Julandid chieftains renounced Umayyad sovereignty, expelled imperial tax collectors and reinstated traditional Omani consultative governance. The autonomous domain resisted caliphal military campaigns for nearly a decade before Umayyad armies under al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf reconquered the coastal ports and mountains. \n\n Status: Autonomous principality; Capital: Nizwa; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Ibadi Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Malik; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 683; Disestablished: 692; Succeeded by: Umayyad Caliphate

name: Zubayrid Caliphate
description: Zubayrid Caliphate was a rival Islamic caliphate established in Mecca by Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr during the Second Fitna in opposition to Umayyad dynastic rule. Rejecting hereditary succession in Damascus, Ibn al-Zubayr proclaimed himself Commander of the Faithful and secured recognition across the Hejaz, Iraq, southern Arabia and parts of Syria. His caliphate maintained widespread authority for nearly a decade until internal factionalism and relentless Umayyad sieges culminated in his defeat and death in 692. \n\n Status: Caliphate; Capital: Mecca; Official languages: Arabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Caliphate; Ruler title: Caliph; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 683; Disestablished: 692; Succeeded by: Umayyad Caliphate

name: Domain of Mukhtar
description: Domain of Mukhtar was a revolutionary Shia polity established at Kufa by al-Mukhtar al-Thaqafi in the tumultuous aftermath of the Battle of Karbala. Championing the Alid rights of Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya and mobilising non-Arab convert mawali, Mukhtar seized control of most of Iraq and western Iran from Zubayrid officials. His regime systematically executed those responsible for Husayn's martyrdom and instituted egalitarian social reforms before being besieged and overthrown by Zubayrid forces under Mus'ab ibn al-Zubayr. \n\n Status: Revolutionary pro-Alid state; Capital: Kufa; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Shia Islam; Government: Theocratic regime; Ruler title: Governor and military commander; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 685; Disestablished: 687; Succeeded by: Zubayrid Caliphate

name: Kingdom of Sussex
label: saxon polities in britain
description: Kingdom of Sussex was an early Anglo-Saxon realm along the English Channel that fell under the political domination of the Kingdom of Wessex. Seated at Chichester, the South Saxon kings had earlier suffered severe territorial ravaging by Caedwalla of Wessex and were subsequently reduced to client sub-kings. Local dynasts managed regional fiscal estates and supported Saxon churches under the supervision of West Saxon overlords until Sussex was completely absorbed into Wessex under King Ecgberht. \n\n Status: Client kingdom of Wessex; Capital: Chichester; Common languages: Old English; Religion: Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Heptarchy; Preceded by: Sub-Roman Britain; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Wessex

name: Conaille Muirthemne
label: irish medieval kingdoms;celtic polities
description: Conaille Muirthemne was an ancient Gaelic kingdom inhabited by the Cruithin that occupied the coastal plains of modern County Louth in eastern Ireland. Governed from chieftains' strongholds near Dundalk, the petty kingdom guarded vital land routes between the Ulaid of Ulster and the southern kingdoms of Leinster and Meath. The dynasty retained independent sovereign status in the Irish annals for several centuries, fiercely resisting raids from neighbouring Cenel nEogain before being annexed in the twelfth century. \n\n Status: Gaelic kingdom; Capital: Dundalk; Common languages: Old Irish; Religion: Christianity; Government: Tanistry; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Medieval Ireland; Disestablished: 1131; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Meath

name: Cyprus Condominium
description: Cyprus Condominium was a unique neutral administrative arrangement over the island of Cyprus established under a treaty between Byzantine Emperor Justinian II and Umayyad Caliph Abd al-Malik. Under this diplomatic agreement, the island was demilitarised and tax revenues were collected by local authorities and divided equally between the treasuries of Constantinople and Damascus. This arrangement shielded the Cypriot population from imperial devastation for almost three centuries until the Byzantine Empire permanently reconquered the island in 965. \n\n Status: Neutral condominium; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Medieval Greek and Arabic; Religion: Christianity and Islam; Government: Joint imperial condominium; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 688; Disestablished: 965; Succeeded by: Byzantine Empire

name: Great Zhou
description: Great Zhou, known historically as the Wu Zhou dynasty, was a Chinese imperial state established when Empress Wu Zetian usurped the Tang throne and proclaimed herself sovereign. Governing from her designated divine capital of Shendu at Luoyang, Empress Wu reformed the imperial bureaucracy, elevated the civil service examinations and promoted Buddhism as the state ideology above Confucianism. Her energetic administration defended the frontiers against Tibetan and Turkic attacks until court ministers forced her abdication in 705 to restore the Tang dynasty. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Luoyang; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Imperial China; Established: 690; Disestablished: 705; Succeeded by: Tang dynasty

name: Chavda Dynasty
description: Chavda Dynasty was a Rajput ruling family that governed the strategic coastal region of Saurashtra and northern Gujarat. Established by King Vanaraja following the downfall of the Maitrakas of Vallabhi, the dynasty founded the great walled trading metropolis of Anahilavada Patan as its capital. The monarchs patronised regional Jain scholars, built substantial Hindu shrines and promoted maritime commerce across the Arabian Sea until their territory passed to the Chaulukya dynasty in 942. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Anhilwad Patan; Common languages: Sanskrit, Prakrit and Old Gujarati; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early Medieval India; Established: 690; Disestablished: 942; Succeeded by: Chaulukya dynasty

name: Mallabhum Kingdom
description: Mallabhum Kingdom was an enduring Hindu principality situated in the forested Rarh region of south-western Bengal, centred at the fortified city of Bishnupur. Founded by the indigenous Malla kings, the realm developed sophisticated earthen ramparts, extensive artificial water reservoirs and distinctive terracotta temple architecture. The monarchs maintained sovereign territorial independence throughout the Delhi Sultanate era, fostering classical Gaudiya Vaishnavite literature and classical music before becoming a British tributary state. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Bishnupur; Common languages: Bengali and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Malla Raja; Historical era: Medieval India; Established: 695; Disestablished: 1761; Succeeded by: British East India Company

name: Kahlur State
description: Kahlur State was a Rajput hill kingdom situated along the upper Sutlej River in the rugged lower Himalayan foothills of modern Himachal Pradesh. Governed from its capital at Bilaspur by the Chandel Rajput dynasty, the principality commanded important mountain defiles and levied duties on riverine transit trade. The rajas maintained territorial autonomy across centuries of regional hill wars and resisted foreign incursions before entering subsidiary treaty relations during the era of British supremacy. \n\n Status: Hill state; Capital: Bilaspur; Common languages: Pahari and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Medieval India; Established: 697; Disestablished: 1815; Succeeded by: Bilaspur Princely State

name: Republic of Venice
label: maritime republics
description: Republic of Venice was a pre-eminent maritime republic founded among the sheltered coastal lagoons of north-eastern Italy. Originating as an autonomous Byzantine naval outpost under an elected doge, the republic transformed itself into a Mediterranean commercial superpower with its administrative heart at the Doge's Palace in Venice. Venice established extensive overseas maritime trade networks, dominated sea lanes across the Adriatic and eastern Mediterranean and preserved an aristocratic republican constitution for over a millennium until the Napoleonic invasion of 1797. \n\n Status: Maritime republic; Capital: Venezia; Official languages: Venetian, Latin and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Aristocratic republic; Ruler title: Doge; Legislature: Great Council; Historical era: Middle Ages and Early modern period; Established: 697; Disestablished: 1797

name: Balhae Kingdom
description: Balhae Kingdom was a multi-ethnic state established across Manchuria, northern Korea and the Russian Far East by Goguryeo refugees and Mohe peoples led by Dae Jo-yeong. Operating from monumental capitals including Shangjing, the kingdom instituted Tang-style administrative departments, civil codes and educational academies, earning Chinese praise as the prosperous country in the east. Balhae maintained diplomatic ties with Japan and resisted Tang expansionism before being conquered by the Khitan-led Liao dynasty in 926. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Shangjing; Common languages: Balhae, Goguryeo and Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism, Shamanism and Confucianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 698; Disestablished: 926; Succeeded by: Liao dynasty

name: Little Goguryeo
description: Little Goguryeo was a transient successor state proposed by historians to have existed on the Liaodong Peninsula following the collapse of the Kingdom of Goguryeo. Formed by Goguryeo refugee communities and frontier garrisons around Liaoyang, the polity retained distinct cultural and political identities while navigating formal Tang protectorate authority. Functioning as a strategic buffer between the Tang Empire and the rising kingdom of Balhae, the territory was eventually absorbed into Balhae in the early ninth century. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Liaoyang; Common languages: Goguryeo and Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism and Korean shamanism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Governor and King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 699; Disestablished: 820; Succeeded by: Balhae Kingdom

name: Türgesh Khaganate
description: Türgesh Khaganate was a nomadic Turkic empire that arose in the Semirechye and Chui River valleys after the dissolution of the Western Turkic Khaganate. Ruling from dual seasonal capitals at Suyab and Taraz, the Türgesh under warlords such as Suluk Khagan fought tenaciously against advancing Umayyad armies in Transoxiana. Escalating internal tribal rivalries between the Yellow and Black factions weakened the state, leading to its destruction by the Karluk confederation in 766. \n\n Status: Steppe khaganate; Capital: Suyab and Taraz; Common languages: Old Turkic; Religion: Tengrism; Government: Nomadic confederation; Ruler title: Khagan; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 699; Disestablished: 766; Succeeded by: Karluk Yabghu

name: Beja Polities
description: Beja Polities comprised a constellation of pastoral and mercantile chiefdoms established by Cushitic-speaking Beja tribes across the Red Sea hills of eastern Sudan and northern Eritrea. Emerging into regional autonomy following the collapse of the Kingdom of Aksum, these tribal kingdoms governed from coastal havens such as Port Sudan and held control over inland gold and emerald mines. The kingdoms maintained independent pastoral lineages and trade links with caliphal merchants before adopting Islam in later centuries. \n\n Status: Tribal chiefdoms; Capital: Port Sudan; Common languages: Beja, Tigre and Arabic; Religion: Traditional animism and Islam; Government: Tribal confederacy; Ruler title: Chieftain; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 701; Disestablished: 1001

name: Breifne
label: irish medieval kingdoms;celtic polities
description: Breifne was a medieval Gaelic overkingdom in north-western Ireland comprising the modern counties of Leitrim, Cavan and adjacent borderlands. Centred at the royal fortress of Dromahair, the kingdom was initially governed by the Ui Briuin clan before passing to the Ua Ruairc dynasty. The realm attained peak influence in the twelfth century under King Tigernan Ua Ruairc, who defended Gaelic borders against early Anglo-Norman incursions before internal dynastic strife split the territory into West and East Breifne. \n\n Status: Gaelic overkingdom; Capital: Dromahair; Common languages: Old Irish; Religion: Christianity; Government: Tanistry; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 750; Disestablished: 1256; Succeeded by: West Breifne and East Breifne

name: Duchy of Aquitaine
label: barbarian kingdoms;frankish polities
description: Duchy of Aquitaine existed as an independent southern French principality south of the Loire River during the eighth century under energetic native rulers such as Duke Eudes and Duke Waiofar. Governed from Toulouse and Bordeaux, the duchy defended its sovereignty against Frankish encroachment from the north and repulsed major Umayyad Caliphate invasions from the south, most notably at the Battle of Toulouse in 721. Aquitanian independence was fiercely maintained until ruthless military campaigns by the Carolingian king Pepin the Short subjugated the territory in 768. \n\n Status: Independent duchy; Capital: Toulouse; Common languages: Old Occitan, Latin and Basque; Religion: Christianity; Government: Feudal duchy; Ruler title: Duke of Aquitaine; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 507; Succeeded by: Carolingian Empire

name: Kanem Empire
description: Kanem Empire was a powerful Central African realm centred in the Lake Chad basin, founded by the nomadic Duguwa dynasty and later governed by the Sayfawa house. Operating from its historic capital of Njimi in modern Chad, the empire commanded vital trans-Saharan caravan routes, trading ivory, salt and horses across the desert to the Mediterranean. The adoption of Islam by its divine rulers bolstered international diplomatic ties and fostered regional commerce, sustaining an imperial state that eventually relocated to Bornu. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Njimi; Common languages: Kanembu, Daza and Arabic; Religion: Traditional animism and Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Mai; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 700; Disestablished: 1380; Succeeded by: Bornu Empire

name: Katyuri Kingdom
description: Katyuri Kingdom was an early medieval Himalayan monarchy that ruled the valleys of Kumaon and Garhwal in modern Uttarakhand and western Nepal. Moving their capital from Joshimath to Baijnath in the Katyur Valley, the kings patronised classical Brahminical temples, stone sculptures and road infrastructure linking Himalayan passes. The dynasty presided over the revival of orthodox Hindu pilgrimage circuits in northern India before internal royal rivalries caused the kingdom to fragment into regional princely states. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Baijnath; Common languages: Sanskrit and Kumaoni; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early Medieval India; Established: 700; Disestablished: 1065; Succeeded by: Chand Kingdom and Garhwal Kingdom

name: Khmer Empire
description: Khmer Empire was an agrarian civilisation in mainland Southeast Asia that grew out of Chenla and established supreme authority across modern Cambodia, Thailand, Laos and southern Vietnam. Governed from the monumental hydraulic capital of Angkor, the realm constructed magnificent temple mountains including Angkor Wat and Angkor Thom under divine monarchs holding the title of chakravartin. The empire directed sophisticated water management networks that sustained extensive rice cultivation until environmental fluctuations, internal rebellions and Siamese invasions precipitated its decline. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Angkor; Official languages: Old Khmer and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Theravada Buddhism; Government: Devaraja monarchy; Ruler title: Chakravartin; Historical era: Post-classical era; Established: 802; Disestablished: 1431; Succeeded by: Post-Angkor Cambodia

name: Kingdom of Harikela
description: Kingdom of Harikela was an ancient coastal realm in south-eastern Bengal that spanned modern Chittagong, Sylhet and adjoining parts of Tripura. Centred at the maritime port of Chittagong, the kingdom engaged in flourishing Bay of Bengal commerce and issued a distinctive series of high-purity silver coinage. Harikela flourished as an independent cultural and commercial crossroad between mainland India and maritime Southeast Asia for centuries before its ports were incorporated into the expanding Chandra dynasty. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Chittagong; Common languages: Sanskrit and Old Bengali; Religion: Mahayana Buddhism and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Early Medieval India; Established: 701; Disestablished: 901; Succeeded by: Chandra dynasty

name: Kingdom of Jarin
description: Kingdom of Jarin was an early medieval Beja monarchy situated in north-eastern Africa between the Gash-Barka riverlands and the Red Sea port of Massawa. Chronicled by early Arab geographers including al-Ya'qubi, the kingdom held strategic hegemony over caravan trade routes traversing the Eritrean coastal hills. Its monarchs collected duties from regional merchant expeditions, preserved Cushitic pastoral customs and defended their borders against neighbouring kingdoms before local clans converted to Islam. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Jarin; Common languages: Beja and Tigre; Religion: Traditional animism and Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 701; Disestablished: 1001

name: Kolathunadu
description: Kolathunadu was an influential maritime kingdom situated along the northern Malabar Coast of modern Kerala, ruled by the Kolattiri dynasty. Governing from royal residences at Ezhimala and Kannur, the monarchy directed lucrative Indian Ocean trade in black pepper, cardamom and timber. The kingdom maintained extensive commercial ties with Arab, Persian and later European merchants, preserving regional matrilineal traditions and autonomous status until the eighteenth-century invasions by the Kingdom of Mysore. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Kannur; Common languages: Malayalam and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Kolattiri Raja; Historical era: Early Medieval India; Established: 701; Disestablished: 1780; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Mysore

name: Protectorate General of Beiting
description: Protectorate General of Beiting was an imperial Chinese administrative command established by the Tang dynasty to govern the northern perimeter of the Tarim Basin in modern Xinjiang. Administered from its fortified citadel at Beiting, the protectorate oversaw frontier garrisons, secured northern Silk Road trading routes and managed diplomatic alliances with nomadic steppe confederacies. Chinese authority persisted despite recurring nomad incursions until Tibetan forces captured the mountain fortress in the late eighth century. \n\n Status: Imperial protectorate of China; Capital: Beiting; Common languages: Middle Chinese and Old Turkic; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Manichaeism; Government: Military protectorate; Ruler title: Protector General; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 702; Disestablished: 790; Succeeded by: Tibetan Empire

name: Land Chenla
description: Land Chenla was an inland Southeast Asian mandala realm that emerged along the middle Mekong River following the division of the pre-Angkorian Chenla polity. Centred around Champasak and the sacred mountain temple sanctuary of Vat Phou, the kingdom relied on intensive riverine agriculture and overland trade with the Khorat Plateau. Local Khmer chieftains maintained decentralised authority across the highland valleys until the regional polities were reunited under the emerging Khmer Empire. \n\n Status: Mandala kingdom; Capital: Champasak; Common languages: Old Khmer and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Decentralised monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Post-classical era; Established: 708; Disestablished: 802; Succeeded by: Khmer Empire

name: Water Chenla
description: Water Chenla was a coastal and deltaic Khmer kingdom formed following the partition of ancient Chenla, covering the Tonle Sap basin and the lower Mekong delta. Governing from major urban centres including Sambor Prei Kuk and Sambhupura, the state controlled vital maritime trade routes between China and India. Fractured by internal succession conflicts and vulnerable to maritime raids from Javanese Shailendra fleets, the maritime realm was consolidated into the unified Khmer Empire by Jayavarman II in 802. \n\n Status: Mandala kingdom; Capital: Sambor Prei Kuk; Common languages: Old Khmer and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Post-classical era; Established: 708; Disestablished: 802; Succeeded by: Khmer Empire

name: Emirate of Nekor
description: Emirate of Nekor was an early Islamic Berber principality established in the mountainous Rif region of northern Morocco by Salih ibn Mansur. Operating from its capital at Nekor, the Banu Salih dynasty governed local Amazigh tribes, fostering orthodox Sunni Maliki jurisprudence while neighbouring realms embraced heterodox movements. The emirate prospered as a Mediterranean coastal trading port, resisting Fatimid incursions and Viking maritime raids until its capital was devastated in the eleventh century. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Nekor; Common languages: Berber and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 710; Disestablished: 1015; Succeeded by: Caliphate of Córdoba

name: Medang Kingdom
description: Medang Kingdom, known also as the Mataram Kingdom, was a flourishing agrarian and maritime empire in central and eastern Java founded by King Sanjaya. Operating from administrative capitals near modern Yogyakarta, the kingdom's rulers of the Sanjaya and Shailendra dynasties constructed monumental religious complexes including Borobudur and Prambanan. The realm commanded vast rice-farming lowlands and overseas trade across the Java Sea before royal authority relocated eastward following catastrophic volcanic eruptions in the eleventh century. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Yogyakarta; Common languages: Old Javanese and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Mahayana Buddhism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Medieval Southeast Asia; Established: 716; Disestablished: 1017; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Kahuripan

name: Kingdom of Asturias
description: Kingdom of Asturias was the foundational Christian monarchy established in north-western Iberia by King Pelagius after defeating Umayyad forces at the Battle of Covadonga. Centred among the Cantabrian Mountains with its royal court at Oviedo, the kingdom successfully repelled Muslim advances and initiated the early territorial expansion of the Reconquista. Asturian monarchs repopulated the Duero basin, fostered Mozarabic art and architecture and safeguarded Christian shrines until transferring their royal capital to León in 910. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Oviedo; Common languages: Latin, Old Leonese and Astur-Romance; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King of Asturias; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 718; Disestablished: 910; Succeeded by: Kingdom of León

name: Kingdom of Mewar
description: Kingdom of Mewar was an enduring Rajput monarchy in southern Rajasthan that achieved prominence under Bappa Rawal of the Guhila dynasty. Centred among the defensive ravines of the Aravalli Range and governed from Nagda and later Chittorgarh, the state earned distinction by checking early Arab incursions into western India. The kingdom maintained a staunch tradition of martial independence, patronising Hindu temple construction and resisting rival sultanates for centuries before establishing Udaipur as its capital. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Udaipur; Common languages: Mewari and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharana; Historical era: Early Medieval India; Established: 728; Succeeded by: Udaipur Princely State

name: Papal States
label: holy roman empire
description: Papal States comprised the sovereign temporal territories across central Italy governed directly by the bishop of Rome following the decline of Byzantine authority. Originating from the Donation of Pepin and the lands of the Roman duchy, the pontifical realm governed from Rome and Avignon, administering extensive estates in Lazio, Umbria, Marche and Romagna. The papacy maintained independent diplomacy, legal courts and armed forces across more than a millennium until the unification of Italy in 1870. \n\n Status: Pontifical state; Capital: Rome and Avignon; Official languages: Latin; Common languages: Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Elective theocratic monarchy; Ruler title: Pope; Historical era: Middle Ages and Early modern period; Established: 754; Disestablished: 1870; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Italy

name: Principality of Serbia
description: Principality of Serbia was an early South Slavic monarchy established in the mountainous interior of the western Balkans by the Vlastimirovic dynasty. Seated at fortified centres including Destinikon and Novi Pazar, the principality successfully repulsed Bulgarian invasions and navigated the geopolitical rivalry between the Byzantine Empire and the First Bulgarian Empire. Under rulers such as Vlastimir and Caslav, the state consolidated Serbian tribal clans and adopted Christian religious institutions before being annexed by the Byzantines in the late tenth century. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Novi Pazar; Common languages: Old Serbian and Proto-Slavic; Religion: Slavic paganism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 730; Disestablished: 971; Succeeded by: Byzantine Empire

name: Saindhava
description: Saindhava was an early medieval Indian dynasty that ruled the western coastal peninsula of Saurashtra in modern Gujarat from their capital at Bhutamabilika, present-day Ghumli. Operating as naval protectors of the western Indian coastline, the rulers commanded maritime trade across the Arabian Sea and patronised elaborate Hindu stone temples in the Barda Hills. Under energetic monarchs such as Agguka I, the dynasty gained distinction by repelling repeated sea attacks by Arab naval forces before succumbing to regional successors. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Ghumli; Common languages: Sanskrit and Prakrit; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Early Medieval India; Established: 735; Disestablished: 920; Succeeded by: Chudasama dynasty

name: Principality of Iberia
description: Principality of Iberia functioned as a tributary Christian principality in eastern Georgia during a period of formal submission to the Umayyad and early Abbasid caliphates. Guided by presiding princes residing at Uplistsikhe after the sack of Tbilisi, the Georgian aristocracy managed local feudal estates while delivering regular tribute to Muslim governors. Despite continuous foreign pressure, the principality safeguarded Georgian Orthodox institutions and laid the administrative groundwork for the rise of the royal Bagrationi dynasty. \n\n Status: Tributary principality of the Arab Caliphate; Administrative seat: Mobile court; Common languages: Old Georgian; Religion: Georgian Orthodox Christianity; Government: Principate; Ruler title: Presiding Prince; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 736; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Iberians

name: Great Meng
description: Great Meng, officially known during its imperial apex as Nanzhao, was a formidable kingdom centred around the Erhai basin of Yunnan in south-western China. Ruling from capitals at Taihe and Dali, the Bai and Nuosu monarchs unified the six tribal confederations of the plateau and created a sophisticated bureaucratic state balancing Tang and Tibetan influences. The kingdom projected military power southward into Upper Burma and northern Southeast Asia, constructing monumental pagodas and fostering Esoteric Buddhist traditions until internal coups dissolved the dynasty. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Dali; Common languages: Bai, Nuosu and Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 738; Disestablished: 902; Succeeded by: Dali Kingdom

name: Confederacy of the Veleti
description: Confederacy of the Veleti was a loose political union of Polabian Slavic tribes that inhabited the lowland forests and river systems of Western Pomerania and north-eastern Germany. Lacking a centralised urban capital, the federation was coordinated through pagan cultic centres and assemblies of tribal elders and war chieftains. The Veleti fiercely defended their indigenous religious rites and territorial independence against Saxon and Carolingian Frankish armies until evolving into the Lutician Federation. \n\n Status: Tribal confederation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Polabian Slavic; Religion: Slavic paganism; Government: Confederal tribal principality; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 740; Disestablished: 990; Succeeded by: Lutician Federation

name: Kingdom of Dál Riata
label: celtic polities in britain;celtic polities
description: Kingdom of Dál Riata was a Gaelic maritime realm encompassing Argyll in western Scotland and north-eastern Ireland that came under the suzerainty of the Pictish kingdom. Centred at the imposing crag fortress of Dunadd, the kingdom's native chieftains were compelled to recognise the overlordship of the Pictish king Oengus mac Fergusa following decisive military defeats. Despite retaining local dynastic lineage and monastic connections with Iona, Dal Riata remained politically subordinate until the two realms merged to form the Kingdom of Alba. \n\n Status: Client kingdom of the Picts; Capital: Dunadd; Common languages: Old Gaelic; Religion: Celtic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 498; Disestablished: 843; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Scotland

name: Emirate of Tlemcen
label: berber kingdoms
description: Emirate of Tlemcen was an early Islamic Kharijite state founded in north-western Algeria by the Berber Banu Ifran tribe following the Great Berber Revolt against the Umayyads. Administered from the inland trading hub of Tlemcen under the leadership of Abu Qurra, the emirate championed Sufri egalitarianism and rejected caliphal hegemony from Damascus. The principality dominated trans-Maghreb caravan routes and contested regional dominance with rival Berber factions until being eclipsed by the rising Rustamid and Idrisid dynasties. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Tlemcen; Common languages: Berber and Arabic; Religion: Sufri Kharijite Islam; Government: Tribal emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 742; Disestablished: 790; Succeeded by: Rustamid dynasty and Idrisid dynasty

name: Barghawata Confederacy
label: berber kingdoms
description: Barghawata Confederacy was an independent Berber tribal state and distinct religious movement that controlled the fertile Atlantic coastal plains of Tamesna in modern Morocco. Established under Tarif al-Matghari following the revolt against Umayyad rule, the confederacy adopted a syncretic Islamic-Berber faith led by self-proclaimed prophets with a Berber-language scripture. The polity repulsed repeated military incursions by neighbouring Idrisid and caliphal armies for three centuries before falling to the Almoravid holy campaigns. \n\n Status: Tribal confederacy; Capital: Casablanca; Common languages: Berber; Religion: Barghawata religion and Kharijite Islam; Government: Confederal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 744; Disestablished: 1058; Succeeded by: Almoravid dynasty

name: Kimek-Kipchak Khanate
description: Kimek-Kipchak Khanate was a powerful Turkic nomadic confederation that dominated the vast steppes along the Irtysh and Ob rivers in modern Kazakhstan and south-western Siberia. Governed by their supreme khagan from seasonal winter and summer headquarters near modern Pavlodar, the confederation brought together seven major tribal groups, including the Kimeks and Kipchaks. The state commanded strategic trans-Siberian fur trade routes and maintained nomadic equestrian warfare until internal migrations caused the Kipchaks to break away and move westwards. \n\n Status: Nomadic confederation; Capital: Pavlodar; Common languages: Old Turkic; Religion: Tengrism and Shamanism; Government: Nomadic khaganate; Ruler title: Khagan; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 744; Disestablished: 1050; Succeeded by: Cuman-Kipchak confederation

name: Uyghur Khaganate
description: Uyghur Khaganate was a nomadic empire that replaced the Second Turkic Khaganate across the Mongolian steppe, established by Qutlugh Bilge Kol following the capture of Otuken. Operating from the expansive fortified capital of Ordu-Baliq on the Orkhon River, the khaganate maintained close diplomatic and mercantile relations with Tang China, frequently intervening in Chinese civil wars to secure substantial silk subsidies. The adoption of Manichaeism as the official state religion nurtured a refined urban culture until the empire was destroyed by Yenisei Kyrgyz invaders in 840. \n\n Status: Steppe empire; Capital: Ordu-Baliq; Common languages: Old Uyghur and Middle Chinese; Religion: Manichaeism, Tengrism and Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Khagan; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 744; Disestablished: 840; Succeeded by: Yenisei Kyrgyz Khaganate and Qocho Kingdom

name: Abbasid Caliphate
description: Abbasid Caliphate was the third major Islamic caliphate, established after the overthrow of the Umayyad dynasty by revolutionary armies that advanced from Khurasan to Kufa. Transforming the administrative and cultural landscape of the Islamic world, the caliphs founded Baghdad as their imperial capital and oversaw the flourishing Golden Age of Islam. The empire integrated Arab and non-Arab Muslim populations, patronised monumental scientific translation movements and established a sophisticated central bureaucracy before peripheral regions fragmented into autonomous regional dynasties. \n\n Status: Caliphate; Capital: Baghdad, Kufa and Samarra; Official languages: Arabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Caliph; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 750; Disestablished: 1258; Preceded by: Umayyad Caliphate; Succeeded by: Mamluk Sultanate

name: Emirate of Multan
description: Emirate of Multan was a prosperous Muslim principality in southern Punjab established around the ancient city of Multan by the Arab Banu Munabbih clan. Governed from the fortified river city, the emirs derived immense wealth from transit commerce along the Indus valley and the collection of offerings at the revered Sun Temple of Multan. The principality preserved autonomous rule outside direct caliphal control through astute local diplomacy until it adopted Ismaili Shiism and was later conquered by Mahmud of Ghazni. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Multan; Common languages: Arabic and Old Punjabi; Religion: Islam; Government: Emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 751; Disestablished: 1010; Succeeded by: Ghaznavid Empire

name: Farighunids
description: Farighunids were an Iranian princely dynasty of Sogdian cultural descent that governed the semi-autonomous mountainous principality of Guzgan in modern northern Afghanistan. Seated at their administrative hub of Yahudiyya near modern Maymana, the princes gained renown as generous patrons of Persian scholars and geographic literature, including the anonymous masterwork Hudud al-Alam. The dynasty preserved stability by paying tribute to the Samanids and Ghaznavids before their domain was peacefully annexed by Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni in 1010. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Maymana; Common languages: Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 750; Disestablished: 1010; Succeeded by: Ghaznavid Empire

name: Kutlehar State
description: Kutlehar State was an ancient Rajput hill principality situated between the Sutlej and Beas river basins in the lower Siwalik hills of modern Himachal Pradesh. Governed from the mountain stronghold of Kot Kutlehar by the indigenous royal family, the state maintained territorial autonomy across centuries of regional hill wars. The rajas defended their secluded mountain valleys, paid tribute to the Mughal court and formed alliances with neighbouring hill monarchs until entering subsidiary treaties during the British colonial era. \n\n Status: Hill state; Capital: Kot Kutlehar; Common languages: Pahari and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Medieval India; Established: 750; Disestablished: 1810; Succeeded by: British East India Company

name: Monte Albán
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Monte Albán was a pre-eminent Zapotec urban state situated atop an artificially terraced mountain ridge overlooking the fertile Valley of Oaxaca in southern Mexico. Serving as a primary ceremonial and civic centre, the city featured monumental stone plazas, ballcourts, carved stelae and subterranean elite tombs. During its terminal classic phase, the city directed regional commerce and tributary networks across the surrounding highlands before diminishing urban authority led to the gradual abandonment of the civic acropolis. \n\n Status: City-state; Capital: Monte Alban; Common languages: Zapotec; Religion: Mesoamerican polytheism; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Ruler title: High Priest and King; Historical era: Mesoamerican Classic period; Established: 500 BC; Disestablished: 900 AD

name: Oghuz Yabgu State
description: Oghuz Yabgu State was an early medieval Turkic nomad realm founded by Oghuz pastoral tribes across the arid steppes between the Caspian and Aral seas. Centred at their winter capital of Yangikent along the lower Syr Darya, the yabgus directed a strategic commercial corridor connecting the Khazar Khaganate with the Muslim cities of Transoxiana. The state was organised as a military confederacy of clan groupings whose internal rivalries and eastward tribal migrations eventually fostered the emergence of the imperial Seljuq dynasty. \n\n Status: Steppe khaganate; Capital: Jankent; Common languages: Old Turkic; Religion: Tengrism and later Islam; Government: Nomadic confederation; Ruler title: Yabgu; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 750; Disestablished: 1055; Succeeded by: Seljuq Empire

name: Imamate of Oman
description: Imamate of Oman was an independent theocratic state established in the mountainous interior of south-eastern Arabia following the election of al-Julanda bin Masud by the Ibadi community. Centred around the historic fortress capital of Nizwa within the protective arc of the Hajar Mountains, the imamate instituted rigorous consultative religious governance under an elected imam. The polity developed extensive Indian Ocean trade networks and maritime connections with East Africa while fiercely preserving its religious autonomy against external caliphal armies. \n\n Status: Imamate; Capital: Nizwa; Official languages: Arabic; Religion: Ibadi Islam; Government: Elective theocratic monarchy; Ruler title: Imam; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 749; Disestablished: 1856; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Muscat and Oman

name: Kingdom of Brittany
label: celtic polities of brittany;celtic polities
description: Kingdom of Brittany was a Celtic state in north-western France that maintained precarious vassal relations with the Carolingian Frankish Empire while resisting complete political assimilation. Governed from administrative and ecclesiastical seats such as Rennes and Vannes, the native Breton counts paid nominal homage to Frankish overlords while preserving customary legal traditions. The territory served as a turbulent march for Carolingian monarchs until King Erispoe defeated Charles the Bald at the Battle of Jengland in 851, securing formal sovereign recognition. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Frankish Empire; Capital: Rennes; Common languages: Old Breton and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 754; Disestablished: 851; Succeeded by: Duchy of Brittany

name: Rashtrakuta Dynasty
description: Rashtrakuta Dynasty was an imperial power that established hegemony across the Deccan and large parts of southern and central India after overthrowing the Chalukyas of Badami. Founded by Dantidurga and operating from their magnificent capital at Manyakheta, the monarchs engaged in the Tripartite Struggle against the Palas and Gurjara-Pratiharas for control of Kannauj. The dynasty was celebrated for outstanding military prowess, tolerant patronage of Jainism and Hinduism and the construction of rock-cut monuments including the monolithic Kailash Temple at Ellora. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Malkhed; Common languages: Kannada and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharajadhiraja; Historical era: Early Medieval India; Established: 753; Disestablished: 982; Succeeded by: Western Chalukya Empire

name: Rashtrakutas of Malkhed
description: Rashtrakutas of Malkhed comprised the imperial southern Indian authority that held jurisdiction over the strategic coastal territories of Goa and the Konkan littoral from their seat at Manyakheta. The imperial administration appointed loyal feudatory governors and supported regional trading corporations that managed flourishing Arabian Sea commerce in Arabian horses and spices. Local coastal affairs were conducted under imperial oversight, ensuring naval defence and regular tribute until the collapse of Rashtrakuta paramountcy in the late tenth century. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Malkhed; Common languages: Kannada and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharajadhiraja; Historical era: Early Medieval India; Established: 753; Disestablished: 964; Succeeded by: Western Chalukya Empire

name: Great Yan
description: Great Yan was a short-lived breakaway Chinese imperial state founded by the rebel Tang general An Lushan during his catastrophic uprising against Emperor Xuanzong. Operating from the northern capitals of Luoyang and Yecheng, the rebel state mobilised Sogdian, Turkic and Han frontier soldiers to seize control of the central Yellow River plains. The rebel dynasty suffered from vicious intra-familial assassinations and factional strife, which enabled allied Tang and Uyghur forces to crush the rebellion and dissolve the regime in 763. \n\n Status: Breakaway empire; Capital: Luoyang; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: An Lushan Rebellion; Established: 756; Disestablished: 763; Succeeded by: Tang dynasty

name: Emirate of Córdoba
description: Emirate of Córdoba was an independent Islamic state in the Iberian Peninsula established by the surviving Umayyad prince Abd al-Rahman I following the Abbasid Revolution. Ruling from the great cultural and intellectual metropolis of Córdoba, the emirate unified Islamic al-Andalus and defended its frontiers against Christian kingdoms to the north. The monarchy established a sophisticated central administration, fostered agricultural and artistic innovations, constructed the magnificent Great Mosque of Córdoba and laid the groundwork for the proclamation of the Caliphate of Córdoba. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Córdoba; Official languages: Arabic; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic and Mozarabic Romance; Religion: Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 756; Disestablished: 929; Succeeded by: Caliphate of Córdoba

name: Zhennan Protectorate
description: Zhennan Protectorate was the temporary imperial designation applied to the Annan Protectorate in northern Vietnam by the Tang dynasty between 757 and 760. Headquartered at the fortified river post of Songping near modern Hanoi, the administration maintained imperial security and managed maritime trade along the Gulf of Tonkin during the disruptions of the An Lushan Rebellion. Tang authorities reverted the administrative title to Annan once regional frontier garrisons restored stability along the southern coastal approaches. \n\n Status: Imperial protectorate of China; Capital: Songping; Common languages: Early Middle Chinese and Austroasiatic dialects; Religion: Mahayana Buddhism and Taoism; Government: Military protectorate; Ruler title: Protector General; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 758; Disestablished: 761; Succeeded by: Protectorate General to Pacify the South

name: Emirate of Sijilmassa
description: Emirate of Sijilmassa was an independent Kharijite state founded in the Tafilalt oasis along the northern rim of the Moroccan Sahara by the Berber Midrarid dynasty. Centred at the prosperous desert city of Sijilmassa, the emirate derived immense commercial power from controlling the northern terminus of the western trans-Saharan gold, salt and caravan trade. The Midrarid rulers maintained religious independence through adherence to Sufrite doctrine and fostered urban agricultural canals until falling to Fatimid invasions in the tenth century. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Sijilmassa; Common languages: Berber and Arabic; Religion: Sufri Kharijite Islam; Government: Emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 758; Disestablished: 1055; Succeeded by: Almoravid dynasty

name: Duchy of Naples
label: byzantine successors in southern italy
description: Duchy of Naples originated as a coastal Byzantine naval command that evolved into a de facto independent maritime duchy along the Tyrrhenian coast of southern Italy. Governing from the ancient walled port of Naples, the elected dukes navigated perilous regional rivalries involving the Lombard princes of Benevento, Saracen raiders and the Holy Roman Empire. The duchy flourished through Mediterranean maritime commerce and preserved Hellenic and Roman legal institutions until it was finally conquered by the Norman King Roger II of Sicily in 1137. \n\n Status: Maritime duchy; Capital: Naples; Common languages: Medieval Latin, Neapolitan and Byzantine Greek; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 661; Disestablished: 1137; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Sicily

name: Kingdom of Kent
label: saxon polities in britain
description: Kingdom of Kent was an ancient Anglo-Saxon kingdom in south-eastern England that fell under the political domination of the Kingdom of Mercia during the Mercian Supremacy. Governed from Canterbury, the Kentish monarchs were reduced to tributary sub-kings who required Mercian royal consent to issue charters or alienate land. Despite sporadic local rebellions seeking to re-establish independence, Kent remained under Mercian hegemony until the West Saxon victory at Ellendun in 825 led to its permanent absorption into Wessex. \n\n Status: Client kingdom of Mercia; Capital: Canterbury; Common languages: Old English; Religion: Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Heptarchy; Preceded by: Sub-Roman Britain; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Wessex

name: Shilahara Dynasty
description: Shilahara Dynasty was a prominent royal house in western India that governed three distinct branches across North Konkan, South Konkan and the Kolhapur plateau. Originating as trusted feudatories of the Rashtrakutas and ruling from coastal strongholds such as Thane, the monarchs managed vibrant Arabian Sea ports and sponsored maritime commercial guilds. The dynasty was celebrated for its religious tolerance, endowing Jain basadis, erecting magnificent Hindu stone temples and patronising classical Sanskrit, Kannada and early Marathi literature. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Thane; Common languages: Sanskrit, Kannada and Old Marathi; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early Medieval India; Established: 765; Disestablished: 1216; Succeeded by: Seuna Yadava dynasty

name: Suket Kingdom
description: Suket Kingdom was an ancient Rajput hill principality established in the upper Beas river basin of modern Himachal Pradesh by Raja Bir Sen. Seated at early capitals such as Pangna and Mandi, the dynasty defended its secluded Himalayan mountain valleys against rival hill rajas and nomadic incursions. The state preserved hereditary royal authority across centuries of regional hill wars, maintaining unique pahari artistic traditions and local religious sanctuaries before acceding to the Indian Union in the twentieth century. \n\n Status: Hill state; Capital: Mandi; Common languages: Pahari and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Medieval India; Established: 765; Disestablished: 1846; Succeeded by: Suket Princely State

name: Ayudha Dynasty
description: Ayudha Dynasty was a northern Indian ruling house that established control over the imperial city of Kannauj following the decline of the Varman dynasty. Commencing with Vajrayudha and later governed by Indrayudha and Chakrayudha, the dynasty struggled to maintain authority amidst the escalating Tripartite Struggle for northern supremacy. The monarchs ruled as clients of Dharmapala of Bengal before Kannauj was captured by the Gurjara-Pratihara emperor Nagabhata II, terminating the dynasty. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Kannauj; Common languages: Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharajadhiraja; Historical era: Early Medieval India; Established: 770; Disestablished: 816; Succeeded by: Gurjara-Pratihara Kingdom

name: Sadakiyans
label: kurdish principalities
description: Sadakiyans formed an early medieval Kurdish Muslim dynasty that established sovereign authority around Lake Urmia in north-western Iran. Founded by Sadaka ibn Ali, the dynasty fortified regional mountain strongholds and directed caravan trade traversing the Azerbaijani highlands outside direct Abbasid control. The rulers balanced alliances with neighbouring Armenian princes and caliphal governors, preserving local Kurdish political autonomy until their territory was integrated into broader regional emirates. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Urmia; Common languages: Kurdish, Persian and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 770; Disestablished: 827; Succeeded by: Sajid dynasty

name: Kingdom of Sussex
label: saxon polities in britain
description: Kingdom of Sussex fell under the direct suzerainty of the Kingdom of Mercia during the expansionist reign of the Mercian king Offa in the late eighth century. Governed from Chichester, the South Saxon monarchs were formally demoted in royal charters from independent kings to mere ealdormen, paying heavy tribute and acknowledging Mercian administrative oversight. This period of Mercian vassalage stifled local political autonomy until Mercian supremacy fractured following the death of King Coenwulf. \n\n Status: Client kingdom of Mercia; Capital: Chichester; Common languages: Old English; Religion: Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Ealdorman; Historical era: Heptarchy; Preceded by: Sub-Roman Britain; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Wessex

name: Fulda Abbey
label: holy roman empire
description: Fulda Abbey was an autonomous Benedictine monastic lordship and imperial abbey centred upon the city of Fulda in the German region of Hesse. Founded by Saint Sturm under the patronage of Saint Boniface, the abbey rapidly became a celebrated intellectual and religious centre of the Carolingian renaissance, housing an illustrious library and scriptorium. Endowed with extensive imperial immunities and territorial estates, the abbey exercised sovereign territorial lordship that eventually developed into an imperial prince-bishopric. \n\n Status: Imperial abbey; Capital: Fulda; Common languages: Old High German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monastic lordship; Ruler title: Abbot; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 744; Disestablished: 1802; Succeeded by: Prince-Bishopric of Fulda

name: Principality of Benevento
label: lombard polities
description: Principality of Benevento was the resilient southern Lombard state that maintained independent sovereignty following Charlemagne's conquest of the Kingdom of the Lombards in northern Italy. Elevating his ducal title to prince, Duke Arechis II made Benevento the political and cultural beacon of Lombard independence across the Mezzogiorno. The principality preserved distinctive Beneventan liturgical and legal traditions, defending its borders against Carolingian and Byzantine incursions until internal partitions split the domain into the rival principalities of Salerno and Capua. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Benevento; Common languages: Vulgar Latin and Lombardic; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Early Middle Ages; Established: 774; Disestablished: 1053; Succeeded by: Principality of Salerno and Papal States
